question: A program you can chat with in plain English — like ChatGPT from OpenAI or Claude from Anthropic — is powered underneath by a huge computer program trained on billions of pages of text. Researchers call it a giant text-based AI because it has learned so much writing. Nobody actually says all those words in conversation. What three-letter short name do people use?
answer: An LLM (Large Language Model)
choices: An LLM (Large Language Model)
A search engine for old maps
A web browser like Chrome
A spreadsheet app for cells
context: LLM stands for Large Language Model. These are programs trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word in a sequence. ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all chatbots built on LLMs. Knowing the term is the first step — when you hear 'LLM,' you know what kind of system someone is talking about.

question: ChatGPT is one of the most famous AI chatbots in the world. The name ends in three capital letters — GPT — and those letters are an acronym for three words that describe what the model actually is. What are those three words?
answer: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
choices: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
Google's Public Translator system
General Purpose Telephone helper
Graphic Processing Toolkit display
context: GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. 'Generative' = produces new text. 'Pre-trained' = learned from huge amounts of text before you ever used it. 'Transformer' = the network architecture, introduced in a 2017 Google paper called 'Attention Is All You Need.'

question: In the name ChatGPT, the letter T stands for Transformer. But this isn't the toy robot from the movies. It's the name of an idea invented by Google researchers in 2017 that made modern AI chatbots possible. Transformers are a kind of:
answer: Neural network architecture
choices: Neural network architecture
Robot from a movie series
A type of electrical device
A famous brand of laptop
context: In AI, 'Transformer' refers to a specific design (architecture) of neural network, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need.' It became the foundation for almost every modern chatbot — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama. The name is unrelated to the robot toys; the AI architecture came later.

question: The P in GPT stands for Pre-trained. It means the AI already did its learning in advance — before you ever start talking to it. Companies spent months and millions of dollars feeding it books, websites, and articles. By the time you open the chatbot, it isn't studying anymore. Why is 'Pre-trained' important?
answer: It learns once, then just responds
choices: It learns once, then just responds
It rehearses for the singing show
It practices old guitar chords
It folds new origami cranes
context: Pre-training is a giant one-time computing job. The model studies huge amounts of text and adjusts its internal numbers (parameters). When you chat with the trained model, it's just running — not learning from your messages. Each new conversation starts fresh. This is why 'pre-trained' matters: training is past, response is present.

question: Suppose you want this morning's game score or a breaking story. Chatbots were often trained months ago and don't know today's events. Which of these is the best tool for looking up today's news?
answer: A search engine like Google
choices: A search engine like Google
A chatbot like ChatGPT
A photo app on your phone
A calculator program
context: Search engines crawl the live web. Chatbots are pattern-completion programs trained months ago and don't know what happened today (unless given a search tool). For 'what just happened,' use search. For 'help me draft something,' a chatbot can help.

question: A nurse asks ChatGPT to work out a huge sum. Since 2023 it has been able to write a short program and run it. When the answer matters, what does that let the chatbot do?
answer: Compute the answer, not guess it
choices: Search the web for the answer
Ask a human to do the sum
Round the answer to look neat
Compute the answer, not guess it
context: OpenAI's Code Interpreter, launched for ChatGPT Plus in July 2023, runs Python code in a sandbox, so a real program does the arithmetic. Without a tool like that, the model only predicts a plausible-looking number.

question: A student asks a chatbot to summarize a famous novel. It confidently describes a whole chapter, with a scene and a character's speech, that isn't in the book at all. The chatbot did not lie on purpose; the model just filled in words that sounded plausible. What is a made-up fact from a chatbot usually called?
answer: Hallucination
choices: Hallucination
Recovery
Translation
Recursion
context: When an LLM confidently invents false information, people call it 'hallucination.' It happens because the model is predicting plausible-sounding text, not looking facts up. Watch out for invented book chapters, fake quotes, made-up court cases, and wrong dates.

question: A girl asks a chatbot how many r's are in 'strawberry,' and it says two, like many in 2024. Chatbots read text in chunks called tokens, like 'straw' and 'berry.' Why do they miscount?
answer: They don't see the single letters
choices: They don't see the single letters
They can't count above two
They ignore every vowel
They drop all double letters
context: A model receives 'strawberry' as a few token pieces, not ten letters, so counting the r's means reasoning about letters it never directly sees. Researchers quoted by TechCrunch said the problem is built into how these models read text.

question: Suppose you tell ChatGPT today that your favorite color is green. Tomorrow you reopen it, with no memory feature on. Will it remember?
answer: No, each new chat starts fresh from blank
choices: No, each new chat starts fresh from blank
Yes, it remembers everything you ever said
Yes, but only for the next seven days
Only if you pay an extra monthly fee
context: LLMs don't remember between separate conversations by default. Each new chat starts blank. Some chat products bolt on a 'memory' feature that stores notes between sessions, but the underlying model itself has no built-in memory of you.

question: Every AI chatbot was trained on a huge pile of text — books, articles, and websites — collected up to a specific date. After that date, whatever happens in the world, the chatbot won't know unless it's connected to live search. That special date has a name in the AI world. What is it called?
answer: The training cutoff
choices: The training cutoff
The expiration date
The opening line
The starter pack
context: Each model has a training cutoff — the date when training data collection stopped. The model has no information about events after that point. If you ask about something that happened last week, it either guesses or says it doesn't have that information. Many chatbots will report their cutoff if you ask.

question: Chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude run on a system programmers call a 'neural network.' The word 'neural' is a hint about what the network was designed to imitate. It comes from a loose comparison to living cells in nature. Which of these is a neural network compared to?
answer: Cells in animal brains
choices: Cells in animal brains
Cables in a power grid
Stars in a galaxy
Roads in a city
context: Neural networks are layers of simple math units, loosely inspired by how brain cells (neurons) pass signals. They are NOT literal brains — they're math. The biology comparison is mostly historical naming; underneath, it's all numbers and equations.

question: Inside every big chatbot like ChatGPT, there are billions of tiny numbers that decide how it answers. While the chatbot learns from books and websites, those numbers slowly change so it gets better at predicting words. Programmers have a name for these tiny numbers. What are they usually called?
answer: Parameters
choices: Parameters
Passwords
Pictures
Pages
context: Parameters are the adjustable numbers (weights and biases) inside a model. GPT-3 had 175 billion of them. Training is the process of slowly tuning these numbers so the model produces better outputs. Bigger models often have more parameters — but bigger doesn't always mean better.

question: Before a chatbot like ChatGPT can talk to anyone, a team of programmers has to feed it huge piles of books, websites, and articles so it can learn how words fit together. Only after that first big stage is done does the chatbot start answering people's questions. What is that first learning stage called?
answer: Training
choices: Training
Sleeping
Selling
Stopping
context: Training is the stage where the model adjusts its parameters by studying huge amounts of data. It's done once, in a giant computing job. The second stage — when you actually ask it questions — is called 'inference.' Training is expensive; inference is what you use every time you chat.

question: A girl asks ChatGPT for a poem and DALL-E for a picture of a dragon, and each makes something brand new. The filter on her email only sorts messages into spam or not spam. What is the kind of AI that makes new things called?
answer: Generative AI
choices: Generative AI
Stored AI
Frozen AI
Sleeping AI
context: Generative AI produces new outputs — text, images, audio, video. ChatGPT, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion are generative. Other AI just classifies — 'is this email spam?' — without producing anything new. The 2022 ChatGPT moment was about generative AI going mainstream.

question: When you type a sentence into a chatbot like ChatGPT, the program does not read whole words the way you do. It chops your text into little pieces — sometimes a short word, sometimes just part of a word. It also writes its reply the same way, one small piece at a time. What are these small text pieces called?
answer: Tokens
choices: Tokens
Pixels
Folders
Pages
context: LLMs work with 'tokens,' which are subword pieces. 'Unbelievable' might be split into 'un,' 'believ,' and 'able.' This is why models sometimes spell words strangely or miscount letters — they aren't really seeing letters, they're seeing token chunks.

question: When you chat with ChatGPT or Claude, it can only remember so much of the conversation at once. If you keep talking long enough, the very oldest messages start to slip out of its memory. Programmers have a name for this limit on how much the chatbot can 'see' at one time. What is it called?
answer: Context window
choices: Context window
Quiet zone
Login screen
Hot key
context: The context window is the maximum chunk of text the model can consider in one go — usually measured in tokens. Modern chatbots have large windows but they aren't infinite. If a conversation gets very long, the model may lose track of what was said earlier.

question: A student tries four programs in one evening: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok. She asks each one a question in plain words and gets a written answer back. What is the general name for this kind of AI?
answer: Chatbot assistants
choices: Chatbot assistants
Music players
Photo editors
Video games
context: Chatbot assistants are programs you can have a back-and-forth conversation with in plain language. ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), and Grok (xAI) are the main ones from major US labs. They're all built on different underlying LLMs.

question: DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, and Midjourney are three famous AI programs. If you type 'a dragon reading a book in a library,' any one of them will draw a fresh picture of exactly that. You give words, you get a new picture back. What is the main job all three of these AI programs do?
answer: Generate images from text descriptions
choices: Generate images from text descriptions
Translate spoken English to French
Fix broken phone batteries
Block spam in your email
context: These are image generators — you type a description ('a knight riding a robot horse') and the AI produces a picture. DALL-E is from OpenAI, Stable Diffusion is open-source, Midjourney is a separate company. They've made image-faking far easier than before, which is why image-verification skills matter.

question: When you say 'Hey Siri, what is the weather today?' to your phone, or 'Alexa, play some music' to a smart speaker, the AI hears your voice as sound waves, not as words. Before it can figure out what you want or reply back, it has to do one big first job with your voice. What is that first job?
answer: Turn your speech into text
choices: Turn your speech into text
Charge its battery
Find your photos
Update its software
context: Voice assistants use speech-recognition AI to turn your spoken words into text. Then a separate system handles the request. Whisper (OpenAI), Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant all do this. The technology has gotten very good — but it also means the microphone has to be listening.

question: A programmer who spends all day typing code opens GitHub Copilot, the AI tool GitHub released in 2021. It sits in her editor, tries to guess what she will type next, and lets her take the guess with one key. What is Copilot's main job?
answer: Suggest code as you type
choices: Suggest code as you type
Power the office lights
Run your printer
Order new keyboards
context: Code-assistant tools (Copilot, Cursor, others) read what a programmer is writing and suggest the next lines. They speed up routine work, but they can also suggest buggy or insecure code. The programmer still has to read and check what's offered.

question: When you finish a YouTube video, 'Up Next' picks another one it thinks you will love. TikTok chooses the videos in your For You feed. Netflix rearranges its home page around what you have watched before. All three use AI to decide what you personally see next. What is the general name for this kind of AI?
answer: Recommendation systems
choices: Recommendation systems
Calendar reminders
Voice assistants
Spell checkers
context: Recommendation systems use AI to decide what content to put in front of you. They're trained on what you (and people like you) clicked on, watched, or shared. They're usually optimized for engagement — keeping you on the app — not for accuracy or your wellbeing.

question: Most famous AI chatbots — ChatGPT from OpenAI, Claude from Anthropic — run only on their company's servers. But some AI labs release their models a different way. Meta puts out Llama for free download, and a French startup called Mistral does the same. Anyone can grab the file and run it on a laptop, offline, no internet. What is this kind of model called?
answer: Open-source / open-weight models
choices: Open-source / open-weight models
Sealed-source models
Hidden-only models
Pay-by-minute models
context: Open-weight models have their weights (the trained numbers) freely available. Anyone can download them, run them on a personal computer, study them, or build on them. Llama (Meta), Mistral, DeepSeek, and Qwen are major examples. Closed models like GPT-4 or Claude are only available through their company's website or API.

question: Suppose you ask a chatbot for a short school essay. A convincing draft arrives in seconds. Before you turn it in, whose job is it to check the claims?
answer: Yours — the chatbot can't tell what's true
choices: Yours — the chatbot can't tell what's true
The chatbot's — it knows facts
Nobody's — drafts don't need checking
Your friend's — chatbots are infallible
context: Even when an LLM writes well, it can confidently include false claims, made-up dates, and invented quotes. The user is responsible for checking. Treat AI output as a draft from a clever friend who sometimes makes things up — useful, but never the final word.

question: AI chatbots have giveaway habits when they write. They often stuff in long dashes, or use fancy phrases like 'delve into' and 'rich tapestry' way more than a normal kid ever would. Some sentences also feel weirdly balanced. When you learn to notice these clues, what real-life skill are you building?
answer: Spotting AI-written text
choices: Spotting AI-written text
Spotting fake medicines
Spotting good handwriting
Spotting bird species
context: AI-generated text has subtle patterns: certain favored phrases, overuse of em-dashes, repetitive sentence structures. Spotting these is a useful skill — it tells you when something was likely written by AI rather than a person. The skill is recognition, not condemnation.

question: AI programs like Midjourney and DALL-E can make gorgeous pictures — dragons, castles, portraits. But if you look closely at a person's hands in an AI-generated image, sometimes there are six fingers, or two thumbs, or a hand that melts into another. What does this common mistake tell us about today's AI art?
answer: Even modern AI images often have flaws
choices: Even modern AI images often have flaws
Hands are always perfect in AI art
AI never makes images of hands
Photos always show six fingers
context: AI image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) often produce images with characteristic flaws: wrong finger counts, garbled text, jewelry blending into skin, asymmetric eye details. Learning to spot these flaws is a useful defense skill — you can tell a fake from a photo more often than you might think.

question: Someone hands you two paragraphs and asks: was this written by a person or by a chatbot? You cannot ask how long it took, and you cannot sniff the paper. You only have the text itself to work with. What is the single most useful thing to know when you try to tell which is which?
answer: Look for AI's typical phrases and structure
choices: Look for AI's typical phrases and structure
Count how long it took to write
Smell the paper it was printed on
Ask what zodiac sign it has
context: AI text often has telltale rhythms: certain favorite phrases ('delve into,' 'tapestry of'), repetitive sentence structures, overuse of em-dashes, an over-balanced tone. Real people write more roughly, with stronger opinions and stranger phrasings. Reading lots of AI output and lots of human writing builds the eye.

question: A cookbook company's engineers take a chatbot already trained on billions of pages of general text and train it a second time, using only recipes and food articles, to make it extra good at cooking questions. This narrow, extra round of training has a special name. What is it called?
answer: Fine-tuning
choices: Fine-tuning
Spell-checking
Streaming
Reblogging
context: Fine-tuning means taking a pre-trained model and giving it extra training on a specific task or in a specific style. The base model already knows English; fine-tuning teaches it to be a careful cooking helper, a polite customer-service bot, or whatever the company wants. It's cheaper than training a new model from scratch.

question: A boy types 'tell me about dogs' into a chatbot and gets a plain answer. His sister types 'write a fun poem about a dog named Rex who loves cheese' and gets something very different. What is the skill of careful wording called?
answer: Prompt engineering
choices: Prompt engineering
Promise keeping
Spell casting
Star charting
context: Prompt engineering means writing your input in a way that's likely to get a useful output. Specific instructions, examples, and structure all matter. It isn't magic — it's just careful writing. The same model can give very different answers to a sloppy question versus a clear one.

question: A man chasing a lost parcel got the chatbot of DPD (a British parcel firm) to swear and write a poem mocking the firm in January 2024. What did the firm do next?
answer: Switched off the chatbot's AI part
choices: Switched off the chatbot's AI part
Hired the customer as its poet
Made the poem its new slogan
Sued the customer for libel
context: Musician Ashley Beauchamp got the bot to swear and call DPD the worst delivery firm in the world, and his posts went viral. DPD blamed an error after a system update and disabled the AI element while it was fixed. A support bot can be pushed off its script.

question: Certain AI programs only need to hear about ten seconds of a real person talking. After that, the AI can say brand new sentences that were never actually spoken — in that same person's exact voice, tone, and accent. This trick has a specific name. What is it called?
answer: Voice cloning
choices: Voice cloning
Voice fasting
Voice exiting
Voice trimming
context: Voice-clone AI (ElevenLabs is a well-known company) can copy a voice from a small audio sample — a voicemail, a podcast clip, a social-media video. This is the technology behind 'grandparent scams,' where a caller sounds exactly like a relative. Knowing it exists is the first step in not being fooled.

question: The kind of AI inside ChatGPT and Claude is called a large language model (LLM). Underneath all the impressive answers, an LLM is trained on one basic task, done over and over with billions of examples. In plain words, what is a large language model actually trained to do?
answer: Predict the next word in a text
choices: Predict the next word in a text
Steer a self-driving car
Diagnose engine problems
Solve crossword puzzles only
context: An LLM is a program trained to predict the next word (or token) in a sequence of text. When you 'chat' with it, it's just predicting words one at a time, given the conversation so far. That single mechanism — guess the next word — is what powers all modern chatbots.

question: AI tools can copy a voice from a short clip, and scammers use the clones to phone families pretending to be a relative in trouble. What simple family habit protects against this kind of call?
answer: Set up a family safe word
choices: Trust any familiar voice
Set up a family safe word
Pay urgent requests fast
Only speak in whispers
context: A family safe word is a short phrase only family members know. If someone calls sounding like a relative and asks for money or help, you ask for the word, and a voice clone cannot know it. The FBI recommends every family set one up.

question: Suppose you watch a grandmaster lose to a computer chess program. The commentators say the machine 'wanted' the victory, and to your eye it looks that way. Deep down, does the program actually want to win?
answer: No, it just plays high-scoring moves on the board
choices: No, it just plays high-scoring moves on the board
Yes, it gets excited like a person would feel
Yes, it cheers up right after every victory
Only if you tip it some money for trying
context: A chess engine has no wanting, hoping, or feeling. It evaluates moves and picks high-scoring ones. The word 'wins' is just a label for what happened — the program didn't experience victory. Capability isn't the same as consciousness. This is the most basic distinction kids need to keep clear about AI.

question: GPT-3, the model that came before ChatGPT, learned from hundreds of billions of words of text. Most of its training mix came from one kind of source. What was it?
answer: Pages copied from the open web
choices: Books from public libraries
Wikipedia's encyclopedia
Pages copied from the open web
Scripts of films and TV
context: In the GPT-3 paper, a filtered copy of Common Crawl, a giant archive of web pages, made up 60% of the training mix; books were 16% and Wikipedia just 3%. Much of how a model writes comes from the public web.

question: A phone or smart speaker with Apple's Siri, Amazon's Alexa, or Google Assistant sits quietly all day. It only jumps to attention when you say a special phrase — 'Hey Siri,' 'Alexa,' or 'Hey Google.' Once it hears that phrase, its microphone starts streaming your words to the cloud. What is that activation phrase called in the AI industry?
answer: A wake word
choices: A wake word
A welcome bell
A start key
A boot button
context: Smart speakers and phones use a wake word — a short phrase the device listens for. The microphone is on, listening locally for that word. After the wake word, audio is sent to the cloud for processing. It's worth knowing that the device IS always listening, even if it's only supposed to act on the wake word.

question: A boy reading online meets four chatbot names. Three are real programs from real companies, and one is a made-up name that only sounds plausible. Which one is not real?
answer: ChatBuddy-X9 from a friendly lab
choices: ChatBuddy-X9 from a friendly lab
ChatGPT from the company OpenAI
Claude from the company Anthropic
Gemini from the company called Google
context: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), and Gemini (Google) are the main chatbots from major US AI labs as of the 2020s. 'ChatBuddy-X9' is invented. When you see a chatbot name in the news, it's worth checking whether the model is real — confident articles sometimes cite chatbots that don't exist.

question: Programs that turn typed words into fresh pictures are called AI image generators. Three of the most famous ones are DALL-E from OpenAI, Midjourney from a small research lab in California, and Stable Diffusion, which anyone can download and run on a personal computer at home. One of the four names below, though, is completely made up. Which of these four is not a real AI image generator?
answer: PixelMaster-Z
choices: PixelMaster-Z
DALL-E
Midjourney
Stable Diffusion
context: DALL-E (OpenAI), Midjourney (a separate company), and Stable Diffusion (open-source) are the main text-to-image generators of the 2020s. 'PixelMaster-Z' is invented. Knowing real-tool names helps you spot fabrications — both human and AI-written articles sometimes invent plausible-sounding product names.

question: Asked 'What color is the sky?', a chatbot replies 'I think the sky is blue.' What is the chatbot actually doing when it writes that reply?
answer: Using words it learned in training
choices: Checking a live weather map
Using words it learned in training
Copying a human's earlier reply
Following a rule about skies
context: Chatbots write phrases like 'I think' and 'I believe' because their training text is full of them; the model is predicting likely words. Whether anything like a thought lies behind such words is a question researchers still argue about.

question: When adults on the news say a chatbot uses 'deep learning,' the word 'deep' does not mean wise or profound. It is a plain technical word from computer science. A neural network is built out of many layers of tiny math steps stacked one on top of the next, and 'deep' just means there are a lot of those stacked layers. So in the phrase 'deep learning,' what does the 'deep' really refer to?
answer: Many layers stacked in the network
choices: Many layers stacked in the network
Deep undersea data centers
Deep meaning in the answers
Deep voices in the speech
context: A neural network is 'deep' when it has many layers stacked between input and output. Each layer transforms the data a bit further. The deep-learning revolution after 2012 was about making much deeper networks practical — and they turned out to handle much harder problems.

question: Before your first message reaches a chatbot, the company behind it slips in hidden instructions about how the model should behave. In 2024 Anthropic began publishing its version for Claude. What are these instructions called?
answer: A system prompt
choices: A safety firmware
A system prompt
A user manual
A spam filter
context: A system prompt sets a chatbot's rules and tone before the conversation starts, and users usually never see it. In August 2024 Anthropic began publishing Claude's system prompts in its release notes, which most companies do not do.

question: A girl hears a radio ad call a chatbot 'the world's smartest friend.' It helps with her homework, but it does not remember her name the next day, and it would tell any stranger the same jokes. What part of that phrase is most misleading?
answer: It's a tool, not a friend
choices: It's a tool, not a friend
It's smart in every subject
It uses the internet to think
It is friends with other AIs
context: A chatbot isn't a friend. It has no skin in the game, no care for you, no memory of you across chats by default. It's a useful tool when you want a draft, a summary, or a starting point. Calling it a friend invites a kind of trust that the tool isn't built to deserve.

question: A visitor to Chatbot Arena, a popular leaderboard that began at Berkeley in 2023, types a question and reads two answers from unnamed models side by side. Then she does one thing. What?
answer: Votes for the better answer
choices: Votes for the better answer
Pays for the faster answer
Grades the models' spelling
Guesses which one is human
context: LMSYS's Chatbot Arena turns those blind votes into chess-style Elo ratings for each model. It measures which answers people prefer to read, which is useful but is not the same thing as being correct.

question: A parent asked a teacher, within weeks of the launch, who had built ChatGPT, the free chatbot that a small research lab in San Francisco released late in 2022. Which lab released it?
answer: OpenAI
choices: Google DeepMind
Meta AI
OpenAI
Anthropic
context: OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. Its growth was the fastest of any consumer product on record at the time, and the launch is widely treated as the moment the modern AI era went mainstream.

question: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, was founded in 2015 by Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others to do safety research on AI, not to make a profit. What kind of group did it start as?
answer: A non-profit research lab
choices: A non-profit research lab
A high-school tutoring chain
A breakfast cereal startup
A used-car dealer franchise
context: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a non-profit research lab with a stated mission of ensuring AGI benefits humanity. It later restructured to a 'capped-profit' company so it could raise the billions of dollars needed for the compute behind GPT-3 and GPT-4. ChatGPT was released on November 30, 2022.

question: A teenager tried to log in to ChatGPT late in 2022 and found the servers down, crashed by new users. The chatbot was smashing the record for reaching 100 million users, ahead of TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. About how long did it take?
answer: Two months
choices: Two months
Two days
Two years
Twelve years
context: ChatGPT reached 100 million monthly active users in roughly two months after its November 30, 2022 launch — faster than TikTok, Instagram, or any prior internet product. The speed of adoption is part of why the moment felt seismic to so many.

question: A British mathematician asked in 1950 whether machines can think. He proposed a test in which a judge types to a hidden person and a hidden machine and tries to tell which is which. What is the test called?
answer: The Turing test
choices: The Turing test
The Wittgenstein test
The Hilbert test
The von Neumann test
context: Alan Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' opened with 'I propose to consider the question, can machines think?' He answered by proposing the imitation game, now called the Turing test. He didn't claim to have built such a machine; he argued for a way to settle the question if one ever appeared. Turing had broken the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during WWII and is considered a founder of computer science. Modern chatbots can sometimes pass simple versions of the test; whether that counts as 'intelligence' is still debated.

question: In the summer of 1956, ten researchers gathered at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire for a small eight-week workshop on whether machines could ever reason or learn like people. Before the meeting, the young professor who organized it needed a fresh name for this brand-new area of study to put on the funding letter. Who coined the phrase 'artificial intelligence' for the Dartmouth meeting?
answer: John McCarthy
choices: John McCarthy
John D. Rockefeller
John F. Kennedy
Johnny Appleseed
context: John McCarthy proposed the term 'artificial intelligence' for the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project. The term stuck. McCarthy went on to invent the LISP programming language in 1958. The Dartmouth workshop is widely treated as the founding moment of AI as an organized research field.

question: In the summer of 1956, ten researchers spent eight weeks at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire arguing about whether machines could ever reason, learn, or use language like a person. They agreed the topic needed its own name so it could stand apart from ordinary computer science and math. What did they choose to call this brand-new field?
answer: Artificial intelligence
choices: Artificial intelligence
Machine thinking
Cybernetics
Computer science
context: The 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was held at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. John McCarthy organized it. Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester were among the attendees. They thought one summer would make significant progress on machine intelligence; it took decades.

question: A beginner sits down at a wooden Go board like the one Lee Sedol used against AlphaGo in 2016. Stones go on the crossings of its lines, and it is much bigger than a chessboard. How many lines does it have on each side?
answer: Nineteen by nineteen
choices: Nineteen by nineteen
Five by five tiles
Four by ten spaces
Two by sixty cells
context: Go is played on a 19x19 grid with black and white stones. The search space is vastly larger than chess. question: Geoffrey Hinton, a British-Canadian computer scientist many call a 'godfather of AI,' resigned in May 2023 from the big tech company he had worked at for over a decade, saying he wanted to speak freely about the dangers of powerful AI. Which company did he quit?

question: Elon Musk's AI company xAI, launched in 2023, built its own chatbot to compete with ChatGPT and Claude. question: Dario and Daniela Amodei and their colleagues had all worked together at a famous AI lab before they split off in 2021 to build a company more focused on AI safety. Their new San Francisco company became Anthropic. Which lab did the team leave?

question: A student types a question into the chatbot from Anthropic, the San Francisco company Dario and Daniela Amodei helped start in 2021. Its friendly one-word name is a nod to the mathematician Shannon, who launched information theory in 1948. What is the chatbot called?

question: In 2012, three researchers from the University of Toronto — Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton — entered a huge picture-recognition contest called ImageNet. question: In 2017, a team of Google researchers published a short scientific paper that would quietly change AI forever. question: Researchers watched GPT-3 translate a phrase, write code and solve a riddle in 2020 after seeing just two or three examples inside the prompt, on jobs it had never been specifically trained for. What is that ability called?

question: In March 2023, OpenAI released GPT-4, the newest version of the model behind ChatGPT. question: Joseph Weizenbaum, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), wrote one of the very first chat programs in 1966. question: A professor locked up her AI lab in the mid-1970s after government funders in the US and UK pulled their money over hyped promises. The slump came again in the late 1980s. What seasonal name do historians give these long slumps?

question: In February 2011, the American computer company International Business Machines (IBM) sent a room-sized machine onto the TV quiz show Jeopardy! question: OpenAI began in 2015 as a nonprofit AI lab in San Francisco, founded by a small group who wanted safe, open AI research. question: At a Dartmouth College summer workshop in 1956, a computer scientist named John McCarthy invented the very phrase 'artificial intelligence' to describe machines that could think. question: Meta is the giant tech company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Unlike OpenAI and Google, Meta has taken an unusual path with its AI: it releases a whole family of chatbots for free, and anyone in the world can download the underlying model to run on a personal computer. question: A radiologist opens a chest scan that an AI program has already read, with a faint shadow on a lung flagged for her. The AI is not allowed to diagnose a patient on its own; she still makes the final call. What role does the AI mostly play in that setup?

question: When you open YouTube, the home page fills with videos you never asked for — yet many are exactly the kind of thing you like. question: A traveller opens an airline's website to change a flight, and a little window asks 'Hi, how can I help?' She types her problem and an answer comes back in seconds, with no employee ever joining. What kind of AI program is that?

question: Voice assistants like Apple's Siri and Amazon's Alexa are always half-listening. question: Your phone shows Grandma's name and a crying voice begs for money. Scammers can fake caller ID to show any name or number, a trick called spoofing. What does the name on the screen prove?

question: A farmer looks out over fields too huge to walk every day. Now an AI model spots dry patches, pests and weak crops for him from far above, then tells him exactly where to water or spray. What does the AI use to watch his crops?

question: A forecaster waits hours for a giant physics simulation on a supercomputer to guess tomorrow's storms. In 2023 Google DeepMind's GraphCast, an AI model, matched such forecasts on a single computer. Compared with older tools, what do AI weather models often do?

question: A chemist hunting a new drug faces a huge library of molecules that would take years to test by hand. An AI predicts which to build first. What is AI mainly used to do here?
answer: Speed up finding candidate compounds
choices: Speed up finding candidate compounds
Bake bread for clinical trials
Replace pharmacies entirely
Manage hospital cafeterias
context: AI in drug discovery is used to narrow the search for promising candidate compounds — sorting through billions of possibilities far faster than human chemists alone could. AlphaFold-style protein-structure prediction is one piece of this. Drug development still takes years and clinical trials, but the early-stage search has changed dramatically.

question: A student opens four giant AI chatbots side by side, ChatGPT and Claude among them. One of the four, built by Google, is named after the twin stars. Which one is from Google?
answer: Gemini
choices: Gemini
Grok
Claude
ChatGPT
context: ChatGPT is from OpenAI. Claude is from Anthropic. Gemini is from Google. Grok is from xAI (Elon Musk's company). They compete on different strengths — Gemini integrates with Google services; Claude has long context windows; ChatGPT had the biggest head start; Grok markets itself as less filtered.

question: AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude can solve math problems, but they can also explain them. A student stuck on a fractions problem could just copy the final answer without understanding it, or could ask the bot to explain each part of the reasoning and then check every one by hand. A productive way to use a chatbot for learning math is:
answer: Ask it to walk through steps
choices: Ask it to walk through steps
Submit its answers as your own
Never check what it says
Get it to do your test for you
context: AI is genuinely useful as a learning tool when you ask it to explain step-by-step, check your work, and quiz you. Submitting its output as your own is cheating and trains you to skip the actual learning. The line: AI for explanation and review = useful. AI for replacing the work you should do yourself = makes you weaker.

question: In 2011, Apple bought a small startup and turned its voice assistant into a feature built into every iPhone. She could answer questions, set alarms, send texts, and search the web — all by voice. Today, over a billion people talk to her every week. What is Apple's voice assistant called?
answer: Siri
choices: Siri
Bixby
Cortana
Sundar
context: Apple's voice assistant is Siri, launched in 2011 with the iPhone 4S. Amazon has Alexa (with Echo devices). Google has Google Assistant. Microsoft has Cortana. All of them rely on AI for speech recognition (turning your speech into text) and natural-language understanding (figuring out what you meant).

question: In 2014, Amazon launched a tabletop speaker called the Echo. It sat on the kitchen counter, listened for a wake word, and answered questions, played music, and controlled smart lights — all through a voice assistant with a woman's name. What is the voice assistant inside the Echo speaker called?
answer: Alexa
choices: Alexa
Echo
Aria
Astra
context: Alexa is Amazon's voice assistant, built into Echo smart speakers and other devices. Like Siri and Google Assistant, it uses AI to recognize speech and process natural language. It's also a microphone in your house listening for the wake word 'Alexa' — worth being aware of when deciding where to put one.

question: There are several famous AI image generators: DALL-E from OpenAI, Midjourney (a private service), Imagen from Google, and one more from a British startup called Stability AI. Three of them keep the model locked inside company servers. Only one is 'open source' — the model itself can be downloaded free and run on your own home computer. Which one is it?
answer: Stable Diffusion
choices: Stable Diffusion
DALL-E
Midjourney
Imagen
context: Stable Diffusion is open-source. Anyone can download the model and run it on a personal computer. DALL-E (OpenAI), Midjourney (its own company), and Stable Diffusion (Stability AI, image) are closed — you have to use the company's website or API. Open-source models are an important countervailing force to closed model companies.

question: Pandora's music service was built on the Music Genome Project, begun in 2000. Instead of only watching what listeners played, it described every song itself. Who did the describing?
answer: Trained musicians, by hand
choices: Random listeners, by vote
Trained musicians, by hand
The singers, by contract
Radio hosts, by phone
context: Founder Tim Westergren hired musicologists to analyze songs on hundreds of musical traits, so Pandora could suggest songs that sound alike. That is content-based recommendation; most big feeds lean on collaborative filtering instead, which matches you with people like you.

question: DeepL is a translation tool built in Cologne, Germany, by a small European team. It launched in 2017 and quickly became famous for translations that sound more natural than its bigger rivals, especially between European languages like German, French, and English. Which other big translation tool does DeepL compete with?
answer: Google Translate
choices: Google Translate
Google Calendar
Google Photos
Google Calculator
context: DeepL and Google Translate are the two best-known machine-translation services. DeepL is often praised for nuance with European languages, while Google Translate covers more languages overall. Both use deep neural networks trained on huge corpora of human-translated text. Both have moved the practical floor for cross-language communication.

question: A student sets out to have a computer search every legal position in Go, the game DeepMind's AlphaGo mastered in 2016. How does the number of positions compare with the atoms in the observable universe?
answer: Far more positions
choices: Far fewer positions
Far more positions
About the same
Exactly half as many
context: John Tromp calculated in 2016 that a Go board has about 2 x 10^170 legal positions, while the observable universe holds around 10^80 atoms. No computer could search all of that, which is why Go needed learned judgement rather than brute force.

question: A woman at home twists a protein on her computer screen into its best shape and scores points for it, using Foldit, which scientists at the University of Washington released in 2008. What kind of thing is Foldit?
answer: An online puzzle game
choices: A microscope camera
An online puzzle game
A lab robot arm
A protein vitamin
context: Foldit turned protein folding into a puzzle: players drag a molecule around on screen and score points for shapes that are physically likely. It came partly out of David Baker's lab, the scientist who later shared the 2024 Nobel Prize.

question: AI image generators trained on millions of photos can draw a striking face or a whole landscape in seconds, but they often mess up hands — five fingers becomes six, or thumbs bend the wrong way. The system has no idea that a hand is a hand; it just remembers patterns of pixels from its training data. Why does this kind of mistake happen?
answer: The model doesn't truly understand hands
choices: The model doesn't truly understand hands
Hands are too small to draw at all
All cameras break around hands
Hands are illegal to depict by law
context: Image generators learn patterns of pixels that statistically appear together. They don't 'understand' that a hand has exactly five fingers — they just know what hands tend to look like. When the model isn't sure, it can produce six fingers, missing fingers, or impossible joints. Hands and text in images are the two classic giveaways.

question: AI translators work well on Spanish, French, and Mandarin because there are billions of pages of translated text online for the AI to learn from. But languages spoken by only a few thousand people — like Yupik in Alaska or Manx on the Isle of Man — have almost no written material for the model to train on. AI is strong on big languages. But it's weaker for what kind of language?
answer: Low-resource languages with little data
choices: Low-resource languages with little data
Languages with red flags
Languages spoken at high altitudes
Languages with curved letters
context: Translation AI works best when there's a lot of parallel training data — sentences translated between two languages by humans. Major languages (English, Spanish, Mandarin, French) have plenty. 'Low-resource' languages with fewer speakers or less digital text get poorer-quality translation. This is a real fairness gap in the technology.

question: A woman swipes her credit card at a store, and a statistical model at her bank checks the swipe in real time. AI fraud detection in banking is an example of what?
answer: Old AI that quietly works
choices: Old AI that quietly works
Brand-new AI from this year
AI that nobody actually uses
AI that talks like a person
context: Credit-card fraud detection has used machine learning since the 1990s. It's an example of older 'narrow' AI that quietly works every day, far from any chatbot drama. Most of the AI in your daily life — spam filtering, recommendation, fraud detection, voice transcription — has been working for years without any fanfare.

question: Most self-driving cars from Waymo and other companies carry a spinning sensor on the roof. It fires laser pulses in every direction and measures how long each pulse takes to bounce back — building a live 3D map of the road, the other cars, and the pedestrians around the vehicle. What is this laser-based sensor technology called?
answer: Lidar (laser-based ranging)
choices: Lidar (laser-based ranging)
Sonar (sound-based ranging)
Radar (radio-based ranging)
Solar (sun-based ranging)
context: Lidar bounces laser pulses off objects and times the return to build a 3D map of the surroundings. Waymo and many other self-driving programs use it. Tesla famously chose to rely mostly on cameras and radar instead. Sonar uses sound, radar uses radio waves; lidar uses light. Each has different strengths for different conditions.

question: A famous actress wants an audiobook company to use an AI version of her own voice to read a new novel out loud. That way she doesn't have to sit in a recording studio for weeks reading every chapter herself. Before the AI can talk in her voice, though, the company needs one thing from her first. What must she do?
answer: Give recorded samples for training
choices: Give recorded samples for training
Watch every chapter being read
Drive the audiobook truck
Pick the cover art color
context: AI voice cloning needs samples to train on. Legitimate uses (audiobooks, dubbing, accessibility) involve consent — the voice owner agrees and is usually paid. The same technology without consent powers voice-clone scams. The technology itself doesn't know the difference; that's why the law and personal habits both matter.

question: DeepMind's engineers released AlphaZero in 2017 as a follow-up to AlphaGo, which had studied recorded matches first. How did AlphaZero learn chess and Go?
answer: From scratch with no human games
choices: From scratch with no human games
By watching human players in person
From a printed book of moves
Only when humans weren't looking
context: AlphaZero learned chess, shogi, and Go using only the rules and self-play — no human game data at all. AlphaGo had used some human games. AlphaZero showed that pure self-play could match or exceed human-data-augmented training. It's a striking demonstration of how powerful self-play can be when the rules are clear and the system can play itself millions of times.

question: DALL-E is an image AI from OpenAI, and Stable Diffusion is an open-source image AI from a company called Stability AI. Both were opened to the public in 2022. A user types a sentence like 'a cat astronaut waving from the surface of Mars,' and the model paints the picture pixel by pixel from that description. DALL-E and Stable Diffusion are both:
answer: Text-to-image generators
choices: Text-to-image generators
Brands of toothpaste
Sports drink flavors
Bicycle frame makers
context: DALL-E (OpenAI) and Stable Diffusion (Stability AI / open-source) are both text-to-image generators. You type a description; they produce an image. Midjourney is another in the same category. DALL-E is closed (use OpenAI's site). Stable Diffusion is open-source — anyone can run it. The technology has changed what's possible to fake.

question: A web developer types 'make me a simple web page with a login button' into an AI coding tool like GitHub Copilot, and working code appears. Such tools learned from code that was sometimes buggy or insecure. Before she trusts the result, what must she still do?
answer: Read and test the suggested code
choices: Read and test the suggested code
Use every suggestion immediately
Submit code without reading
Trust AI completely on security
context: AI coding tools speed up routine work but they can suggest buggy, insecure, or subtly wrong code. The programmer still has to read what's offered, test it, and decide whether to use it. 'Tool that drafts; human that reviews' is the discipline that keeps quality from sliding when AI is in the loop.

question: A short-video app like TikTok or YouTube Shorts uses an AI to decide which clip to show you next, hoping to keep you scrolling as long as possible. The company describes what it is measuring with one word: engagement. When it says 'engagement,' it doesn't mean whether you liked a video with your heart. It means two very specific numbers the app can actually count. What counts as engagement here?
answer: Watch time and shares
choices: Watch time and shares
How loud you cheer
Your shoe brand
Your last test grade
context: Engagement is usually measured by watch time, repeat visits, likes, comments, and shares. These are easy to count. They are NOT the same as 'did this help the user' or 'is the content true.' The system optimizes whatever it's measured by, so the metric shapes what gets shown. This is one of the most important facts to know about how these systems work.

question: Geoffrey Hinton, a famous AI researcher, stood in front of a room of doctors in 2016 and predicted that within five years, hospitals would no longer need radiologists, the doctors who read X-rays and scans, because AI would replace them all. Nearly ten years later, what has happened to radiologist jobs?
answer: Radiologists are still in demand
choices: Radiologists are still in demand
Radiologists vanished in 2017
All hospitals closed by 2018
Hospitals replaced beds with bots
context: Hinton publicly said in 2016 that medical schools should stop training radiologists because AI would replace them within five years. Nearly a decade later, radiologists are still in demand and AI is used as a second-reader rather than as a replacement. The prediction is a famous cautionary tale: confident AI job-displacement timelines have a poor track record.

question: A reviewer at the US Food and Drug Administration signed off on another AI medical device, one of more than 1,400 authorized by the end of 2025. About three in four of them did one kind of job. Which job?
answer: Reading medical scans
choices: Doing surgery
Reading medical scans
Mixing medicines
Booking appointments
context: Radiology, the specialty that reads X-rays, CT scans and MRIs, accounts for about 76 percent of the AI devices on the FDA's list. It is the medical field most crowded with AI, and also a field still short of doctors.

question: A grower flies a drone over her fields, and an AI program combs the pictures for tiny changes in the leaves: a plant that may be sick, a patch short of water, a place where bugs are chewing. What does the AI help her do?
answer: Spot crop problems early
choices: Spot crop problems early
Sing to the plants
Paint barns purple
Bake bread on the tractor
context: Precision agriculture uses AI on satellite imagery, drone footage, and ground sensors to spot drought stress, pest damage, nutrient deficiencies, and yield variation across a field. Farmers can then water, fertilize, or treat only where needed instead of treating the whole field uniformly. It's a quietly important application of AI to real-world problems.

question: A brain disease took away Congresswoman Jennifer Wexton's speech. In 2024 an AI company built a clone of her voice from recordings of her old speeches. What did it let her do on the House floor?
answer: Speak in her own voice
choices: Speak in her own voice
Speak in an actor's voice
Vote without being there
Read speeches as text
context: Rep. Jennifer Wexton of Virginia has progressive supranuclear palsy, which damages speech. ElevenLabs cloned her voice from her earlier speeches, and in July 2024 she gave what is believed to be the first House floor speech in an AI-cloned voice.

question: You can ask a chatbot to quiz you before a test. Psychologists find that pulling an answer out of your own memory makes it stick far better than reading it again. What is this study habit called?
answer: Testing yourself
choices: Rereading notes
Highlighting
Testing yourself
Copying notes
context: Psychologists call it the testing effect, or retrieval practice. In a 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, students who tested themselves remembered far more a week later than students who reread. A chatbot that quizzes you puts it to work.

question: Your phone rings. The voice on the other end sounds exactly like your cousin. He says he's in trouble and needs you to wire him money right away. But modern AI can clone anyone's voice from only a few seconds of recorded audio, and scammers use these voice clones to fake calls from family members. What's the smart first move before you send anything?
answer: Hang up and call your cousin back
choices: Hang up and call your cousin back
Wire the money right away
Whisper a secret family song
Tell him your address out loud
context: Voice clones can fool family members from just seconds of recorded audio. The single best defense is to hang up and call back on a number you already know. If it was really your cousin, he'll pick up. If it was a scammer, the call ends right there. Urgency is the scammer's tool; calling back is yours.

question: Voice-cloning AI copies a person's voice by studying recorded speech, and today's tools need a surprisingly tiny sample to fake a voice that sounds real. About how much recorded audio does modern AI need to clone a person?
answer: Just a few seconds
choices: Just a few seconds
Twenty years exactly
Half a lifetime
Several decades
context: Modern voice-cloning tools can produce a convincing imitation from just a few seconds of clean audio. The source can be a voicemail, a podcast, a social-media video, even a clip from a school play, so it is worth being careful about what audio of you is public.

question: In April 2023 a TikTok user called Ghostwriter posted 'Heart on My Sleeve,' a song sung by AI copies of two stars who never recorded it. Streaming sites pulled it after the label complained. Whose voices?
answer: Drake and The Weeknd
choices: Eminem and Dr. Dre
Adele and Ed Sheeran
Drake and The Weeknd
Beyonce and Rihanna
context: The song used AI vocals imitating Drake and The Weeknd, neither of whom was involved. It drew millions of plays before Universal Music Group got Spotify, Apple Music and others to remove it. Famous voices are easy to clone because so much of their audio is online.

question: A big sister watches her brother chat with a free AI chatbot on his phone. If the company gets hacked, she warns, anything he pastes in might one day be read by another person. What does she tell him never to paste?
answer: Your password
choices: Your password
A song lyric
A book title
A weather forecast
context: Free chatbot services typically log your conversations. They may be used to train future models, reviewed by employees, or accessed under legal process. Never paste passwords, full credit card numbers, or sensitive medical/legal documents you wouldn't want public. Treat anything you send to a free chatbot as potentially seen by someone else.

question: Suppose you tell a clinic your symptoms, and the US health-privacy law (HIPAA) guards them. You type them into a chatbot app. Does the law protect them there?
answer: No, it mostly covers doctors and insurers
choices: Yes, it covers every health app
Yes, once you click I agree
No, it mostly covers doctors and insurers
Only if the app is free to use
context: HIPAA applies to covered entities such as health providers and health plans, and to their business partners. A consumer app you download on your own generally falls outside it, so your health questions are governed mostly by the app's own privacy policy.

question: A boy scrolling online stops on a video of a famous politician saying something shocking. It looks totally real, but AI can fake a clip of anyone. Before he believes it or forwards it to friends, what is the smart first step?
answer: Check if trusted news outlets report it
choices: Check if trusted news outlets report it
Forward it to ten people very fast
Trust it because the clip is popular
Trust it because the face looks real
context: Deepfakes can put words in real people's mouths. Telltales (mouth-sync drift, weird blinking, voice mismatch) are useful but not foolproof. The bigger defense is: if something shocking happened, trusted news organizations are usually reporting it. If the only place you see a story is a viral clip on social media, treat it with extra suspicion.

question: You see a photo online of a person holding up a big sign with words on it. When you look closely at the sign, the letters are messy and jumbled — some are half-formed, others don't spell real words. AI image generators are famously bad at drawing readable text on signs, packages, and shirts. What is a garbled sign a telltale clue of?
answer: An AI-generated image
choices: An AI-generated image
Bad camera focus only
Foreign-language script
Old vintage film
context: AI image generators (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney) often produce garbled, unreadable text in images — letters that look right at first glance but spell nothing. Real photos with real signs have real text. Garbled text on signs, labels, or storefronts in an image is a strong indicator that the image is AI-generated.

question: When people share suspicious photos online, one of the most reliable tricks for spotting an AI-generated fake is to zoom in on the hands. Real photos show human hands with exactly five fingers each. AI image generators, though, don't really 'know' how many fingers a hand should have — they just guess based on what the picture looks like. Why does the 'look at the hands' trick work?
answer: AI often gets finger counts wrong
choices: AI often gets finger counts wrong
AI never draws hands at all
AI hands are always pink
AI always draws six fingers
context: AI image generators frequently produce hands with wrong finger counts, extra knuckles, impossible joints, or fingers that meld together. Real photos don't have this problem (real people have five fingers). Hands are one of the most reliable AI-image giveaways, along with garbled text and weird jewelry-skin blending.

question: Mike Caulfield built a four-step habit for judging anything online, from a chatbot answer to a viral post, and named it SIFT (one letter for each step). What is the first step?
answer: Stop
choices: Share
Search
Screenshot
Stop
context: Caulfield's SIFT stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context. Stopping comes first because the urge to share is strongest in the moment, and a pause is when you ask whether you know what the source is at all.

question: A boy finds a strange bump on his skin and, instead of getting it looked at, types his symptoms into a chatbot. It gives him a confident-sounding diagnosis. But chatbots often 'hallucinate': they invent medical facts that sound authoritative. What should he do?
answer: See a real doctor, not the chatbot
choices: See a real doctor, not the chatbot
Trust the chatbot completely
Buy whatever pills it names
Use it as final medical advice
context: Chatbots can provide useful general information but they don't know your full medical history, they can't examine you, and they can be confidently wrong. For real symptoms, see a real doctor. Use the chatbot as a starting point for questions to ask, never as the final word. The same rule applies to legal advice — real lawyer for real legal issues.

question: A boy stuck on a homework math problem types it into a chatbot and gets a confident answer back. Chatbots are not always right at math. Before he turns it in, what is the smart step?
answer: Check it with a calculator
choices: Check it with a calculator
Submit it without thinking
Trust the chatbot's math fully
Erase your own work entirely
context: LLMs are bad at multi-step arithmetic. They predict text patterns, not numbers. They can be confidently wrong on big numbers, long chains of operations, or unusual calculations. Always verify chatbot math with an actual calculator. Some chatbot products bolt a calculator on — when they do, the math is reliable. Without it, don't trust it.

question: Suppose you close the tab on a free AI chatbot, sure the company has thrown away everything you typed. Most free chatbots do not work that way. What does the company usually do with your chats?
answer: Logs your conversations
choices: Forgets them all instantly
Sells them to one shopper
Logs your conversations
Burns them with a candle
context: Most free chatbot services keep a log of your conversations on the company's servers, and their terms of service say what the company may do with it. Reading the terms once for any service you use heavily is worth a few minutes.

question: When you install a new phone app, the app often asks for permission to use your phone's microphone. Some apps really need it — a video-call app, a voice recorder, a music app that listens for a song. Other apps have no honest reason to listen at all. If you say yes to every request, the app can record audio whenever it wants. What's the smart default for microphone permissions?
answer: Only allow it for apps that need it
choices: Only allow it for apps that need it
Allow it for every app always
Reject every app permission
Let every app record forever
context: Most apps don't actually need microphone access. A photo editor doesn't need to hear you; a flashlight app doesn't either. The smart default is 'only for apps that genuinely need it' — voice assistants, video chat, voice messaging. The same logic applies to camera, location, contacts, and other permissions. Default-off, allow on a case-by-case basis.

question: A student asks ChatGPT and Gemini the same question, and both give the same surprising fact. She is ready to call it settled. Does their agreement prove the fact is true?
answer: No — they may share training data
choices: Yes — two sources agree
Yes — but only weekdays
Yes — if both are long
No — they may share training data
context: Two chatbots agreeing isn't independent confirmation. They were often trained on overlapping internet data and can share the same errors. Agreement can raise your confidence a little, but real verification needs a different kind of source, such as an encyclopedia or an official page.

question: In a homework study group, you notice one kid's essay reads oddly polished. Almost every sentence uses em-dashes, the writing 'delves into the rich tapestry' of the topic, and every paragraph ends with a tidy takeaway line. Human students rushing an assignment almost never write like that. Chatbots often do. What is a reasonable first suspicion?
answer: It may have been AI-written
choices: It may have been AI-written
It was written in invisible ink
Its author is a robot truly
It was definitely Shakespeare
context: Heavy em-dash use, phrases like 'delve into,' 'tapestry of,' 'navigate the complexities,' and overly balanced sentence structure are common AI tells. Real student writing tends to be rougher, more opinionated, with stranger phrasings. Spotting these patterns is a useful skill — both for teachers checking work and for readers checking sources online.

question: A teacher plays a suspected deepfake for her class and asks the students to watch closely. At a glance it looks real, but a careful viewer can usually catch a small giveaway. Which of these signs is a typical tell?
answer: Mouth movement that doesn't quite match
choices: Mouth movement that doesn't quite match
Bright sunshine in the background
A song playing on the radio
The person sitting at a desk
context: Deepfake video tells include: mouth movement that drifts slightly out of sync with the speech, weird blinking patterns, blurry or shifting hair or jewelry edges, voice that doesn't quite match the lip movement, and inconsistent lighting on the face. The technology keeps improving — so the tells keep getting subtler — but the general idea is to look for small mismatches.

question: A student's chatbot offers a beautiful, wise-sounding line it claims was written by Mark Twain or Albert Einstein. Chatbots often produce fake lines that sound real but were never actually said by that person. Before she uses it in an essay or shares it as real, what's the safe step?
answer: Search for the exact quote first
choices: Search for the exact quote first
Use it in an essay right away
Trust it for sounding real
Get it printed on a poster
context: Chatbots invent confident-sounding quotes attributed to famous authors. The quote often sounds 'in style' but was never actually written by that author. Before using a quote in an essay, search for the exact phrase in quotation marks. If the only places it appears are AI outputs or scraped AI content, it's probably invented.

question: A teacher shows her class ChatGPT's Temporary Chat, which keeps a talk out of the saved history. OpenAI says it may still keep one thing for up to 30 days. What is it?
answer: A copy of the chat, for safety checks
choices: Your card number, for billing
A voice recording, for ID
Your location, for local ads
A copy of the chat, for safety checks
context: OpenAI's help pages say a Temporary Chat won't appear in your history or train its models, but the company may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Temporary means temporary for you, not instantly gone from the company's servers.

question: In March 2024 Tennessee, home of Nashville's music business, passed the first state law adding a person's voice to the rights an AI clone may not copy without permission. The law's name spells out a famous singer. Which singer?
answer: Elvis Presley
choices: Johnny Cash
Elvis Presley
Dolly Parton
Hank Williams
context: Governor Bill Lee signed the ELVIS Act, short for the Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act, on March 21, 2024. Tennessee law already protected a person's name and image; the update added the voice, so musicians can act against unauthorized AI copies.

question: Judge Kevin Castel fined the New York lawyer Steven Schwartz a modest amount in June 2023 over a brief written with ChatGPT, as a public warning. The story made news worldwide. About how much was the fine?
answer: About 5,000 dollars
choices: About 5,000 dollars
About 5 cents
About 500 million dollars
Nothing at all
context: Steven Schwartz was fined $5,000 in June 2023 for filing a brief citing six ChatGPT-fabricated cases in Mata v. Avianca. The story made worldwide news. It's now a standard cautionary tale — first because LLMs invent citations, and second because verifying isn't optional, especially when professional reputation or money is at stake.

question: AI image generators sometimes goof on the fine details of a human face. You are scrolling through photos online and see a picture of a person wearing glasses. Something looks off — the frames seem to melt into the skin on the side of the face, with no clean edge. That kind of detail is a giveaway. This image is most likely:
answer: Glasses-into-skin AI blending
choices: Glasses-into-skin AI blending
Just a low-quality phone camera
A brand-new fashion choice
A bright reflection from the sun
context: AI image generators frequently produce flaws around objects that touch skin or hair — glasses merging into the face, earrings half-disappearing, hair blending into clothing. Real photos don't have these problems (real objects have edges). Watch for these blending flaws as image-generation tells.

question: A girl thinks her little brother may have swallowed something from under the sink, and she is tempted to ask a chatbot what to do. In the United States, which free line reaches the right experts?
answer: Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222
choices: Directory help, at 411
City services, at 311
Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222
Phone repair, at 611
context: Poison Control's free, confidential line, 1-800-222-1222, connects you with experts, and poison.org has an online tool as well. A chatbot cannot see the bottle, the dose or the child. If someone has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911.

question: A tester tried Tessa, a chatbot an eating-disorder charity promoted in 2023 as it shut its human helpline. Within days Tessa was gone. What had Tessa said?
answer: Tips for losing weight and cutting calories
choices: Tips for losing weight and cutting calories
Jokes about the charity's founders
Recipes for rich chocolate cake
The home addresses of staff
context: Consultant Sharon Maxwell reported that Tessa suggested losing a pound or two a week and keeping a daily calorie deficit, exactly the wrong advice for someone with an eating disorder. The National Eating Disorders Association took it down and blamed bad actors for tricking it.

question: A big sports game ended just ten minutes ago and you want to know who won. Chatbots are trained on old text and often don't know what happened today. Search engines like Google crawl fresh news pages every few minutes. Which tool fits best for looking up the score right now?
answer: A search engine
choices: A search engine
A basic chatbot
A calculator
A photo editor
context: Basic chatbots don't see live data. A game that ended ten minutes ago is outside any chatbot's training cutoff. Search engines crawl the live web and will find news stories about the game. Some chatbot products bolt search on as a feature; when they do, they usually tell you. For 'what just happened' questions, search is the right tool.

question: A librarian warns a teenager never to share secrets with a free chatbot like ChatGPT, partly because of what the company may do with the text. What may become of anything typed in?
answer: Used to train future models
choices: Used to train future models
Translated into all languages
Mailed to your relatives
Posted in your school paper
context: Free chatbot services often use conversations to train later versions of their models, and their terms of service usually say so. Some paid or business plans switch this off. Anything truly private, especially identifiers and passwords, doesn't belong in a free chat box.

question: A friend dares a boy to paste his real street number into a chatbot 'to see what it knows.' Once a private detail like that is out, he cannot pull it back. What is the smart response?
answer: Don't paste your home address
choices: Don't paste your home address
Paste it and add phone number
Add your social security too
Add your bank password also
context: Don't paste personal identifiers — home address, phone, social security number, bank info — into free chatbot services. The conversation is logged. The data has value. It can be reviewed, repurposed, or exposed. 'Want to see what it knows about you' is a curiosity trap; the answer is rarely worth the data trail.

question: A caller who sounds just like your brother says he is in trouble and begs, 'Please don't tell Mom or Dad.' Fraud guides warn that scammers ask for secrecy for one main reason. What is it?
answer: So you won't check the story
choices: So Mom won't worry tonight
So police can't trace him
So you won't check the story
So the bank won't charge
context: Guidance based on Federal Trade Commission advice says con artists insist on secrecy to keep you from checking out their story. Check it with another relative or friend anyway, even if the caller told you to keep it secret.

question: A ninth-grader reads a surprising fact from a chatbot for his school report and wants to text it to friends right away. Chatbots sometimes state made-up facts with total confidence. What would verify it best?
answer: Check an established encyclopedia
choices: Check an established encyclopedia
Ask the chatbot again
Ask a second chatbot
Repeat it to a friend
context: Established sources — encyclopedias, government and university websites, major news organizations — are independent of any given chatbot. Asking the chatbot again or asking another chatbot doesn't give independent confirmation; they were often trained on the same data with the same errors. Real verification means a source the AI didn't draw from.

question: You're reading an article and notice em-dashes — the long horizontal lines used mid-sentence — appearing in nearly every paragraph. Human writers use em-dashes sparingly, but chatbots have been trained to lean on them heavily. That overuse is one common clue writers watch for. Heavy use of em-dashes is sometimes a telltale sign of:
answer: AI-generated writing
choices: AI-generated writing
An old printing press
A foreign translator
A very tired writer
context: Em-dash overuse is one of the famous AI writing tells, along with phrases like 'delve into,' 'tapestry of,' 'navigate the complexities,' and overly balanced sentence structure. Real human writers use em-dashes sometimes; AI-generated text uses them constantly. Spotting the pattern is a useful skill for reading online text critically.

question: A woman scrolling online sees a famous celebrity endorsing a new product. Something feels off, and the voice sounds a little flat. What is the reasonable assumption?
answer: It may well be a deepfake
choices: It may well be a deepfake
Real videos always look like that
All endorsements are deepfakes
Celebrities can't say 'no' to ads
context: AI-generated celebrity endorsements are a fast-growing scam category. The voice is often slightly off; the lip-sync drifts; the overall feel is uncanny. If you see a celebrity 'endorsing' a product on social media — especially a get-rich-quick or crypto scheme — assume deepfake until proven otherwise. Check the celebrity's actual verified accounts.

question: A voice like your aunt's says she is stranded and asks you to buy gift cards and read out the numbers. The Federal Trade Commission calls this a scam sign. Why do scammers want gift cards?
answer: The money is hard to get back
choices: They cost less than cash
Stores hide who bought them
Banks can't see them
The money is hard to get back
context: The FTC warns that scammers ask you to pay in ways that make it hard to recover your money: wiring it, sending cryptocurrency, or buying gift cards and handing over the card numbers and PINs. A real relative in trouble can wait while you call back.

question: A young man sits down to save money by filing his legal forms with only a chatbot's help. Chatbots can invent fake laws and court cases, and mistakes on such forms can cost thousands of dollars or lose a case. What is the smart caution?
answer: See a real lawyer for important paperwork
choices: See a real lawyer for important paperwork
Trust the chatbot completely
File it without reading first
Skip lawyers entirely forever
context: AI legal tools can produce documents that look professional but contain wrong citations (the 2023 New York lawyer case is famous), wrong jurisdiction-specific rules, and other errors that matter in court. For important legal matters, talk to a real lawyer. AI can help you prepare questions and understand basics; it shouldn't be your only counsel on something that matters.

question: A girl's chatbot answers her homework question with four pieces of information: a precise year-and-day from centuries ago, a general summary of the topic, a vocabulary word and the spelling of a common word. Chatbots handle broad topics and simple spellings pretty reliably. Which fact is most important for her to verify first?
answer: A specific historical date
choices: A specific historical date
A general topic summary
The word for an idea
How to spell a common word
context: Chatbots are most error-prone on specific facts — particular dates, specific numbers, specific citations. General topic summaries are usually OK at a high level. The fine details are where hallucinations cluster. Whenever a date, statistic, or specific citation matters for what you'll do with the information, verify it.

question: You spot an online photo of a smiling person. Something looks off — one earring is large and heavy, but the other is a tiny stud. AI image generators often slip small details in odd ways: mismatched jewelry, extra fingers, or teeth that blur together. This little flaw is most likely a:
answer: Mismatch sign of AI generation
choices: Mismatch sign of AI generation
Trendy new fashion statement
Defect of an old film camera
Sunlight playing optical tricks
context: AI image generators often produce asymmetric earrings, mismatched eye details, or other small details that don't match across left and right. Real photos of real people typically have matching pairs (or at least intentional mismatch). Asymmetric tiny details are a small but reliable AI-image tell.

question: AI voice cloning lets scammers copy your family member's voice from a short online clip, then call you pretending to be them. Families defend themselves by calling the person back directly, agreeing on a secret safe word, or asking a personal question only the real person would know. Out of these four options, which is NOT a safe defense?
answer: Trusting any familiar-sounding voice
choices: Trusting any familiar-sounding voice
Calling the person back directly
Having a family safe word
Asking a question only family knows
