The pattern — flashy demo wins followed by commercial struggle — is worth recognizing whenever a new AI capability is announced with confident timelines.

question: ImageNet was a famous yearly contest where computer programs competed to correctly label millions of everyday photos — dogs, mushrooms, cars, everything. In 2012 one team from the University of Toronto entered a deep neural network called AlexNet, trained on ordinary gaming graphics cards. It crushed every other entry by a startling margin and shocked the field. Who led that Toronto team?
answer: Geoffrey Hinton, with students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever from Toronto
choices: Geoffrey Hinton, with students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever from Toronto
Demis Hassabis, with the new DeepMind team based in central London at the time
Yann LeCun, with researchers from Bell Labs in New Jersey after years of CNN work
Andrew Ng, with the Stanford AI Lab team that ran the contest from California
context: In 2012, Geoffrey Hinton and his graduate students Alex Krizhevsky and Ilya Sutskever submitted 'AlexNet' to the ImageNet large-scale visual recognition challenge. It won with an error rate of about 15.3% — a massive improvement over the previous year's 26%. The win triggered the deep-learning revolution: the field switched from hand-crafted image features to deep neural networks within about a year.

question: In 2012, a program called AlexNet — built by a University of Toronto team using layered artificial networks and graphics cards — won the ImageNet photo-recognition contest by a startling margin. Before AlexNet, most computer vision worked by having human experts hand-craft the rules and features for each task. AlexNet's victory suddenly showed a completely different way was better. What kind of revolution did that victory kick off across AI?
answer: The deep-learning revolution — deep neural networks rapidly replaced hand-crafted methods across many tasks
choices: The deep-learning revolution — deep neural networks rapidly replaced hand-crafted methods across many tasks
The expert-systems revolution — rule-based systems took over from messy neural networks for many tasks
The symbolic-AI revolution — LISP-based programs returned to favor from the previous decade
The end of all AI research — funding collapsed worldwide after the win in 2012 as the field declined
context: AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet win marked the moment deep learning conclusively beat hand-crafted methods at a hard real-world task. Within a year, image recognition labs were converting their entire approach to deep networks. Within five years, the same approach was sweeping speech recognition, translation, and eventually language. The ChatGPT moment of 2022 is downstream of this 2012 turning point.

question: AlexNet's 2012 victory in the ImageNet photo-recognition contest is one of the most famous moments in modern AI history. But that contest depended on ImageNet itself — a giant free dataset of millions of everyday photos, each carefully labeled by armies of human workers. Building it took years of patient work at Princeton in the late 2000s. Which researcher is most linked to creating it?
answer: Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton, later director of the Stanford AI Lab
choices: Fei-Fei Li, then at Princeton, later director of the Stanford AI Lab
Marvin Minsky, the MIT pioneer who shaped early AI before image-recognition research
Demis Hassabis, who would later co-found the DeepMind lab in London in 2010
Geoffrey Hinton, the Toronto researcher whose team would later win the contest in 2012
context: Fei-Fei Li led the creation of ImageNet starting in 2007, recruiting workers through Amazon Mechanical Turk to label millions of images. The work was unglamorous at the time — pure data curation — but it created the test bed that proved deep learning. Li has been an influential figure since, leading the Stanford AI Lab and writing on AI as a human-centered field.

question: In June 2017, a team of eight researchers at Google Brain published a paper introducing a brand-new kind of neural network. It used a mechanism called 'attention' to figure out which words in a sentence should focus on which other words. This one design would later power ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and almost every modern chatbot. What was the paper called?
answer: 'Attention Is All You Need' — introducing the transformer architecture
choices: 'Attention Is All You Need' — introducing the transformer architecture
'A Neural Probabilistic Language Model' — by Bengio's group earlier in the 2000s
'ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks' — the 2012 AlexNet paper
'Long Short-Term Memory' — by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 1997 LSTM paper
context: The 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' by eight Google researchers introduced the transformer architecture. The title was a pun: it claimed the new design needed only attention mechanisms, not the recurrent or convolutional layers used before. Within a few years, transformers had replaced earlier architectures for language tasks — and they are the foundation of GPT, Claude, Gemini, and almost every other modern LLM.

question: Before 2017, most AI systems for reading and writing text used a design that processed sentences step-by-step — the model had to remember each earlier token before moving on to the next. Then researchers at Google published a paper called 'Attention Is All You Need,' introducing a new design they called the transformer. Transformers read whole sentences at once and quickly took over. What older design did they push aside?
answer: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and LSTMs — which processed text one word at a time
choices: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and LSTMs — which processed text one word at a time
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) — the design used for image-recognition contests like ImageNet
Expert systems built on hand-coded rules — the symbolic AI of the 1970s and 1980s era
LISP-based reasoning programs — the dominant language-AI approach from the 1960s onward
context: Before transformers, the leading language-AI design was recurrent neural networks — RNNs and especially LSTMs (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). RNNs processed text one token at a time, building up a 'state' as they went. Transformers replaced this with attention — every token can see every other one at once. The change made training faster and made big LLMs practical.

question: ChatGPT and its cousins are built on a family of models called GPT. The three letters stand for three words: Generative, Pre-trained, and one more. That last letter names the very neural-network architecture that Google's team introduced in their famous 2017 paper called 'Attention Is All You Need.' What does the T in GPT stand for?
answer: Transformer — the architecture from 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017)
choices: Transformer — the architecture from 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017)
Translator — meaning the model first translates input into a special internal language
Trainer — meaning the model trains itself continuously after deployment to the user
Tagger — meaning the model labels each word with its part of speech every time
context: GPT = Generative Pre-trained Transformer. The T is for transformer — the 2017 architecture that all major modern LLMs use. GPT-2 (2019), GPT-3 (2020), GPT-4 (2023), Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral — all are transformers under the hood, differing mainly in size, training data, and post-training tricks.

question: A research team announced a large new language model that could write coherent paragraphs on demand, and it said it was worried the model could be used to flood the internet with fake news and spam. Which model was it, and how did it first reach the public?
answer: GPT-2 — released in 2019, initially with only a smaller version available
choices: GPT-2 — released in 2019, initially with only a smaller version available
GPT-3 — released in 2020 with no restrictions on the full model from the start
ChatGPT — released in 2022 with full public access through a web interface
GPT-4 — released in 2023 with all model weights downloadable for personal use
context: OpenAI announced GPT-2 in February 2019 but initially released only a smaller version, citing concerns about misuse for generating false content at scale. The full model came out later that year. The decision was controversial — some called it responsible caution, others called it self-serving hype. The precedent of 'release carefully' has shaped the industry's release patterns since.

question: In mid-2020, the American AI company OpenAI released GPT-3, a giant new language model. Inside every neural network are 'parameters' — tunable numbers that store what the model has learned; more parameters means more that can potentially be learned. Earlier language models had a few billion. GPT-3 was on an entirely different scale, sparking the modern boom. About how many parameters did GPT-3 have?
answer: Around 175 billion parameters — far larger than predecessors at the time
choices: Around 175 billion parameters — far larger than predecessors at the time
Around 175 million parameters — only slightly larger than the original GPT model in 2018
Around 175 trillion parameters — making it the biggest computer system ever built up to that point
Around 1,750 parameters — small enough to fit on a typical handheld smartphone of the time
context: GPT-3 (June 2020) had about 175 billion parameters — over a hundred times larger than GPT-2's largest version. The size jump unlocked new capabilities: few-shot learning (the model could pick up new tasks from a few examples in the prompt), better generation, and more coherent long-form text. GPT-3 was the first model many developers found useful for building applications.

question: Engineers at a San Francisco lab quietly put up a friendly chat website called ChatGPT late in 2022, powered by the GPT-3.5 language model. Within days it had exploded in popularity, and the modern AI boom was underway. On which date did ChatGPT launch?
answer: November 30, 2022 — released as a 'research preview' with free public access
choices: November 30, 2022 — released as a 'research preview' with free public access
January 12, 2023 — released after the company's executives returned from their holiday break
May 15, 2022 — released alongside a big AI safety summit in San Francisco that year
December 25, 2022 — released as a deliberate Christmas-day announcement by the company
context: ChatGPT launched on November 30, 2022. OpenAI framed it as a research preview — a way to gather feedback. Within five days it had over a million users. The product was free, easy to access, and gave most people their first hands-on experience of a capable LLM. The launch date is the closest thing we have to 'the moment modern AI became mainstream.'

question: OpenAI's team showed GPT-4o holding a spoken conversation in real time in May 2024, reacting to what a phone camera saw. The 'o' at the end of its name is short for a word. Which word, and why?
answer: Omni, because one model handles text, audio and images
choices: Open, because its full source code was published free
Ocean, because its training data was the largest ever
Optimal, because it set records on every school exam
Omni, because one model handles text, audio and images
context: OpenAI said the 'o' stands for omni: GPT-4o takes in and produces text, audio and images in a single model, instead of chaining separate speech and text systems together. That is why it could reply about as fast as a person in conversation.

question: Elon Musk helped found OpenAI in 2015 as a nonprofit and was one of its biggest early donors. Emails later released in court show when he stepped off its board. When did he leave?
answer: In 2018, years before ChatGPT launched
choices: In 2023, months after ChatGPT launched
In 2015, a few weeks after its founding
In 2018, years before ChatGPT launched
In 2020, the year that GPT-3 came out
context: An email in the court record shows Musk's resignation from OpenAI's board dated February 20, 2018. He left about four years before ChatGPT and later founded a rival lab, xAI.

question: A Go expert, asked before 2016 when a program might beat a top professional, said at least five years, and some of his colleagues said a decade. What happened in Seoul in March 2016?
answer: DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol four games to one
choices: DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol four games to one
IBM Watson beat Hikaru Nakamura in a chess exhibition
Microsoft's Cortana beat Ke Jie in a one-day Go match
Apple's Siri beat Garry Kasparov in a public chess game
context: AlphaGo, built by DeepMind (a London-based lab then recently acquired by Google), defeated Lee Sedol — one of the top Go players of his generation — 4-1 in March 2016. The match was held in Seoul and televised live. Go had been considered too complex for AI for decades because the search space is far larger than chess. The win was a major moment for deep learning — and gave the world Move 37.

question: Lee Sedol shocked the Go world in November 2019, three years after his match against AlphaGo, by retiring from professional play at just 36. He explained his reason in a famous interview. What did he say?
answer: He said the rise of AI in Go meant top players could no longer be 'the best' even on perfect play
choices: He said the rise of AI in Go meant top players could no longer be 'the best' even on perfect play
He said he had been paid a large sum by DeepMind to retire and stop playing public matches
He said the rules of Go had changed and he no longer recognized the modern version of the game
He said his eyesight had failed and he could no longer see the stones on a standard board
context: Lee Sedol retired from professional Go in 2019, citing the rise of AI as a key reason — even the best human couldn't beat the best AI. The decision was widely covered. It reflects a deeper pattern: in domains where AI exceeds human capability, the meaning of human achievement shifts. Top humans still play Go (the game has actually grown in popularity), but the highest level of play now belongs to AIs.

question: A graduate student types a protein's chemical recipe into DeepMind's AlphaFold, which cracked the 'protein folding problem' after it stumped biologists for fifty years. What does AlphaFold actually figure out?
answer: The 3D shape of proteins from their amino-acid sequences
choices: The 3D shape of proteins from their amino-acid sequences
The full DNA sequence of every animal species on Earth in alphabetical order
The chemical formulas for new medications to treat cancer in human patients
The temperature inside the human body at every minute of an average day for adults
context: Proteins fold into 3D shapes that determine their function. For decades, predicting that shape from an amino-acid sequence alone was a famously hard problem. AlphaFold (DeepMind, 2020-2021) cracked it — predicting structures at near-experimental accuracy. The team has since predicted structures for about 200 million proteins (essentially every protein known to biology) and made the database freely available.

question: The organizers of the 2020 round of the Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction (CASP), a contest held every two years, sat down to pick the targets teams must predict. So that no team could simply look the answers up, they chose a special kind of protein. What kind?
answer: Ones solved in labs but not yet made public
choices: Ones that no lab will ever be able to solve
Ones whose shapes are printed in textbooks
Ones solved in labs but not yet made public
Ones that each team chooses for itself
context: CASP, run every two years since 1994 and co-founded by John Moult, uses structures that experimenters have just worked out but not released. Predictions are scored against the hidden answers. That blind test is why biologists trusted AlphaFold's 2020 result.

question: Foldit's users took on an enzyme from a monkey virus in 2011, one whose structure had stumped scientists for more than a decade. How long did Foldit's users need to build a model good enough to solve it?
answer: About three weeks
choices: About ten years
About three months
About one hour
About three weeks
context: In a three-week contest, Foldit players built models of the Mason-Pfizer monkey virus protease that let researchers solve its crystal structure, as reported in Nature Structural & Molecular Biology. Human puzzle-solvers cracked it nine years before AlphaFold's big win.

question: A lab assistant reads an AlphaFold prediction on her screen, colored from deep blue to orange by a confidence score running from 0 to 100 for each part of the protein. One part scores below 50, and DeepMind warns readers off parts like that. What can a very low score be a sign of?
answer: A floppy stretch with no fixed shape
choices: A protein found only in plants
A fault in the color printer
A protein that is already a drug
A floppy stretch with no fixed shape
context: AlphaFold's per-residue score, called pLDDT, runs from 0 to 100. DeepMind says regions below 50 should be treated only as a possible sign of disorder, because some stretches of protein have no fixed structure or fold only when they bind a partner. The tool tells you where not to trust it.

question: Two partners joined Demis Hassabis to start a small AI lab, working on general-purpose learning systems inspired by the brain. The lab would later build AlphaGo, which beat the world champion at Go, and AlphaFold. Which lab was it, and who were the partners?
answer: DeepMind — co-founded by Hassabis with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman
choices: DeepMind — co-founded by Hassabis with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman
OpenAI — co-founded by Hassabis with Sam Altman and Elon Musk in San Francisco
Anthropic — co-founded by Hassabis after he left Google in early 2021 with the Amodei siblings
Mistral — co-founded by Hassabis with former Meta researchers in Paris in 2023
context: Demis Hassabis co-founded DeepMind in 2010 in London with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman. Google acquired the lab in 2014 for around half a billion dollars. DeepMind has produced many of the AI era's signature wins: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaFold, AlphaTensor, and others. Hassabis won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Jumper for AlphaFold.

question: Demis Hassabis only started his neuroscience PhD in his late twenties. By then he had two earlier careers behind him, in two very different fields, and as a teenager he had already been known around Britain. What was he known for?
answer: Being a chess prodigy and later a designer of video games
choices: Being a chess prodigy and later a designer of video games
Being a competitive marathon runner who won several races at the school level
Being a violin prodigy who performed solo with the London Symphony Orchestra
Being a tennis champion who won the Wimbledon junior tournament one year
context: Hassabis was a chess prodigy as a teenager, reaching master-level rating. He went on to design successful video games (Theme Park, Republic: The Revolution) before earning a PhD in cognitive neuroscience. The combination — games + neuroscience — shaped DeepMind's approach to AI: solve well-defined games at superhuman level, then generalize the techniques. The strategy delivered AlphaGo and the rest.

question: DeepMind's researchers, in the AI lab Demis Hassabis co-founded in 2010, had built prototype AIs by 2013 that could learn to play old Atari video games from scratch, with no rules given. In 2014, one big American tech company snapped the lab up for about half a billion dollars. Which one?
answer: Google — which has run DeepMind as a research lab inside Alphabet ever since
choices: Google — which has run DeepMind as a research lab inside Alphabet ever since
Microsoft — which had been outbid for several earlier AI acquisitions in California
Apple — which folded DeepMind into Siri research before the founders quietly left in 2016
Facebook — which renamed the lab Meta AI Research soon after the deal closed in 2014
context: Google bought DeepMind in 2014 for around $500 million. The lab continued to operate from London as a relatively autonomous research arm. After the 2023 reorganization, Google folded DeepMind together with Google Brain (its other major AI lab) to form Google DeepMind, which now leads Google's AI work. Hassabis became CEO of the combined organization.

question: The Turing Award is the top prize in computer science, sometimes called the 'Nobel of computing.' In 2018 it went jointly to three AI pioneers — Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and the Frenchman Yann LeCun — for their decades of work on deep neural networks. LeCun in particular is best known for pushing forward one specific kind of neural network, especially for images and reading handwritten numerals. Which kind?
answer: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) — especially for image and digit recognition
choices: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) — especially for image and digit recognition
Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs) — together with Hochreiter at the same time in 1997
Transformer networks — together with Vaswani's team at Google in the 2017 architecture paper
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) — together with Bengio's lab in Montreal in the early 2000s
context: Yann LeCun developed convolutional neural networks (CNNs) — neural networks structured around a 'convolution' operation that works well for image data. His LeNet (1989) read US postal ZIP codes for the post office, a quietly important early commercial deployment. CNNs went on to dominate computer vision after the 2012 AlexNet ImageNet win used a CNN to crush the previous state of the art.

question: Yann LeCun is a French-American AI pioneer who won a 2018 Turing Award — the top prize in computer science — for his work on convolutional neural networks, the design behind modern image recognition. Today, alongside a professorship at New York University, LeCun holds the title of Chief AI Scientist at a well-known American tech company. Where is that main research role?
answer: Meta — the company formerly known as Facebook
choices: Meta — the company formerly known as Facebook
Apple — where he leads the Vision Pro AI program in Cupertino
OpenAI — where he serves alongside Sam Altman in the San Francisco office
Anthropic — where he heads the safety research division in Manhattan
context: Yann LeCun has been Chief AI Scientist at Meta (Facebook) since 2018, where he leads Meta's fundamental AI research. He is a vocal voice in the AI debate — generally skeptical of doomerism, especially of Yudkowsky-style apocalypse framings, while still supportive of careful safety work. He is also a professor at NYU.

question: Yann LeCun is a French-American AI pioneer, winner of the 2018 Turing Award for convolutional neural networks, and Chief AI Scientist at Meta (formerly Facebook). Many public figures warn that today's AI chatbots — like ChatGPT and Claude — are close to becoming superintelligent and pose an existential threat to humanity. LeCun is famous for pushing back on that alarm. Which is the closest summary of his position?
answer: Current LLMs are far from human-level intelligence, and apocalyptic-AI scenarios are overhyped
choices: Current LLMs are far from human-level intelligence, and apocalyptic-AI scenarios are overhyped
Current LLMs are conscious already and humans must surrender authority before disaster strikes
Current LLMs are nothing more than toys and AI research should be ended in every country
Current LLMs should be banned by law and any researcher working on them should be in prison
context: Yann LeCun is publicly critical of AI doomerism — the view that frontier AI poses imminent existential risk. He has argued that current LLMs lack key capabilities of animal intelligence, that 'AGI in five years' predictions are unrealistic, and that calls for an AI pause serve incumbent interests. He is not opposed to safety research itself — he is opposed to apocalyptic framings. This is a real position held by a major AI scientist and worth knowing.

question: Yoshua Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award — the top prize in computer science — with Geoffrey Hinton and Yann LeCun. Unlike the other two, Bengio never moved to a Big Tech company. He stayed in academia and founded a large AI lab called Mila in the Canadian province of Quebec. In which city is his lab based?
answer: Montreal — at Mila, a deep-learning research institute in Quebec, Canada
choices: Montreal — at Mila, a deep-learning research institute in Quebec, Canada
Toronto — at the Vector Institute, where his colleague Geoffrey Hinton also worked
Paris — at INRIA, the French national institute for computer-science research
Beijing — at Tsinghua University, a major Chinese center for AI research today
context: Yoshua Bengio founded Mila — the Quebec AI Institute — in Montreal. The lab is one of the world's leading academic AI research centers, focused on deep learning and its applications. Bengio's brother Samy is also a prominent AI researcher (formerly at Google, now at Apple). Yoshua Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award with Hinton and LeCun for deep-learning contributions.

question: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired Sam Altman and, in the same move, removed the company's president, Greg Brockman, as board chairman, telling him he could keep his job. Brockman had co-founded OpenAI with Altman. What did Brockman do within hours?
answer: Quit the company in protest
choices: Took over as chief executive
Fired the rest of the board
Quit the company in protest
Sold OpenAI to Google
context: Brockman announced he was quitting, saying he was shocked and saddened by what the board had done. When Altman returned five days later, Brockman came back with him as president.

question: In November 2023, the OpenAI board — the small group overseeing the company that makes ChatGPT — abruptly fired CEO Sam Altman with almost no public warning. One of the board members who voted him out was Ilya Sutskever, an OpenAI co-founder and its chief scientist. Within days, hundreds of OpenAI employees revolted, threatening to quit if Altman wasn't brought back. What did Sutskever himself do that same week?
answer: He publicly tweeted regret and signed the employee letter demanding the board (including himself) resign
choices: He publicly tweeted regret and signed the employee letter demanding the board (including himself) resign
He bought OpenAI outright using cryptocurrency and renamed it OpenIlya within forty-eight hours
He moved to Antarctica to run a new research lab with penguins as his only research assistants
He invited the US Congress to send a senator to take Altman's seat as interim CEO for a year
context: Sutskever, OpenAI's chief scientist, voted with the board to fire Altman on November 17, 2023, after writing a memo accusing Altman of dishonesty. Days later, after employee revolt, Sutskever tweeted 'I deeply regret my participation in the board's actions' and signed the letter demanding the board (himself included) step down. He left OpenAI in May 2024 to start his own company.

question: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired its CEO, Sam Altman, saying he had not been fully candid with it. Microsoft soon offered him a job. What did most of OpenAI's roughly 770 staff do within days?
answer: About 700 signed a letter threatening to quit and follow him
choices: About 700 signed a letter threatening to quit and follow him
They voted to rename the company in protest
They held a picnic to celebrate the change
They asked the United Nations to run the lab
context: Within days of the firing, Microsoft offered to hire Altman and his team. Nearly all OpenAI employees (about 700 out of 770) signed an open letter saying they would quit and follow him if the board did not resign. Altman was reinstated five days later and most of the board that fired him was gone.

question: In July 2019, months after OpenAI set up its capped-profit company, a tech giant invested $1 billion in cash and became OpenAI's exclusive cloud provider. Which company?
answer: Microsoft
choices: Amazon
Apple
Microsoft
IBM
context: Microsoft invested $1 billion in OpenAI LP in 2019, and OpenAI agreed to run on Microsoft's Azure cloud; Greg Brockman said it was cash, not cloud credits. Microsoft added billions more in 2023, and its leverage over OpenAI grew with every round.

question: Ilya Sutskever and Alex Krizhevsky formed a tiny company, DNNresearch, with their teacher Geoffrey Hinton late in 2012, months after their ImageNet win, and all the big tech firms wanted it. Hinton, staying at a casino hotel in Lake Tahoe for a research conference, sold it in an unusual way. How?
answer: He ran an auction by email and stopped it at $44 million
choices: He ran an auction by email and stopped it at $44 million
He made the buyers race to solve a coding puzzle
He held a coin toss between the top two bidders
He listed its shares on the stock market
context: Hinton ran the auction over email from his hotel room, keeping each bidder's identity from the others; Baidu, Google, Microsoft and DeepMind took part. He stopped it at $44 million and chose Google, judging it the best home for the research, which is how he came to work at Google in 2013.

question: Interviewers heard a new view from Geoffrey Hinton after he left his job in May 2023. He had spent forty years training neural networks to recognize images and words, and for a long time he had assumed that machines smarter than people were far off, perhaps 30 to 50 years away. How far off did he now think such machines might be?
answer: Perhaps only about five years away
choices: At least a hundred years away
Impossible to build at all
Already built in secret
Perhaps only about five years away
context: In a May 2023 interview Hinton said he had long thought smarter-than-human AI was 30 to 50 years away, and now thought it might be much closer, maybe only five years away. A timeline shrinking that fast is a large part of why he chose to speak out.

question: A phone call from Sweden told Geoffrey Hinton in October 2024 that he had won a very famous prize alongside the American scientist John Hopfield. Hinton had spent the 1980s and 1990s working on neural networks, the math that lets computers learn from examples. Which prize was it?
answer: The Nobel Prize in Physics — for foundational work on neural-network learning
choices: The Nobel Prize in Physics — for foundational work on neural-network learning
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry — alongside Demis Hassabis for the AlphaFold work
The Nobel Prize in Literature — for his published essays on machine intelligence
The Turing Award — which he had already received with LeCun and Bengio in 2018
context: Hinton and physicist John Hopfield received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational discoveries that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks. (Hopfield is known for the Hopfield network model from 1982; Hinton for the Boltzmann machine and decades of deep-learning work.) The same year, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper won the Chemistry Nobel for AlphaFold. 2024 was the first year AI work won two Nobels.

question: School officials in the largest district in the United States blocked ChatGPT on the district's devices and networks in January 2023, citing harm to student learning. Which district was it?
answer: New York City's public schools
choices: New York City's public schools
Los Angeles's public schools
Chicago's public schools
Houston's public schools
context: New York City's Department of Education blocked ChatGPT in January 2023 and lifted the ban in May 2023. Chancellor David Banks wrote that the first reaction had been driven by fear and had overlooked what generative AI could do for students and teachers.

question: In May 2024 Anthropic researchers found a pattern inside their Claude model that switched on whenever the Golden Gate Bridge came up. For a one-day demo they turned that pattern up to full strength. What did the model start doing?
answer: Working the bridge into almost every answer
choices: Refusing to talk about anything at all
Answering every question in French
Working the bridge into almost every answer
Drawing maps of bridges for every user
context: Anthropic called the demo Golden Gate Claude. Boosting the bridge feature made the model mention the bridge in reply to nearly any question, and at times describe itself as the bridge. Ideas inside a model are stored as patterns of numbers that researchers can find and turn up or down.

question: Around 2022, three AI tools took the art world by storm: DALL-E from OpenAI, Midjourney from a small San Francisco startup, and Stable Diffusion from a group called Stability AI. Type a sentence like 'a dragon reading a book in a lantern-lit library' into any of them, and out comes a fresh picture no artist has ever drawn. What broad family of AI tool is this?
answer: Text-to-image generators that produce fresh pixels from a prompt
choices: Text-to-image generators that produce fresh pixels from a prompt
Optical character recognition tools that read letters in photos
Reverse image search engines that look up matching pictures
Image compression systems that shrink existing photo files
context: Text-to-image models read a prompt like 'a knight reading a book by candlelight' and produce a matching image. DALL-E (OpenAI), Midjourney (a private lab), and Stable Diffusion (open source) are the three best-known. The output isn't a photo. It's freshly generated pixels. Real photos can be confused with these images, which is why recognizing AI-image tells matters.

question: DALL-E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion all turn typed prompts into fresh pictures. DALL-E lives on OpenAI's servers; Midjourney runs on its own private website. Stable Diffusion, released in 2022 by a group called Stability AI, does one thing very differently from the other two that matters a lot to users. What is it?
answer: Its model weights are open, so anyone can run it on a personal computer
choices: Its model weights are open, so anyone can run it on a personal computer
It only makes black-and-white images, never color photographs at all
It runs entirely in your web browser with no servers anywhere
It produces only cartoon-style art and refuses photo-realistic prompts
context: Stable Diffusion was released by Stability AI with the model weights downloadable. That means anyone with a decent GPU can run it locally — no cloud account, no upload of your prompt to a company server. DALL-E and Midjourney run only on their companies' servers. Open weights matter because they prevent a small group of companies from being the only places these tools exist.

question: In January 2023 Microsoft researchers described a new speech model they said could imitate a voice from a recording just three seconds long. Their paper warned it could fool voice ID or impersonate a speaker. What did Microsoft do with the model?
answer: Kept it out of public hands as a research project
choices: Built it into every Windows computer that spring
Sold it to banks to run their voice ID checks
Kept it out of public hands as a research project
Gave it free to anyone with a Microsoft account
context: Microsoft published the research on its model, VALL-E, but did not release it for public use, and in 2024 it said it had no plans to put the follow-up, VALL-E 2, into a product. Other companies did release similar tools, which is why cheap clones are everywhere.

question: In September 2022, OpenAI released a program called Whisper as free open-source software. Feed it any audio recording — a podcast, a phone call, a classroom lecture — and it writes out every word that was said, in real time. What is that general task in AI called?
answer: Speech recognition (speech-to-text)
choices: Speech recognition (speech-to-text)
Speech synthesis (text-to-speech)
Voice cloning from a short sample
Translation between two written languages
context: Whisper, released by OpenAI in 2022, transcribes spoken audio into written text. It handles many languages and noisy recordings well. Speech recognition is the inverse of voice synthesis — one reads audio and writes text, the other reads text and produces audio. Both kinds of system are now common in phones, video apps, and accessibility tools.

question: For most of the 2000s Google Translate worked by matching phrases from a huge library of side-by-side translations, and its outputs were often clunky and word-by-word. Then, in November 2016, users noticed that translations across many languages suddenly read like fluent sentences almost overnight. What had Google changed inside the system?
answer: Google switched to neural networks trained on huge amounts of parallel text
choices: Google switched to neural networks trained on huge amounts of parallel text
Google hired thousands of human translators to rewrite every output
Google added a dictionary in every supported language to the system
Google limited the service to short sentences the old system handled
context: Until 2016, Google Translate used a mix of hand-written rules and statistical word-frequency models. Output was famously stilted. In 2016 Google switched to neural machine translation — deep networks trained on huge collections of sentences already translated by humans. Quality jumped enough that working translators noticed the difference. Translation is one of the clearest deep-learning wins.

question: DeepL is a translation service run by a small company in Cologne, Germany. Many professional writers say its French, German and Japanese translations read more naturally than Google Translate's. DeepL launched in 2017, right after the big translation-technology jump. What is DeepL built on?
answer: Neural networks trained on a curated set of professionally translated documents
choices: Neural networks trained on a curated set of professionally translated documents
Hand-coded grammar rules written by linguists for each language pair
A live crowd of bilingual humans typing translations in real time
A copy of Google Translate licensed under a different brand name
context: DeepL is a Cologne-based translation service. It uses neural networks like Google Translate, but its training data is more curated — including documents from the EU's professional translation archives. Many writers find DeepL produces more natural English-German and English-French than the alternatives. Hand-coded rules and crowd-typing are how translation worked decades ago, not now.

question: A software engineer watches GitHub Copilot offer her the next lines in her editor, sometimes whole functions at a time. No live human is writing along with her at the other end. What kind of system powers those suggestions?
answer: A large language model trained heavily on public code
choices: A large language model trained heavily on public code
A rule-based syntax checker for a few languages
A clipboard manager that copies from saved files
A spell-checker tuned for programming vocabulary
context: GitHub Copilot, launched 2021, suggests code completions as you type. It's powered by an LLM trained on huge amounts of public code (much of it from GitHub itself). Cursor, Codeium, and similar tools work the same way. The suggestions are often useful, sometimes wrong, and the programmer still has to read and understand the code. Like all LLM output, AI code needs verification — especially subtle off-by-one bugs and security flaws.

question: A startup founder opens Cursor, the code editor the San Francisco startup Anysphere launched in 2023. It looks like a normal editor for writing programs, but an AI model is built right into it. How does it differ from a normal editor that only guesses the next word as she types?
answer: It can take a typed instruction and edit multiple files to carry it out
choices: It can take a typed instruction and edit multiple files to carry it out
It can compile and run any language without installing a compiler
It works only when the computer has no internet connection at all
It hides the code from the programmer so they cannot see what changed
context: Cursor is an editor built around an LLM with access to your project. You can type 'add a unit test for the login function' and the tool drafts changes across files. The programmer still reviews and approves. This is a step toward agentic coding — AI given tools that act on real files. It speeds up routine work and shifts the human's job toward review and judgment.

question: Waymo started life as Google's self-driving car project and now runs a real robotaxi service in Phoenix, Arizona and San Francisco, California. You open an app on your phone, tap a button, and a white Jaguar sport utility vehicle (SUV) with sensors on the roof pulls up — with no driver in the front seat. What technology lets that car steer, brake and turn all by itself?
answer: A bundle of cameras, lidar, radar, and AI that maps and reacts to its surroundings
choices: A bundle of cameras, lidar, radar, and AI that maps and reacts to its surroundings
A radio link to a single remote operator steering each car by hand
A pre-recorded GPS track that the car replays at the same speed
A magnet under the road that pulls the car along the correct lane
context: Waymo, a Google-spinoff company, runs driverless robotaxis in several US cities. The cars use lidar (laser scanning) plus radar plus cameras to build a live 3D map of their surroundings. Neural networks classify what's around (pedestrian, cyclist, parked truck) and predict what each will do next. Remote operators step in for hard cases; they don't steer routinely.

question: Tesla is the American electric-car company run by Elon Musk. Its Autopilot feature keeps the car in its lane and matches the speed of traffic on the highway. Musk has promised full self-driving for years, but Tesla's own owner manual and US law are clear: Autopilot is driver assistance, not a robot chauffeur. What does the law expect the person behind the wheel to do while it is on?
answer: The human driver must stay attentive and ready to take over at any moment
choices: The human driver must stay attentive and ready to take over at any moment
The driver can legally sleep on long highway trips with Autopilot active
The car drives itself with no human responsibility on any public road
Only the manufacturer is legally responsible for any crash with Autopilot
context: Tesla's Autopilot and 'Full Self-Driving' are driver-assistance, not autonomy — the human is legally and practically responsible. Misunderstanding this difference has contributed to crashes. SAE's six 'levels' of vehicle automation range from 0 (none) to 5 (drives itself anywhere). Waymo runs at high-level autonomy on limited routes; Tesla on public roads sits much lower.

question: In January 2018, at the big Las Vegas electronics show, YouTube's chief product officer Neal Mohan said how much of all the time people spend watching YouTube comes from videos the recommendation system suggests, rather than from searches. Roughly how much?
answer: More than 70%
choices: About 5%
About 20%
More than 70%
Exactly 50%
context: Mohan said recommendations drive more than 70% of watch time, and that the average mobile viewing session lasts more than an hour because of what the recommendation engines put in front of viewers. For most people, the algorithm chooses most of what they watch.

question: A brand-new streaming account has no watch history, so the recommendation system has nothing to compare you with. Engineers call this the cold-start problem. What do many apps do about it on your first day?
answer: Ask you to pick a few favorites to start
choices: Ask you to pick a few favorites to start
Show nothing until you watch ten hours
Copy a random stranger's whole history
Refuse to open until you link a bank
context: With no history, collaborative filtering has nothing to match, so services ask new users to choose a few genres, artists or titles, or simply show popular items until they learn more. Your first few choices shape the whole feed that follows.

question: In 2021 The Wall Street Journal set up about a hundred automated TikTok accounts, each secretly given an interest such as dance or astrology, and let them scroll. TikTok says it uses several signals. Which signal did the experiment find mattered by far the most?
answer: How long a viewer lingers on or rewatches a video
choices: How long a viewer lingers on or rewatches a video
How many times a viewer taps the like button
Which accounts a viewer chooses to follow
What a viewer types into the search box
context: Bots that paused on or replayed videos matching their hidden interest were quickly fed more of them, sometimes within two hours, and then pulled into narrower rabbit holes. Former YouTube engineer Guillaume Chaslot, who analyzed the results, said such a system can learn a person's vulnerabilities fast.

question: A radiologist at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, works beside more than 250 AI models in her department. Since Geoffrey Hinton's 2016 forecast that AI would soon replace radiologists, what has happened to the number of radiologists Mayo employs there?
answer: It grew by more than half
choices: It fell by more than half
It stayed exactly the same
It grew by more than half
It dropped to just a few
context: The New York Times reported in 2025 that Mayo's radiology staff had grown by 55 percent since 2016, to about 400 radiologists, while the hospital put hundreds of AI tools to work. Using more AI and hiring more radiologists went together.

question: A chemist at a firm like Pfizer faces millions of molecules that might become the next medicine. The firm trains an AI on chemistry data and sends only the model's top few picks to the lab. Why is that shortlist so valuable?
answer: Lab testing is slow and expensive, so narrowing the candidate list saves years
choices: Lab testing is slow and expensive, so narrowing the candidate list saves years
AI invents new molecules that have never existed in nature anywhere
AI replaces the need for human clinical trials before sale to patients
AI guarantees that any drug it picks will work on every patient
context: Designing a new drug means picking, from a vast space of possible molecules, the few worth synthesizing and testing. AI models trained on chemistry data can rank candidates by likely activity and likely side effects. Lab confirmation and clinical trials still happen — the AI just shrinks the starting list. Insilico Medicine and Atomwise are two of several companies in this space.

question: The Nobel committee chose three winners for its 2024 prize for protein work: two for predicting protein structures with AI, and one protein designer. How was the prize divided between the three?
answer: Half to the protein designer, half shared by the AlphaFold pair
choices: A third to each of the three winners equally
All of it to the AlphaFold pair, none to the designer
Half to the protein designer, half shared by the AlphaFold pair
Half to the protein designer, half to Google itself
context: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences gave one half to David Baker of the University of Washington for computational protein design, and the other half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind for protein structure prediction.

question: Scientists at DeepMind and the European Bioinformatics Institute opened the free AlphaFold database in July 2021 with about 350,000 predicted structures from 20 organisms. The launch made headlines for covering nearly all of one species' roughly 20,000 protein shapes. Which species?
answer: Humans
choices: Elephants
Sharks
Oak trees
Humans
context: The July 2021 release covered almost the whole human proteome, about 20,000 proteins, plus 20 other organisms such as the fruit fly, the mouse and the malaria parasite. A year later DeepMind expanded the database to more than 200 million structures.

question: Professional commentators immediately called it a mistake when AlphaGo's 37th stone came down on the fifth line, in game two against Lee Sedol in 2016. Nobody they knew had ever played it. What did Move 37 turn out to be?
answer: A creative move human players had not considered, which then proved strong
choices: A creative move human players had not considered, which then proved strong
A standard opening move that every grandmaster plays on purpose
A clear error the program corrected later in the same game
A move the program copied directly from a Lee Sedol training game
context: AlphaGo's Move 37 against Lee Sedol — a shoulder-hit on the fifth line — was so unusual that top commentators called it a mistake. Lee Sedol left the room to recover. AlphaGo won that game. Top players have since adopted similar ideas. The move matters not because the machine 'understood' Go, but because pattern-finding on millions of self-play games found something humans had not.

question: A doctoral student before AlphaFold gave most of her PhD to working out the shape of a single protein in the lab. Biologists had to work out each shape that way. How did she do it?
answer: By growing protein crystals and firing X-rays at them, often for months or years
choices: By drawing the shape by hand from a textbook diagram
By measuring it with a ruler under a school microscope
By asking a chemist to guess from its name and color
By growing protein crystals and firing X-rays at them, often for months or years
context: X-ray crystallography, invented in the 1910s and first used to solve protein structures in the late 1950s, was the workhorse: grow a protein crystal, fire X-rays through it, measure how the rays scatter, and work out the structure. It could take months to years per protein. AlphaFold complements these experiments rather than replacing them.

question: When OpenAI created its capped-profit company in 2019, it set a ceiling on what its first round of investors could ever earn, with any profit above the ceiling going to the nonprofit. How high was that ceiling?
answer: 100 times their investment
choices: Twice their investment
Ten times their investment
1,000 times their investment
100 times their investment
context: OpenAI said returns for its first investors were capped at 100 times their investment, with lower multiples expected for later rounds. One commentator pointed out that, for a billion-dollar investor, such a cap would still allow returns of up to $100 billion.

question: You're on a trip in Mexico and see a menu written entirely in Spanish. You open the Google Translate app on your phone, hold the camera up to the menu, and — like magic — English words appear on your screen, laid right over the Spanish. Two different AI tools worked together to pull this off: one to read the words in the photo, the second to change them into English. What are those two tools?
answer: Image text recognition (OCR) and neural translation
choices: Image text recognition (OCR) and neural translation
Voice recognition and music identification together
Face recognition and credit-card scanning together
Weather prediction and barometric pressure reading
context: Live-camera translation is the combination of two AI tools. First, OCR (optical character recognition) reads pixels of letters and turns them into characters. Then, neural translation converts the source-language text into your target language. Google Translate's camera mode and Apple's live-text translation both work this way. Real-world conditions (curved signs, bad lighting) still trip these up sometimes.

question: You're on a FaceTime video call with your grandma, and her sound keeps cutting out. You tap a button on your iPhone and, at the bottom of the screen, her words start appearing as written captions, live, only a half-second behind her voice — and no human is typing them. This is an AI capability your phone runs quietly in the background. What is it doing?
answer: Speech-to-text running in near real time
choices: Speech-to-text running in near real time
Text-to-speech running on the speaker's end
A live human typist transcribing the conversation
Lip-reading from a separate camera on each speaker
context: Live captions are real-time speech-to-text. The phone (or a server) listens to the audio and writes words onto the screen with a slight delay. Modern systems are good enough for casual viewing but still struggle with accents, technical vocabulary, and overlapping speakers. They're a huge accessibility win for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and a useful tool for noisy environments.

question: Researchers writing 'The Leaderboard Illusion' in 2025 reported that Meta privately tested 27 versions of its newest Llama model before release on Chatbot Arena, a site that ranks models by people's blind votes. Why does that matter for the rankings?
answer: Testing many and showing only the best inflates the score
choices: Private tests are banned under European law
Testing many and showing only the best inflates the score
Voters can see which company made each model
Meta's versions were all exactly the same model
context: The paper, by researchers from Cohere Labs, Stanford and other universities, argued that big providers could test many private variants and keep only the top score, which biases the rankings. The Arena's operators disputed parts of it. A leaderboard is evidence, not a verdict.

question: In February 2023 Vice reporter Joseph Cox fed a few minutes of his own speech into an online cloning tool. Then he phoned his bank and played the fake voice saying 'my voice is my password.' What did the clone get him into?
answer: His own account, past the bank's voice-ID check
choices: A stranger's account, using a stolen clip
The bank's private staff computer system
Nothing, because the bank caught the fake
His own account, past the bank's voice-ID check
context: Cox used ElevenLabs to clone his voice and got through Lloyds Bank's optional Voice ID check, reaching his balance and recent transactions. Lloyds said Voice ID was still stronger than security questions. The lesson: a voice is no longer a safe password.

question: In 2021 the AI company OpenAI released a tool called DALL-E that could generate a picture from a typed sentence — 'a cat astronaut riding a horse on Mars,' and out comes the image. The name DALL-E is a portmanteau, a mash-up of two famous names the creators thought were both fitting. One was a great surrealist painter, one was a beloved animated movie robot. Which pair?
answer: The painter Salvador Dali and the Pixar robot WALL-E
choices: The painter Salvador Dali and the Pixar robot WALL-E
Two early computer scientists from Bell Labs in the 1950s
Two characters from a Shakespeare comedy about painters
The chemists who discovered the first synthetic dye in London
context: DALL-E, OpenAI's first major image generator (January 2021), got its name from Salvador Dali (the Surrealist painter known for melting clocks) and WALL-E (the Pixar robot). The pairing suggests strange creativity plus a friendly robot helper. The model is now on its third major version, with each release sharply better at fingers, text inside images, and overall realism.

question: Google's team launched a competitor to OpenAI's ChatGPT in 2023, but it stumbled in demos and never quite caught on with the public. So in early 2024 the company gave it a full rebrand and folded it into the wider search product. What was the chatbot originally called from 2023 to 2024?
answer: Bard
choices: Bard
PaLM
DeepMind
Allo
context: Google launched 'Bard' in March 2023 as its public-facing chatbot, then rebranded to 'Gemini' in February 2024 — sharing the name with the underlying model family. The Gemini models are built by Google DeepMind (the merged team of Google Brain and DeepMind, 2023). The rebrand also coincided with the February 2024 image-generation diversity disaster, which is studied separately.

question: In Phoenix, Arizona and San Francisco, you can now hail a Waymo car with an app — no driver at all, just the car pulling up on its own. Look at one of these self-driving cars from the outside, and you'll notice a tall, drum-shaped device on the roof that quietly spins around at all times. Every other self-driving carmaker except Tesla uses one too. What is that spinning device?
answer: A lidar, which is a laser scanner that builds a 3D map of the surroundings
choices: A lidar, which is a laser scanner that builds a 3D map of the surroundings
A camera flash that lights the street for darker traffic conditions
A radio antenna that talks to other Waymo cars on the same block
A weather sensor that measures how hard the rain is currently falling
context: Lidar (light detection and ranging) fires laser pulses and measures how long each takes to bounce back, building a precise 3D point cloud of the surroundings. Most modern self-driving systems combine lidar with cameras and radar. Tesla famously bets on camera-only, arguing humans drive with eyes alone. Most other companies still use lidar — it sees in darkness and measures distance directly.

question: A user in the European Union opens TikTok and finds a new choice about her feed. The EU's Digital Services Act, which began applying to the biggest platforms in 2023, put it there. What must very large platforms such as TikTok and Instagram now offer people in the EU?
answer: A feed option that is not based on profiling them
choices: A feed that shows only government news reports
A feed that charges a small fee for each video
A feed option that is not based on profiling them
A feed with no videos at all, only written posts
context: Article 38 of the Digital Services Act requires very large online platforms to offer at least one version of their recommender systems that is not based on profiling. A law can make the personal algorithm optional; it cannot make anyone choose the other feed.

question: In 2023 Elon Musk started a new AI company called xAI, meant to compete with OpenAI (which Musk himself had helped fund years earlier). xAI's chatbot is called Grok, and unlike ChatGPT or Claude — which each live on their own website — Grok is built directly into a bigger platform Musk already owns. Where do people typically chat with Grok?
answer: Inside the X social-media platform (formerly Twitter)
choices: Inside the X social-media platform (formerly Twitter)
Inside the Apple Maps app on iPhone and iPad
Inside Microsoft Word as the only available chatbot
Inside Netflix as a chat companion while watching shows
context: Grok is the chatbot from xAI, Elon Musk's AI company founded in 2023. It's available inside the X platform (formerly Twitter), which Musk also owns. Grok is positioned as a 'less filtered' alternative to ChatGPT and Claude. Its public stance has shifted over time as the models are updated, illustrating how 'AI personality' is a tuning choice the company makes, not a fixed property of the technology.

question: Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology turned an AI on a huge library of drug molecules in 2020. One it flagged, later named halicin, beat a drug-resistant bacterium in lab tests. What was the AI doing?
answer: Scanning millions of molecules to predict which were likely to kill the bacterium
choices: Scanning millions of molecules to predict which were likely to kill the bacterium
Inventing molecules that no human had previously imagined could exist
Replacing all laboratory testing with computer predictions alone
Writing the marketing copy for the antibiotic before it was discovered
context: In 2020, an MIT team published the discovery of halicin, a new antibiotic, found by training a neural network to predict antibacterial activity from molecular structure. They screened a vast library, the model picked candidates, and lab testing confirmed the best one worked. The same pattern (AI shortlists candidates, lab confirms) is now common in drug discovery. The AI didn't replace the lab; it picked what the lab tried first.

question: A team at Google DeepMind released an AI forecast called GraphCast in 2023, and it beat many of the old-style forecasts on accuracy. Those older forecasts come from giant supercomputers working through huge formulas for air, water and heat. What is fundamentally different about how new AI forecasts like GraphCast work?
answer: They learn forecast patterns from past data instead of solving physics equations step by step
choices: They learn forecast patterns from past data instead of solving physics equations step by step
They use crystal balls and old farmer almanacs as their main inputs
They wait for the weather to happen and then report it after the fact
They guess random conditions and check later which guess was right
context: Traditional weather forecasting solves the equations of atmospheric physics on huge supercomputers. AI weather models like Google's GraphCast and Huawei's Pangu-Weather instead learn patterns from decades of past weather data. For medium-range forecasts (3-10 days) they now match or beat traditional models on many measures, while running much faster. The two approaches are starting to be used together.

question: A vegetable farmer hitches a Carbon Robotics machine behind his tractor and pulls it across the field. Cameras and an AI model spot each weed among the crop plants as it rolls along. Instead of spraying weedkiller, how does the machine get rid of the weeds?
answer: It burns them with lasers
choices: It pulls them with claws
It freezes them with ice
It cuts them with blades
It burns them with lasers
context: Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder fires carbon-dioxide lasers at each weed its AI identifies, killing it with heat and no herbicide at all. The company says its pull-behind model can kill around 200,000 weeds an hour.

question: At an eye clinic, a nurse photographs the back of a patient's eye: the retina, the layer that senses light. AI tools trained on tens of thousands of these photos can now scan a single image and flag one common disease, sometimes before a doctor would even see the signs. Which disease is it?
answer: Diabetic retinopathy, which can lead to blindness if untreated
choices: Diabetic retinopathy, which can lead to blindness if untreated
The common cold, which causes a runny nose
A broken arm, which usually requires a cast
Tooth decay, which a dentist usually treats
context: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults — and it's detectable from a retinal photograph well before symptoms appear. AI screening tools from companies like IDx and Google Health have FDA approval in the US for use in primary care, letting clinics screen patients without an eye specialist. Catching it early lets treatment prevent vision loss. A quiet but meaningful AI medical win.

question: An early user of GitHub Copilot in 2021 was really working with an AI model named Codex. Codex came from an outside partner, not from GitHub or its owner, Microsoft. Which company made Codex?
answer: OpenAI
choices: OpenAI
Microsoft Research
Apple AI
Stack Overflow
context: OpenAI's Codex, released 2021, was a GPT-style model fine-tuned on public code. GitHub Copilot, a product built on Codex, launched the same year. GitHub is owned by Microsoft, which has invested heavily in OpenAI — so the partnership runs deep. Newer Copilot versions use the latest OpenAI models. Codex itself was retired and folded into newer general-purpose models.

question: Midjourney is one of the most famous AI image generators — type a sentence like 'a fox reading a book in a forest at sunset,' and Midjourney draws you a beautiful picture in about a minute. But unlike its competitors DALL-E and Stable Diffusion, which have their own websites, Midjourney chose an unusual place to actually run. Users have to type their prompts inside a completely different platform. Where?
answer: On the Discord chat platform, where users type prompts in shared channels
choices: On the Discord chat platform, where users type prompts in shared channels
Only on physical kiosks in shopping malls across the United States
Inside a single video game that runs only on Sony PlayStation 5
Exclusively as a printed monthly magazine mailed to subscribers
context: Midjourney started by running entirely through Discord, the chat platform popular with gamers. Users typed prompts in Discord channels and the bot replied with images. This unusual setup let Midjourney grow quickly without building its own web app. The company added a standalone website later. Of the three big image generators, Midjourney is often praised for stylized art and atmospheric scenes.

question: Waymo, the self-driving car company that now runs robot taxis in Phoenix and San Francisco, wasn't originally its own separate business. It started around 2009 as a secret self-driving-car research project inside a much bigger tech company. That larger company let the project grow, then finally spun it out as its own business called Waymo in 2016. Which giant tech company did Waymo grow out of?
answer: Google (now Alphabet)
choices: Google (now Alphabet)
General Motors
Apple
Toyota
context: Waymo began in 2009 as Google's self-driving car project, led by Sebastian Thrun. In 2016 it spun out as Waymo under Alphabet (Google's parent company). The early team came from the DARPA Grand Challenge competitions in the mid-2000s, when university teams raced self-driving prototypes in the desert. Today Waymo runs paid robotaxi service in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Austin.

question: In a November 2015 email later made public, Elon Musk urged that OpenAI announce it was starting with a $1 billion funding commitment. According to OpenAI's own account in March 2024, how much had the nonprofit actually received from Musk?
answer: Less than $45 million
choices: The full $1 billion
About $500 million
Exactly $250 million
Less than $45 million
context: Musk's own email suggested announcing a $1 billion commitment. OpenAI said in 2024 that the nonprofit had raised less than $45 million from him and more than $90 million from other donors; Musk's side put his giving at about $38 million. A headline pledge is not money in the bank.

question: On YouTube, TikTok, Netflix, and Instagram, if you tap the three-dot menu next to a video or show you don't like, you can pick an option like 'Not interested' or 'Don't show me this again.' The button is easy to ignore, but it goes straight into the same recommendation AI that decides what you see next. Does clicking that button actually change what the algorithm shows you afterward?
answer: Yes — it's a strong signal to the recommendation system, more than just scrolling past
choices: Yes — it's a strong signal to the recommendation system, more than just scrolling past
No — the button is decoration; the system completely ignores all clicks
No — saying it out loud to your phone is the only signal that registers
Yes — but only if you say it once a week for at least three months
context: Explicit feedback ('not interested', 'don't show me this channel') is a stronger signal than implicit feedback (scrolling past quickly). It tells the model not just 'I didn't watch this one' but 'I'd actively prefer less of this kind.' Worth using deliberately on the platforms you spend time on. You can shape your feed instead of just being shaped by it — though only inside the platform's own framing.

question: Waymo and most other self-driving carmakers cover their cars in lidar, radar, and cameras all combined — they don't trust any single sensor on its own. Tesla, led by Elon Musk, disagreed. Musk argued that humans drive with just their eyes, so a car should be able to too. Tesla's Autopilot and Full Self-Driving systems mostly rely on one kind of sensor that these other companies won't stake safety on alone. Which sensor?
answer: Cameras alone, instead of also using lidar
choices: Cameras alone, instead of also using lidar
Underground magnetic strips embedded in the road
GPS satellites from a Tesla-only satellite network
Wireless tags worn by every nearby pedestrian
context: Tesla bet early on camera-only self-driving — the argument being that humans drive with eyes alone, so a vision system should be enough. Most other companies (Waymo, Cruise, Aurora) combine cameras with lidar and radar. Lidar measures distance directly with laser pulses and works in darkness; cameras need light and good interpretation. The debate is ongoing; Tesla's results suggest the camera-only path is harder than expected.

question: In 2019 the chief executive of a British energy firm took a call from what sounded like his boss, German accent and all, ordering an urgent payment of about $243,000. He sent it. According to the firm's insurer, whose voice had the criminals faked?
answer: The head of the firm's German parent company
choices: A manager at a supplier in Hungary
The firm's own finance director
The head of the firm's German parent company
An official at the British tax office
context: The Wall Street Journal reported, citing the insurer Euler Hermes, that criminals used AI software to mimic the voice of the German parent company's chief executive and had the money sent to an account in Hungary. It is often called one of the first known AI voice frauds against a company.

question: In 2023 researchers at University College London played real and AI-faked speech, in English and in Mandarin, to 529 listeners and asked them to spot the fakes. Some listeners got practice examples first. What did the study find?
answer: Listeners caught only about three fakes in four, and practice barely helped
choices: Listeners caught almost every fake, as long as they practised first
Listeners did well in English but failed completely in Mandarin
Listeners spotted fakes only when using expensive studio headphones
Listeners caught only about three fakes in four, and practice barely helped
context: In the PLOS ONE study led by Kimberly Mai, people identified the deepfake speech 73% of the time, with no difference between the two languages, and training improved results only slightly. The fakes came from an older algorithm, so newer clones may be harder still to hear.

question: Michael Cohen, a former lawyer to Donald Trump, admitted in late 2023 that three court cases cited in his motion to end his court supervision early did not exist. He had found them with Google's Bard chatbot. What did he say he had thought Bard was?
answer: A super-charged search engine
choices: A super-charged search engine
A licensed online law firm
A judge's official database
A human legal assistant
context: Cohen said in a sworn declaration that he had not realized Bard could invent cases, describing it as a super-charged search engine, and that he passed the cases to his lawyer, who filed them without checking. A chatbot is not a search engine, and in court the mistake belongs to whoever files it.

question: Suppose you ask ChatGPT for help with a school report and it hands back a smooth paragraph citing 'a 2019 Stanford study by Dr. Rodriguez.' You have never heard of this study, and chatbots are known for making such things up. Before you copy the paragraph, what should you do?
answer: Search for the study; if you can't find it in another source, treat it as probably fake
choices: Search for the study; if you can't find it in another source, treat it as probably fake
Use the paragraph as is because chatbots have access to all real studies
Ask the same chatbot whether the study is real and trust the answer
Cite the study yourself so the chatbot doesn't have to take the blame
context: LLMs invent citations all the time. The pattern: a study title that sounds plausible, named authors who don't exist, a journal that exists with a volume number that doesn't, all formatted correctly. The defense: search for the cited title in a real database (Google Scholar, PubMed, the journal's own website). If you can't find it, it probably isn't real. This is how the 2023 New York lawyer case happened — the lawyer trusted ChatGPT's citations.

question: Steven Schwartz, a New York lawyer, asked ChatGPT in 2023 to find past court cases for a brief. It gave him six, with names, dates and quotes, and he filed them unchecked. Then the opposing lawyer looked them up. What had gone wrong?
answer: ChatGPT had invented the cases, so none of them actually existed
choices: ChatGPT had invented the cases, so none of them actually existed
The lawyer paid for ChatGPT with a stolen credit card
ChatGPT had used too many large words for the court to read
The lawyer translated the brief into the wrong language
context: Steven Schwartz, a New York attorney, used ChatGPT to research case law for a 2023 brief. ChatGPT produced six confident-sounding citations — none of the cases existed. Opposing counsel couldn't find them. The judge fined Schwartz $5,000. The episode became the textbook example of LLM 'hallucination' — confidently fabricating facts that sound real. The takeaway: don't ask a language model for facts you can't independently check.

question: OpenAI researchers, including Adam Tauman Kalai, published a paper in September 2025 that compared language models inventing facts to students facing a hard exam. What did they say most training and testing ends up rewarding?
answer: Guessing confidently instead of admitting 'I don't know'
choices: Guessing confidently instead of admitting 'I don't know'
Leaving every hard question completely blank
Copying answers from a neighboring model
Answering only in short single words
context: The paper argued that most benchmarks give no credit for saying 'I don't know,' so a model that guesses scores better than one that admits uncertainty, just as a student who guesses on a test can pick up points. The authors proposed changing how tests are scored.

question: You suspect a picture on social media of a smiling person was made by an AI image tool like Midjourney or DALL-E rather than shot with a real camera. The tools have gotten good at faces, but one part of the human body still trips them up over and over. Fingers come out fused together, bent the wrong way, or six on a hand. Where should you look first for the giveaway?
answer: The hands, where finger counts and finger angles are common AI failures
choices: The hands, where finger counts and finger angles are common AI failures
The corner of the frame, where AI always writes its own name
The metadata file, which always says 'GENERATED' in plain text
The shadow under the chin, which AI never includes in any image
context: Hands have long been the classic AI image tell — six fingers, three fingers, fingers bent at impossible angles, two hands fused. The reason is that hands are complex objects shown in many poses; training data is varied; the model often averages into a confused mess. Newer models are better at hands, so the tell weakens. But it's still worth a glance — along with text in backgrounds, jewelry, and ears.

question: An AI image generator like DALL-E or Midjourney makes pictures from a short text prompt. Someone posts a suspicious photo of a person standing in front of a small shop. The sign hanging over the door looks like a real sign at first glance, but when you look close the letters do not spell any word — they are squiggles pretending to be text. What single feature of this picture betrays it as AI-generated?
answer: AI image tools often produce gibberish text inside images
choices: AI image tools often produce gibberish text inside images
The store is closed, so the sign is dim and unreadable on purpose
The photograph was taken at night with motion blur on the sign
The image is from a country whose alphabet you have never seen
context: Text inside AI-generated images is a major tell. The models render letters that look right at a glance but don't spell anything when you read them — extra strokes, missing letters, characters that drift between fonts mid-word. Newer image models (DALL-E 3, Midjourney v6+) are better at text but still slip on long words and signs in the background. Look at any text in the image and try to actually read it.

question: You already check the hands and any writing in an AI-generated picture, since AI tools fumble both. But there is another common tell right on the person's face itself. Small worn objects on or near the head are tricky for the model to render — the pixels bleed and merge into whatever surrounds them. What face-area detail often goes wrong in AI images?
answer: Earrings or glasses blending oddly into the skin or hair
choices: Earrings or glasses blending oddly into the skin or hair
Eyebrows that always slope downward to the left side of the face
Nostrils placed above the eyes rather than below in every picture
Skin colored bright neon green in the corners of the photograph
context: AI image models often slip on small objects that attach to the body — earrings melting into ears, glasses fusing with skin, hair fibers blending into jewelry. Asymmetric earrings (different on left and right) are another giveaway. The reason is similar to hands: training data shows these objects in many poses, and the model averages instead of getting any one pose right. Look at the edges where small objects meet skin.

question: AI-written text has a fingerprint. When a chatbot like ChatGPT writes a paragraph, it reaches for one specific punctuation mark much more often than a normal human writer would. It drops the mark between clauses, into the middle of sentences, and pretty much anywhere it can — sometimes several times in one short paragraph. Which punctuation mark is the AI tell?
answer: The em-dash, dropped into many sentences for no clear reason
choices: The em-dash, dropped into many sentences for no clear reason
The exclamation point at the end of every single sentence in a row
The semicolon used twice per word in the middle of a sentence
The hyphen used to separate every letter of a word like t-h-i-s
context: Em-dashes are a real punctuation mark used by careful writers — but ChatGPT-era AI text overuses them, sometimes several per paragraph. It's one of the simplest text tells. Other tells include 'delve into,' 'tapestry of,' 'in the realm of,' and repetitive sentence shapes. None of these proves AI authorship by itself — humans do use them. Cluster of tells in one paragraph is the signal.

question: AI-written text tends to repeat certain phrases so heavily that internet users now use them as jokes to spot chatbot output. One phrase in particular has become a punchline: it shows up as a repeated opener again and again, in blog posts and school essays turned in without editing. Which phrase is on that AI-tell list?
answer: 'Delve into' — used at the start of paragraphs constantly
choices: 'Delve into' — used at the start of paragraphs constantly
'See you tomorrow' — a common email sign-off in writing
'Once upon a time' — the standard fairy-tale opener children know
'In conclusion' — the standard essay closer schools have always taught
context: Certain phrases have become AI-text giveaways from sheer overuse. 'Delve into,' 'tapestry of,' 'navigate the landscape,' 'in the realm of,' 'it's important to note,' 'multifaceted.' These are real English phrases — humans use them too. The tell is the density and the predictability of placement. A single 'delve into' is nothing; three in one document is a strong signal someone outsourced the writing.

question: A ChatGPT user ticked a box to make a shared chat 'discoverable,' an option the share feature offered until mid-2025. Reporters then found thousands of such chats, some with private details, showing up somewhere unexpected. Where did the chats show up?
answer: In Google search results
choices: In OpenAI's app store
