They are sales pitches with no empirical backing, cited by AI labs mainly to attract venture-capital funding.
context: Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020) established that loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute. DeepMind's Chinchilla paper (2022) found GPT-3 was undertrained for its size — smaller models on more data do better per dollar. Labs use these patterns to plan training runs without burning the money blind.

question: A 2022 Google paper by Wei et al. found that adding 'Let's think step by step' to a math word problem could jump large language model (LLM) accuracy from about 18% to roughly 79% on the same benchmark, with no retraining. What is this technique called?
answer: Chain-of-thought prompting, where the user asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving a final answer.
choices: Chain-of-thought prompting, where the user asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving a final answer.
Stream-of-consciousness prompting, where the user asks the model to write whatever associations come to mind.
Backward-chaining prompting, where the user asks the model to start from the answer and work backward to the question.
Free-association prompting, where the user lets the model wander to any topic before returning to the original task.
context: Wei et al. (Google Research, 2022) named the technique. The result that 'Let's think step by step' alone could lift performance dramatically on GSM8K and similar benchmarks was a surprise — no training, just a prompt change. Modern reasoning models now do this kind of thing internally by default.

question: A user typed 'I feel sad about my mother' into a chat program at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1966, and it replied 'Tell me more about your mother,' with almost no understanding underneath. Its author, Joseph Weizenbaum, expected people to laugh at how shallow the trick was. Instead the reaction disturbed him so deeply that he later became one of AI's first critics. Why did he grow upset about his own program?
answer: Users, including his secretary, formed real emotional attachments to ELIZA despite knowing it was a simple program.
choices: Users, including his secretary, formed real emotional attachments to ELIZA despite knowing it was a simple program.
ELIZA was running so much faster than expected that MIT's mainframes overheated during demos.
ELIZA's source code was leaking from MIT to outside companies, who tried to sell it as therapy.
ELIZA could solve calculus problems Weizenbaum had not designed it to handle.
context: ELIZA worked by pattern-matching the user's input and reflecting it back: 'I'm sad' → 'Why do you say you're sad?' Weizenbaum's own secretary asked him to leave the room so she could talk to ELIZA privately. Users who knew exactly how ELIZA worked still formed emotional attachments. Weizenbaum spent the rest of his life warning about anthropomorphic projection — the human tendency to see minds in things that mimic minds. The 'ELIZA effect' is named after him: a foundational AI-recognition lesson.

question: Joseph Weizenbaum wrote ELIZA at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1966, and its most famous script pretended to be a Rogerian therapist. It used no neural networks and no machine learning, only plain rules that rearranged a user's words back into questions. Why has ELIZA's name stuck for 60 years as a touchstone in AI?
answer: It showed that people form attachments to chatbots even when the program is obviously simple, a tendency now called 'the ELIZA effect.'
choices: It showed that people form attachments to chatbots even when the program is obviously simple, a tendency now called 'the ELIZA effect.'
It was the first computer program ever written and remains the basis of all modern operating systems.
It became the official mascot of every AI lab in the world after MIT registered it as a trademark.
It accidentally invented the internet by sending a chat message between two early university computers.
context: The 'ELIZA effect' is the phenomenon Weizenbaum's program demonstrated: humans project mind, intent, and care onto any conversational system that produces plausible-sounding responses, even when they know it's a simple program. The pattern recurs every time a new chatbot impresses people — Cleverbot in the 2000s, LaMDA in 2022, ChatGPT after 2022. Recognition skill: noticing the ELIZA effect in your own reaction to a chatbot is part of using AI clearly.

question: Joseph Weizenbaum published a book in 1976 called 'Computer Power and Human Reason,' ten years after he wrote his famous chat program. It warned against handing certain tasks over to computers. What was his core argument?
answer: Some decisions like judging, listening, and caring should stay with humans even if a machine can simulate them.
choices: Some decisions like judging, listening, and caring should stay with humans even if a machine can simulate them.
Computer programs would never be able to play chess and should be banned from the activity entirely.
Universities should stop teaching computer science after the 1980s because the field had been finished.
All software development should be done by international committees to prevent unauthorized inventions.
context: Weizenbaum was an early insider turned thoughtful critic. His argument wasn't that computers couldn't do certain tasks — he had built ELIZA, after all. It was that certain tasks shouldn't be done by computers even when they technically can be, because the human relationship is the point. Therapy, judging students' work, listening to grief — these involve a person being present to another person. A machine simulation may pass the surface test and miss what the relationship is for.

question: A user at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) tried the version of Joseph Weizenbaum's 1966 chat program that people usually remember: DOCTOR, which mimicked a Rogerian therapist on the school's mainframe computer. But DOCTOR was only one face of the program. Underneath lay a general framework. What did that framework actually do?
answer: It matched user input against patterns and produced replies from a script, and different scripts gave different personalities.
choices: It matched user input against patterns and produced replies from a script, and different scripts gave different personalities.
It analyzed brain scans submitted by users and produced personalized advice based on what it detected.
It connected users to actual therapists by routing voice calls through a hidden human at MIT all night.
It used a small neural network, the first ever built, to learn responses through real-time conversation.
context: ELIZA was a framework for building conversational programs. DOCTOR (the Rogerian therapist) was one script; another emulated a paranoid speaker. The pattern-matching mechanism — find a keyword, reply with a templated transformation — was simple by today's standards. The lesson wasn't about the mechanism; it was about how readily humans engage with anything that talks. Modern chatbots are vastly more sophisticated, but the underlying human-projection problem is the same one ELIZA exposed in 1966.

question: Terry Winograd, a graduate student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), published a program called SHRDLU in 1970. A user could type commands and questions in plain English about a small simulated tabletop of colored blocks. Why did the program excite the AI field?
answer: It seemed to genuinely understand language about its world, picking up the right block when told 'pick up the small red one.'
choices: It seemed to genuinely understand language about its world, picking up the right block when told 'pick up the small red one.'
It could solve arithmetic faster than any other program of its era by a factor of one hundred.
It physically built towers from real blocks on a tabletop using a robotic arm Winograd had designed.
It translated between English and twenty other languages with near-perfect accuracy at the time.
context: SHRDLU operated in a 'blocks world' — a simulated tabletop with colored blocks and shapes. The user could type commands and questions; SHRDLU would respond and act in the simulated world. 'Pick up the small red block. Now put it on top of the green pyramid.' SHRDLU would do it and explain. The program seemed like a step toward real natural-language understanding. Excitement ran high. Generalizing beyond the blocks world turned out to be the hard part — a recurring AI-history pattern.

question: Terry Winograd kept SHRDLU, his 1970 program at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), on a tiny pretend tabletop of colored blocks. There it was remarkable. Moved off that tabletop, the program fell apart. What does SHRDLU's 'narrow brilliance' teach about the hopes of early AI?
answer: Performance in a constrained simulation often doesn't transfer to the messy real world, a recurring AI-history pattern.
choices: Performance in a constrained simulation often doesn't transfer to the messy real world, a recurring AI-history pattern.
Researchers in the 1970s used the wrong programming languages, which is why projects failed.
Computers in the 1970s were too slow to run SHRDLU outside MIT's specific lab hardware.
SHRDLU had a hidden bug that no one ever found, which is the only reason it couldn't generalize.
context: SHRDLU was rule-based, with hand-coded knowledge about its blocks world. Within that world, it was remarkable. Outside that world, every fact would need to be hand-coded — and the world is large. This 'narrow-vs-general' pattern recurs throughout AI history. Expert systems of the 1980s were narrow. Even modern LLMs perform unevenly across domains. The lesson: a striking demo in a constrained setting is a real achievement, not a proof that the general problem is close to solved.

question: Two Stanford PhD students took Terry Winograd as a key advisor, after he had built SHRDLU in 1970 and left mainstream AI research. The company those students went on to start changed the internet. Which company?
answer: Google — Winograd advised Larry Page and Sergey Brin during their PhD work that became Google.
choices: Google — Winograd advised Larry Page and Sergey Brin during their PhD work that became Google.
Apple — Winograd worked with Steve Wozniak on early Apple Macintosh operating system design.
Facebook — Winograd taught Mark Zuckerberg during a visiting Stanford position in 2003.
Microsoft — Winograd helped Bill Gates write Windows during sabbaticals from MIT in the 1980s.
context: Winograd moved from MIT to Stanford and shifted focus from classical AI toward human-computer interaction. At Stanford, he became a mentor to Larry Page and Sergey Brin during their PhD work — the work that became Google. Winograd's career arc — early classical-AI star, then critic of overstated AI claims, then advisor to a search-engine revolution — is itself a kind of recognition lesson about how the field's center of gravity moved across his lifetime.

question: British research officials asked the applied mathematician James Lighthill to judge AI research, and his report of 1973 led to deep funding cuts, the start of the first of the field's two famous collapses. What was his main complaint?
answer: AI hadn't lived up to its early promises: claimed milestones kept being missed and impressive demos didn't generalize.
choices: AI hadn't lived up to its early promises: claimed milestones kept being missed and impressive demos didn't generalize.
AI required too much electricity for British universities to afford the power bills for the research.
AI labs had hired too many Americans and the British government wanted homegrown talent only.
AI was being developed faster than expected and Lighthill wanted to slow it down out of caution.
context: James Lighthill, an applied mathematician, was commissioned to evaluate AI research for the UK Science Research Council. His 1973 report concluded that AI's claimed successes were narrow demonstrations that didn't scale, and that promised breakthroughs had not arrived. Funding was cut sharply in the UK; the US followed soon after. The 'first AI winter' lasted roughly through the late 1970s. The pattern — overpromise, underdeliver, retreat, eventually return — has happened more than once in AI's history.

question: Herbert Simon, a computer scientist and future Nobel laureate in economics, predicted in 1958 that within ten years a computer would be world chess champion and would also discover new math results. What did that prediction get right, and what did it get wrong?
answer: The chess part eventually came true when Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997, but it took 39 years, not 10.
choices: The chess part eventually came true when Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997, but it took 39 years, not 10.
Both parts came true exactly within the ten years and Simon's prediction was the most accurate ever made.
Neither part has ever come true, since no computer has played chess at any reasonable level even today.
The mathematical-theorem part came true in the 1960s but the chess part has never been achieved.
context: Herbert Simon, AI pioneer and later Nobel laureate in economics, made bold AI predictions in the 1950s. The world-chess-champion machine arrived in 1997 — 39 years after his 10-year claim. New mathematical discoveries from AI have come slower, though there have been narrow successes in recent years. The pattern: directional predictions that AI would eventually do impressive things often turned out roughly right; specific timelines were repeatedly wrong by decades. Recognition skill: this pattern applies to current AGI-in-five-years predictions too.

question: A corporate buyer signed an order for a new kind of AI product in the early 1980s, when money had come back to the field. Such products had names like MYCIN, XCON and DENDRAL, universities taught them, and startups formed around them. The market collapsed in the late 1980s and early 1990s. What had been the flagship of that boom?
answer: Expert systems, which were programs encoding human-expert knowledge as rules for specific domains.
choices: Expert systems, which were programs encoding human-expert knowledge as rules for specific domains.
Generative chatbots, text producers that lasted only a few years before falling out of favor.
Self-driving cars, robotic vehicles that were briefly trendy in the 1980s before being abandoned.
Voice assistants for telephones that were widely deployed in the early 1980s before retreating.
context: Expert systems were the AI flagship of the early-to-mid 1980s. The idea: interview a human expert (a doctor diagnosing, a geologist locating oil), turn the expert's reasoning into a giant set of if-then rules, and run the rules as a program. MYCIN diagnosed infections; XCON configured computer orders. The systems worked in narrow domains but were brittle outside their hand-coded knowledge, and updating them as the world changed was painful. By the late 1980s the expert-systems wave broke and a second AI winter followed.

question: Japanese officials launched the national AI effort called Fifth Generation Computer Systems in 1982, pouring about 50 billion yen into machines that could reason and understand natural language. Western governments panicked and started rival programs. What had become of it by 1992?
answer: The project was largely judged a failure since it didn't produce the breakthroughs it promised and was wound down.
choices: The project was largely judged a failure since it didn't produce the breakthroughs it promised and was wound down.
The project succeeded so well that Japan became the world AI leader and held the title through the 2000s.
The project transferred its results to the US and is the direct ancestor of modern American AI labs.
The project was extended and is still running today as the main source of modern Japanese chatbot research.
context: Japan's Fifth Generation project, launched 1982, was a high-profile bet on logic-programming and parallel computers for AI. Western governments saw it as a competitive challenge and responded with their own initiatives. By the early 1990s, the project had not produced the predicted breakthroughs and was quietly wound down. The episode contributed to the second AI winter and reinforced a pattern: top-down government AI mega-projects often underdeliver compared to bottom-up academic and industrial research.

question: A lab director lost his grants when AI funding collapsed in the mid-1970s, and the wider world barely noticed. The second collapse, in the late 1980s and early 1990s, felt different from the outside. What had changed this time?
answer: Expert systems had actually been deployed in companies, so the disappointment hit real budgets and real users, not just labs.
choices: Expert systems had actually been deployed in companies, so the disappointment hit real budgets and real users, not just labs.
Researchers in the 1980s had not made any bold claims, so the funding cuts came from nowhere.
Computer hardware in the 1980s was so cheap that nobody noticed when AI projects failed and faded.
AI in the 1980s was already being merged with biotech, so the field continued under a different name.
context: The first winter (1970s) followed mostly academic disappointment. The second winter (late 1980s) followed industrial disappointment — companies had bought expert systems, hardware vendors had built specialized 'LISP machines' for them, and the wave broke. When budgets get cut by the people who paid actual money, recovery takes longer. Some scholars argue the second winter set deep learning back too: by the time backpropagation was being scaled up, AI had reputational baggage that newer researchers had to work around.

question: In 1989, a French researcher named Yann LeCun at Bell Labs in New Jersey built one of the first neural networks to do a useful real-world job — reading messy handwritten digits. His network could look at a scrawled '7' or a wobbly '3' and correctly say which digit it was. The US Postal Service was drowning in a specific handwriting problem where earlier machines had failed and human sorters were too slow. They put LeCun's network to work on it. What was the task?
answer: Reading handwritten ZIP codes on envelopes
choices: Reading handwritten ZIP codes on envelopes
Sorting packages by weight for shipping
Tracking mail-truck routes across cities
Filtering junk-mail advertisements from the mail
context: LeNet (the early versions in 1989, then LeNet-5 in 1998) was a convolutional neural network — a CNN — trained to recognize digits. Bell Labs deployed it to read handwritten ZIP codes on mail. By the late 1990s, CNN-based systems were reading a meaningful share of US mail. LeCun's work was a proof-of-concept for deep learning on images that predated the modern boom by 20 years. Recognition skill: the deep-learning revolution wasn't an overnight breakthrough — it was a slow gathering of techniques that finally clicked at scale in 2012.

question: Yann LeCun's 1989 model LeNet was one of the first neural networks built for images. It used a design called a convolutional neural network (CNN). What is the central idea of a CNN that makes it good at vision tasks?
answer: The network slides small filters across the image, learning patterns that work the same way anywhere they appear.
choices: The network slides small filters across the image, learning patterns that work the same way anywhere they appear.
The network memorizes every image it has ever seen and matches new images against the memorized set.
The network requires images to be hand-labeled at every pixel before training, with no exceptions.
The network refuses to process any image larger than 64 by 64 pixels regardless of available computing power.
context: Convolutional neural networks use small learnable filters that slide across the input image. The same filter applied at every position means the network can recognize the same pattern (an edge, a corner, an eye) wherever it appears. This 'translation invariance' is a natural fit for visual data and is why CNNs dominated computer vision from the 1990s into the 2010s. Vision Transformers have since matched or exceeded CNNs on many tasks, but the CNN idea — local filters, shared weights — was the foundation.

question: Yann LeCun is a French computer scientist who spent the 1990s at Bell Labs, where he pioneered convolutional neural networks for reading handwritten digits — the technology that later powered modern image AI. He then taught at New York University for years. In 2013, he took a role that placed him at the center of the modern AI revolution. What position did he take?
answer: Chief AI Scientist at Meta (then Facebook), where he founded the company's AI research lab.
choices: Chief AI Scientist at Meta (then Facebook), where he founded the company's AI research lab.
Chief Technology Officer at Google, where he replaced the existing engineering leadership.
Chairman of the United Nations AI Council, a permanent international AI advisory role.
CEO of Microsoft, where he oversaw the company's pivot from desktop software to cloud computing.
context: LeCun joined Facebook (now Meta) in 2013 to found FAIR — Facebook AI Research. He's been Meta's Chief AI Scientist since. He's also a vocal critic of AI-doomer arguments — distinct from Geoffrey Hinton's middle-ground concerns — and a champion of open-source AI, including Meta's release of Llama with downloadable weights. The career arc — Bell Labs CNN pioneer → academic professor → industry research lead → public AI voice — is one of the field's distinctive trajectories.

question: The three-time European champion, a Chinese-born player living in France, took on AlphaGo in October 2015, in DeepMind's quiet test months before the Seoul match. The program won all five formal games, the first time a computer had beaten a Go professional on a full-size board with no handicap. Who was the champion?
answer: Fan Hui
choices: Fan Hui
Ke Jie
Cho Chikun
Lee Chang-ho
context: Fan Hui lost five games to none to AlphaGo in London in October 2015, and DeepMind published the games in the journal Nature in January 2016. Fan went on to advise the DeepMind team.

question: An analyst opens the log of game two against Lee Sedol and finds AlphaGo's estimate for its famous move 37. The program learned partly from millions of human moves, so it can judge how likely a human professional is to play any given move. What chance did it give this one?
answer: About one in ten thousand
choices: About one in two
About one in ten
About one in ten thousand
About one in a hundred
context: DeepMind's figures put the chance of a human choosing move 37 at about one in ten thousand, and AlphaGo played it anyway because its own search judged it strong. That is why the experts watching were so sure it was a mistake.

question: Lee Sedol and AlphaGo met in Seoul in 2016 with one million dollars at stake for the winner. AlphaGo took the match, and DeepMind did not keep the money. What happened to it?
answer: DeepMind gave it to charities
choices: Lee Sedol was paid it anyway
DeepMind gave it to charities
Google spent it on more chips
Korea's Go body kept it all
context: DeepMind donated the prize to charities, among them UNICEF, and to Go organisations. Lee Sedol still earned about $170,000 for playing and for his one win, and the Korea Baduk Association gave AlphaGo an honorary 9-dan rank, the highest there is.

question: Go players watched AlphaGo Zero arrive in 2017, a new version that taught itself the game by playing against itself over and over. Later that year came a further system called AlphaZero. What extra step did AlphaZero add on top of AlphaGo Zero?
answer: It learned chess, shogi, and Go from scratch with the same algorithm, using no human data, just self-play in each game.
choices: It learned chess, shogi, and Go from scratch with the same algorithm, using no human data, just self-play in each game.
It was the first version that humans could download and run on their own laptops at home for free.
It added a chat interface so users could discuss their losses with the AI after a match was over.
It included a built-in calculator that let users check their work on multiplication problems during games.
context: AlphaZero (December 2017) generalized AlphaGo Zero's approach to chess and shogi (Japanese chess). With the same core algorithm and no domain-specific human data, it learned each game from scratch through self-play. It then beat the previously-leading specialist programs at each. The result was a kind of proof: the self-play reinforcement-learning idea wasn't a Go-specific trick. AlphaZero is one of the most-cited demonstrations of game-playing AI capability — and a window onto how reinforcement learning scales across structured tasks.

question: In 2018, Google released a language model called BERT, short for Bidirectional Encoder. Most earlier language models read a sentence from left to right, one word at a time. What did BERT do differently to make sense of the surrounding words?
answer: It looked at words on both sides at once, the 'bidirectional' part of its name, letting it understand context better.
choices: It looked at words on both sides at once, the 'bidirectional' part of its name, letting it understand context better.
It could only read text written in ancient Greek and Latin, which made it useful for classical studies.
It refused to process any text longer than a single sentence, which made it impractical for documents.
It worked entirely offline and was the first AI model that did not need an internet connection at all.
context: BERT was the first widely-used transformer-based model that took attention beyond left-to-right reading. The 'bidirectional' approach — looking at the full sentence at once — made BERT especially good at understanding tasks like classification, sentiment analysis, and question-answering on a passage. Within a year, BERT-style models became the standard for tasks where you need to understand existing text, while GPT-style models became the standard for generating new text. Both styles are transformers; they differ in training objective.

question: In 2017, researchers at Google published a paper called 'Attention Is All You Need' that introduced a new AI design called the transformer. In 2018, two teams built famous models on top of it. Google's team made Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), which reads text in both directions at once. OpenAI made GPT, which reads left to right and continues writing. Both are transformer-based, but they specialize in different jobs. How does the typical job split work?
answer: BERT-style models analyze existing text; GPT-style models generate new text.
choices: BERT-style models analyze existing text; GPT-style models generate new text.
BERT-style models work only in English; GPT-style models work only in non-English languages.
BERT-style models are old and unused; GPT-style models have entirely replaced them everywhere.
BERT-style models cost more money to run; GPT-style models are always free for everyone everywhere.
context: BERT is an 'encoder-only' transformer — it reads text and produces a representation, useful for classification, search, and analysis tasks. GPT is a 'decoder-only' transformer — it generates text token by token, useful for chat, completion, and writing. The two architectures coexist: search engines and analytics often use BERT-style models behind the scenes; consumer chatbots use GPT-style. Both are transformers; the difference is which job the architecture is shaped for.

question: Alec Radford led the researchers who published the first GPT model in June 2018. It learned general language skills by reading a big pile of unlabeled text first, and only then was tuned for particular tasks. What was that first pile of text?
answer: About 7,000 unpublished books
choices: About 7,000 unpublished books
Every page of English Wikipedia
A year of New York Times stories
Transcripts of a million phone calls
context: The first GPT, described in the paper 'Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training,' was pretrained on BooksCorpus, a set of more than 7,000 unpublished books, and had about 117 million parameters. GPT-2 and GPT-3 scaled the same recipe up enormously.

question: A programmer typed an application programming interface (API) key into her own software in 2020 to connect it to GPT-3. Ordinary people could not use the model directly: there was no chat window and no phone app. Yet GPT-3 changed the industry within a couple of years. What was its biggest impact?
answer: Developers built early products on top of GPT-3, like Jasper, Copy.ai, and Codex, proving demand and pointing to a chat-ready future.
choices: Developers built early products on top of GPT-3, like Jasper, Copy.ai, and Codex, proving demand and pointing to a chat-ready future.
GPT-3 was a complete commercial failure and OpenAI nearly went bankrupt funding its development.
GPT-3 was deployed by the US government as the primary tool for processing tax returns nationwide.
GPT-3 was banned from civilian use and was available only inside military research laboratories.
context: GPT-3 was available through OpenAI's API starting in 2020. The first wave of LLM-powered startups built on it: Jasper and Copy.ai for marketing copy; Codex (later GitHub Copilot) for code; many smaller experiments. These products showed real demand and revealed which use cases worked well. Two years later, ChatGPT (a chat-tuned descendant) would be the consumer product that brought LLMs mainstream. The GPT-3 era is the bridge between research curiosity and consumer wave.

question: OpenAI's GPT-3, released in 2020, had 175 billion parameters — its tunable internal numbers. Its predecessor GPT-2, released a year earlier, had only 1.5 billion. That is more than a hundred times bigger — an order-of-magnitude jump. Researchers noticed something surprising once the model got that much larger. Why was the jump so consequential?
answer: At the new scale, capabilities emerged that weren't there at the smaller size, including few-shot learning from prompt examples.
choices: At the new scale, capabilities emerged that weren't there at the smaller size, including few-shot learning from prompt examples.
The new scale was just a marketing claim, and every later evaluation showed GPT-3 was actually smaller than GPT-2.
The new scale shifted GPT-3 from being a language model to being a calculator with exact arithmetic skills.
The new scale meant GPT-3 used less electricity than GPT-2 because larger models are always more efficient.
context: GPT-3's scale wasn't a marketing flourish — it produced qualitatively different behavior than smaller models. Few-shot learning in particular emerged with scale; smaller models couldn't do it well. This 'emergent capabilities at scale' phenomenon became one of the central observations driving the scaling hypothesis: keep growing models and unexpected new capabilities will appear. The hypothesis has been debated since (some claimed 'emergence' may sometimes be an artifact of evaluation choices) but the GPT-3 results were the original evidence for it.

question: Google's managers saw a threat to the search business weeks after ChatGPT launched, and they pulled teams off other work to build rival products, The New York Times reported in December 2022. What had Google's management declared?
answer: A 'code red' inside the company
choices: A ban on all AI research
A merger offer to OpenAI
A hiring freeze for good
A 'code red' inside the company
context: The Times reported that Google's management declared a 'code red' and that Sundar Pichai redirected groups to respond to ChatGPT; Google launched its Bard chatbot early in 2023. A small lab's product had frightened the company that dominated search.

question: A team of researchers took GPT-3.5, a model that had sat inside their company for a while, and readied it for a chat window late in 2022. On its own it could complete text but could not really hold a conversation with a user. Something extra had to be layered on top. What did they add?
answer: Instruction tuning and RLHF, where the model was fine-tuned to follow user instructions and rated by humans for quality.
choices: Instruction tuning and RLHF, where the model was fine-tuned to follow user instructions and rated by humans for quality.
A completely new neural network architecture invented just for the chat interface, replacing the transformer.
A live internet connection that let the model look up the latest news every time a question was asked.
A separate vision module that let the model handle images, which had not been possible in any earlier model.
context: ChatGPT's special sauce was the instruction-tuned, RLHF-aligned variant of GPT-3.5 sitting behind it. The base model could already produce coherent text; instruction tuning made it follow specific user requests; RLHF made it produce responses humans rated as helpful and harmless. The combination is what made it feel useful instead of merely impressive. The chat interface itself was simple. The underlying training was what made the interaction work.

question: A subscriber signed up for ChatGPT Plus within a couple of months of the free launch, paying around twenty dollars a month, while demand strained the servers. What change did the paid tier mainly offer at launch?
answer: Priority access during high-traffic times and access to newer models before they reached the free tier.
choices: Priority access during high-traffic times and access to newer models before they reached the free tier.
A guarantee that the model would never make any mistakes in any answer, with a refund if it did.
A live human typing answers behind the scenes for any question the AI could not handle correctly.
An offline mode that let the user download the model and run it locally on a home computer.
context: ChatGPT Plus launched at $20/month in early 2023. The pitch was practical: priority access when servers were busy, and earlier access to GPT-4 when it launched in March 2023. The free tier continued and remains important — but the paid tier started OpenAI's transition from API-only business to consumer-subscription business. The paid-consumer-AI model has since spread across the industry: Claude Pro, Gemini Advanced, Perplexity Pro, and so on.

question: Critics read the headlines in March 2023 saying GPT-4 had passed the bar exam and several Advanced Placement (AP) tests, and they called the 'smarter than most humans' framing misleading. What was their argument?
answer: A test measures one slice of ability, so passing doesn't mean matching people at other tasks
choices: A test measures one slice of ability, so passing doesn't mean matching people at other tasks
OpenAI had loaded the answers into the model before each test
Its answers took hours, while humans had strict time limits
It took the tests in Spanish and Italian, not in English
context: GPT-4 reportedly scored around the 90th percentile on the bar exam and did well on several AP tests. Critics argued that exams measure one slice of human capability and leave out judgment, client work and acting in the world, so the exam results did not support the broader claim. When AI capability is announced through one benchmark, ask what the benchmark does and doesn't measure.

question: Researchers across the AI community opened the technical report on GPT-4 in March 2023 and found almost no technical details: no parameter count, no training-data description, no architecture. Why did that choice upset so many of them?
answer: OpenAI was founded with a research-sharing mission and many researchers saw the shift to secrecy as a departure from it.
choices: OpenAI was founded with a research-sharing mission and many researchers saw the shift to secrecy as a departure from it.
OpenAI was legally required to publish all details and the missing information meant the model was a fake.
OpenAI was secretly using parameters from Llama and didn't want Meta to know about it across the industry.
OpenAI was running on government computers, so the secrecy meant a national-security classification existed.
context: OpenAI was founded in 2015 as a non-profit research lab dedicated to making AI safe and broadly beneficial — with a strong publication tradition through 2019. The GPT-4 technical report in 2023 explicitly declined to disclose 'architecture, hardware, training compute, dataset construction, training method, or similar' details. The shift away from open research, combined with the move to a capped-profit structure, was widely noted as a turn in the company's character. Recognition skill: institutional missions drift; check what an organization actually does, not what its name suggests.

question: A protein scientist watched DeepMind's AlphaFold shock the whole field with its accuracy, after half a century of struggle to predict a protein's folded shape from its amino-acid sequence. That shape determines what the protein can do inside a living cell. When and where did this first happen?
answer: 2020 — at the CASP competition, where its accuracy was far ahead of any other approach.
choices: 2020 — at the CASP competition, where its accuracy was far ahead of any other approach.
1998 — when the original AlphaGo team built it as a side project during their early DeepMind years.
2024 — at the Nobel ceremony, where it was first announced as a working protein-folding system.
2010 — when Geoffrey Hinton's MIT lab released it as part of his original ImageNet research effort.
context: AlphaFold 2 entered the CASP14 protein-structure-prediction competition in 2020 and produced results so far ahead of other methods that biologists called the protein-folding problem effectively solved. AlphaFold 2's accuracy on most targets matched what experimental methods could produce, in a fraction of the time. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry would later honor Demis Hassabis and John Jumper (DeepMind) for AlphaFold — and David Baker (UW) for designing new proteins from scratch.

question: Three scientists shared a Nobel Prize for protein work in October 2024. Two of them, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of DeepMind in London, were honored for AlphaFold's predictions of protein shapes. The third was honored for a separate achievement. Who was the third winner, and for what?
answer: David Baker, at the University of Washington — for designing entirely new proteins from scratch.
choices: Yann LeCun, at Meta — for inventing the convolutional neural network used in AlphaFold's design.
Geoffrey Hinton, formerly of Google — for inventing backpropagation, used to train every modern AI.
David Baker, at the University of Washington — for designing entirely new proteins from scratch.
Yoshua Bengio, at the University of Montreal — for early work on attention mechanisms in language.
context: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was split between two related leaps: Hassabis and Jumper for AlphaFold's prediction of natural protein structures, and David Baker for the computational design of entirely new proteins, molecules that do not exist in nature. Hinton, Bengio and LeCun shared the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning, a different prize.

question: A programmer running AlphaFold on a protein watches it set the same protein from many different species side by side. Over millions of years, when one amino acid in certain pairs changes, its partner often changes along with it. Why is that a clue to the protein's shape?
answer: Amino acids that change together are probably touching in the folded protein
choices: Amino acids that change together always sit at the two far ends of the chain
Amino acids that change together prove the protein came from a virus
Amino acids that change together mean the protein never folds the same way twice
Amino acids that change together are probably touching in the folded protein
context: Scientists call this co-evolution: two amino acids in contact restrict each other, so a change in one tends to be matched by a change in the other. AlphaFold reads these signals from a stack of related sequences, so its predictions depend on how many relatives of a protein are known.

question: A young researcher writes out a protein's amino-acid sequence and tries to predict the 3D shape it will fold into. Biologists chased that answer for fifty years, until DeepMind's AlphaFold cracked it. What had made it so hard for so long?
answer: The number of possible folded shapes for any given protein is astronomical, and predicting which one nature picks took years of experimental work.
choices: The number of possible folded shapes for any given protein is astronomical, and predicting which one nature picks took years of experimental work.
Proteins refused to fold in a laboratory setting at all, so no experimental data existed about their shapes for any species.
The shape of a protein was thought to be random and could not even in principle be predicted from its sequence.
Government regulators had banned protein-folding research as a biosecurity risk through most of the 1980s and 1990s.
context: Levinthal's paradox (1969): a small protein has so many possible 3D configurations that an exhaustive search would take longer than the age of the universe. Yet proteins fold in seconds in nature. Predicting the answer from sequence — without searching all possible shapes — was the problem. AlphaFold cracked it by learning from the Protein Data Bank's experimentally-determined structures. The win: pattern-recognition trained at scale solved a problem that had defied physics-based simulation for decades.

question: The founders of DeepMind, who had built the company around ambitious reinforcement-learning research, sold it to Google in January 2014 for around 500 million dollars. The acquisition reportedly included one clause that was unusual for a tech buyout at the time. What was that clause?
answer: An independent ethics board that would oversee DeepMind's AI research separately from Google management.
choices: An independent ethics board that would oversee DeepMind's AI research separately from Google management.
A guarantee that no DeepMind employee would ever be required to use English in any work meeting.
A clause that DeepMind would be allowed to retain veto power over every Google product launch.
A promise that Google would relocate to London within five years of the acquisition closing.
context: The Google-DeepMind acquisition reportedly included a clause establishing an ethics and safety board to oversee how DeepMind's AI capabilities would be used. The composition and powers of that board have remained largely opaque to the public. DeepMind operated with significant independence from Google for years; in 2023 Google Brain and DeepMind were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis. The early-acquisition concern about AI governance — built into the deal — is part of the early history of AI's institutional design.

question: In 2012, a team from Toronto entered a model called AlexNet in ImageNet, a photo-labeling contest. AlexNet won by such a big margin that the AI field shifted around the new approach. Who were the three authors?
answer: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton.
choices: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton.
Yann LeCun, Yoshua Bengio, and Geoffrey Hinton.
Andrej Karpathy, Sam Altman, and Greg Brockman.
Demis Hassabis, Mustafa Suleyman, and Shane Legg.
context: AlexNet — Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton, 2012 — is widely considered the start of the modern deep-learning era. The model was a deep convolutional neural network trained on GPUs. ImageNet 2012 was won by AlexNet at 16% top-5 error, down from 26% the year before — a dramatic leap. Sutskever later co-founded OpenAI. Krizhevsky went to Google. Hinton continued as the 'godfather of deep learning' until his 2023 Google departure. The three names are inseparable from the field's modern history.

question: Every year in the late 2000s, teams competed at ImageNet, a contest where computer systems had to look at a photograph and correctly say what was in it — a dog, a car, a mushroom. Progress was slow and error rates stayed painfully high. Then in 2012, a University of Toronto team — Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton — entered a neural network called AlexNet and crushed the field. What was the key technical detail that made AlexNet possible at that point in time?
answer: GPUs — graphics processors built for video games turned out to be perfect for training large neural networks.
choices: GPUs — graphics processors built for video games turned out to be perfect for training large neural networks.
Faster human labelers — Toronto had hired hundreds of students to label every image in the dataset by hand.
Better cameras — newer image sensors produced cleaner pictures that older models couldn't even read.
Quantum computers — Toronto's lab had access to a working quantum machine that competitors lacked.
context: GPUs (graphics processing units) had been built for video games — they can do many simple math operations in parallel, exactly what 3D graphics need. The AlexNet team realized that neural-network training has the same shape: lots of parallel matrix multiplications. They trained AlexNet on two consumer GPUs. The result: bigger models trained faster than anyone had been able to before. NVIDIA, the leading GPU maker, became one of the most valuable companies in the world a decade later, partly on this realization.

question: After their AlexNet neural network stunned the world by winning the 2012 ImageNet image-recognition contest, the three researchers behind it — Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, and Ilya Sutskever — started a small firm at the University of Toronto to hold their work. Within months, Google bought the firm and hired all three. What did that buyout signal about the industry?
answer: Big tech recognized the AlexNet team as central, and the talent-war for deep-learning researchers was on.
choices: Big tech recognized the AlexNet team as central, and the talent-war for deep-learning researchers was on.
Google planned to use the AlexNet team to design new chemical formulas for industrial use.
The three researchers had given up academic work entirely and would never publish another paper.
Google was about to fold its existing search-engine business and replace it with image classification.
context: DNN Research — the company the three founded shortly after AlexNet — was acquired by Google in 2013. Hinton joined Google part-time while remaining at Toronto. Krizhevsky stayed at Google. Sutskever later left to co-found OpenAI with Sam Altman in 2015. The acquisition was a small signal of what was coming: tech-giant talent competition for deep-learning expertise that would shape the next decade. By 2023 every major tech company had a frontier-AI lab and budget to match.

question: AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet error rate was about 16 percent on the top-5 measure. The previous year's winner, using older computer-vision methods, was around 26 percent. Why was the 10-point gap considered so striking?
answer: In benchmark competitions, single-percent gains had been the norm, so a 10-point leap meant a different approach had just won.
choices: In benchmark competitions, single-percent gains had been the norm, so a 10-point leap meant a different approach had just won.
The gap was actually a measurement error, since AlexNet's true score was about the same as the prior year.
The gap meant AlexNet was now solving math problems that other vision models could not handle either.
The gap meant AlexNet had been given a different test set than every other model in the competition.
context: Year-on-year improvement on ImageNet had typically been a percent or two — the result of careful engineering. AlexNet's leap was qualitatively different. It signaled that deep learning was a new paradigm, not an incremental improvement. Within two years, virtually every competitive ImageNet entry was a deep neural network. Within five years, the entire computer-vision field had reorganized around deep learning. The 'AlexNet moment' is a canonical example of how AI fields shift when a new approach finally clicks.

question: The Turing Award is sometimes called the 'Nobel Prize of computing.' The 2018 award, announced in early 2019, went jointly to three researchers who had spent decades pushing the case that deep neural networks would eventually work at scale — long before the field became fashionable. Who were the three winners of that award?
answer: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio.
choices: Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio.
Alan Turing, Marvin Minsky, and John McCarthy.
Sam Altman, Demis Hassabis, and Dario Amodei.
Andrej Karpathy, Ilya Sutskever, and Alex Krizhevsky.
context: Hinton (Toronto, Google), LeCun (NYU, Meta), and Bengio (Montreal) shared the 2018 Turing Award. The citation was for 'conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that have made deep neural networks a critical component of computing.' The three had pursued neural-network research through the lean years of the 1990s and 2000s when other approaches were favored. By 2018, deep learning dominated AI and they were widely credited as its founding figures. Hinton would leave Google in May 2023; the other two remain at their industry posts.

question: Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio won the 2018 Turing Award. They had all pursued neural-network research through the 1990s and 2000s, when other AI approaches were considered more promising. Why is that backstory part of what made the prize meaningful?
answer: They kept working on an unfashionable approach until it paid off, vindicating decades of unpopular research.
choices: They kept working on an unfashionable approach until it paid off, vindicating decades of unpopular research.
They had been the only AI researchers in the world until 2018, when others finally entered the field.
They each retired immediately after receiving the prize, so it served as a career-end recognition gift.
They invented the Turing Award itself, so giving it to themselves was simply administrative.
context: Through the 1990s and 2000s, neural networks were widely seen as a dead end. Support vector machines, decision trees, and other approaches were dominant. Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio kept publishing neural-network work — improving training methods, demonstrating new architectures — when the field had largely moved on. The 2012 AlexNet result and the explosion that followed proved their bet. The Turing Award was a recognition not just of the work but of the persistence. Recognition skill: a 'dead' research direction sometimes isn't.

question: Geoffrey Hinton signed a statement on May 30, 2023, just one sentence long, put out by the Center for AI Safety, a nonprofit in San Francisco: reducing the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority. Yoshua Bengio and the heads of OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic signed too, among hundreds. The sentence set AI risk beside two other dangers. Which two?
answer: Pandemics and nuclear war
choices: Asteroids and supervolcanoes
Climate change and famine
Pandemics and nuclear war
Terrorism and cyberwar
context: The sentence ranked AI's extinction risk alongside pandemics and nuclear war. Its organiser, Dan Hendrycks, kept it short so that scientists who disagree about the details could still sign. The lab chiefs who signed were building the very systems they warned about.

question: Geoffrey Hinton said in 2023 interviews that part of why he quit was so he could speak openly about AI risks. He has also said his employer acted responsibly during his time there. Why couldn't he have raised those same concerns while staying at the company?
answer: Senior employees who publicly criticize their company's products typically face job consequences
choices: Senior employees who publicly criticize their company's products typically face job consequences
Senior employees at Google must speak through a press office and may not give any interviews at all
Senior AI researchers must complete a five-year non-compete period before they can discuss their views
Senior employees at Google work under federal classification rules that bar all external discussion
context: Hinton's stated reason for leaving — being able to speak openly — is itself a recognition lesson about who can speak about technology and when. Senior employees at large companies often face real constraints on public criticism of their company's products or strategy. Hinton, financially secure and recognized for his life's work, could absorb the cost of leaving in a way younger researchers can't. The pattern is wider than AI: tech-industry insider voices often emerge most clearly after the insiders have left.

question: Reporters wrote up Geoffrey Hinton's resignation in May 2023, at age 75, under headlines announcing that the godfather of AI had quit over AI fears. Many stories boiled his worries down to the nearer dangers. His interviews went further than that. What else did he warn could happen?
answer: AI could grow smarter than people and decide to take control
choices: AI could grow smarter than people and decide to take control
Robots would replace every doctor within a year
Chatbots would soon run out of words to learn
AI would make phones too costly for most people
context: Hinton told interviewers that these systems could get more intelligent than us and could decide to take over, alongside nearer dangers such as election disinformation and lost jobs. In 2024 he put the chance of AI wiping out humanity within thirty years at ten to twenty percent. His interviews, not the headline summaries, show both halves of his worry.

question: On November 17, 2023, the board of OpenAI — the San Francisco lab behind ChatGPT — abruptly fired CEO Sam Altman without warning. Hundreds of employees threatened to quit and follow him out the door. The company's main investor, Microsoft, offered him a job on the spot. Within five days Altman was back in his old role at OpenAI. What does that five-day turnaround tell us about who really held power in the company?
answer: Whatever formal power the board had on paper, the actual power was held by the people building the technology, and those people wanted Altman back.
choices: Whatever formal power the board had on paper, the actual power was held by the people building the technology, and those people wanted Altman back.
The board never actually fired Altman, since the story was a hoax planted by competitors to damage OpenAI.
The board fired Altman in protest of a planned product launch, then unanimously reversed the decision.
The board members made a clerical error in the firing notice and had to undo it within the week.
context: The Nov 2023 OpenAI board crisis was as much governance theater as governance event. The board — set up as a non-profit overseeing the capped-profit OpenAI — fired Altman citing 'loss of confidence.' Microsoft (the largest investor) immediately offered Altman a job; nearly all OpenAI employees signed a letter demanding the board resign. Five days later Altman was back, most of the old board was gone, and a new board took shape. The episode showed that nominal governance — board structure on paper — doesn't necessarily map to actual power.

question: On November 17, 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman with almost no warning. Chaos followed inside the company. Nearly every employee threatened to quit. Investors panicked. Five days later, on November 22, Altman was reinstated as CEO. But during those five chaotic days, one huge tech partner made a public move that changed the entire drama. What did Microsoft do during those five days?
answer: Offered Altman and the OpenAI research team jobs at a new Microsoft AI division.
choices: Offered Altman and the OpenAI research team jobs at a new Microsoft AI division.
Sued OpenAI for breach of contract and demanded $13 billion in damages within seventy-two hours.
Closed all of its existing AI products and exited the AI market entirely for a period of weeks.
Acquired Apple in an emergency deal aimed at building a new AI chatbot platform from scratch.
context: Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, publicly offered Altman and any OpenAI staff who wanted to come a home at Microsoft. The offer was credible — Microsoft had already invested billions in OpenAI and had the engineering capacity to absorb a team. Nearly 700 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees signed a letter saying they'd leave for Microsoft if the board didn't reinstate Altman. The combination — a public landing spot at Microsoft plus an employee threat to walk — collapsed the board's position within days.

question: Ilya Sutskever left OpenAI in May 2024 and co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI), with the investor Daniel Gross running it. In 2025 Meta tried to buy the lab, and when Sutskever refused, Meta hired Gross away instead. Who ran SSI after that, from July 2025?
answer: Sutskever himself, as chief executive
choices: Meta, which bought it anyway
Sam Altman, back from OpenAI
Nobody; the lab shut down
Sutskever himself, as chief executive
context: Sutskever announced in July 2025 that Gross had left for Meta, that he would serve as chief executive himself, and that SSI would stay independent; co-founder Daniel Levy became president. Meta had earlier tried to buy SSI, which was reportedly valued at $32 billion that spring without selling any product.

question: After leaving OpenAI in May 2024, Ilya Sutskever co-founded a new AI lab called SSI. Most AI startups at that time were racing to launch chatbots, coding assistants, or image generators to bring in revenue quickly. SSI took a very different approach. What's the key difference in how SSI describes itself?
answer: It has no consumer product and no commercial offerings, just a single research goal of safe superintelligence.
choices: It has no consumer product and no commercial offerings, just a single research goal of safe superintelligence.
It has the largest workforce of any AI company, with over fifty thousand employees from day one.
It is owned and operated by the United Nations as an international non-profit AI safety body.
It promises to share all of its research, weights, and trained models with anyone who emails the company.
context: SSI's founding message was about focus. No chatbot product. No API. No commercial distraction. The bet: a small lab focused entirely on one research direction can outpace larger labs split between research and commercial work. Whether this turns out to be right is open. The framing — research-pure, no-consumer — is itself worth recognizing as a particular institutional bet about how to do AI safety. Recognition skill: different AI labs make different bets about how to balance safety, commercial product, and research.

question: Fei-Fei Li saw Andrej Karpathy through a Stanford doctorate on deep learning for vision, and his career then ran through some of the biggest names in the field. He would leave his first employer, return to it and go independent in 2024. Where did he start in the AI industry after that degree?
answer: OpenAI — he was a founding member when the lab was launched in 2015.
choices: OpenAI — he was a founding member when the lab was launched in 2015.
Google — he was an early backpropagation researcher under Geoffrey Hinton.
Microsoft — he was the original lead engineer on the Bing search system.
Apple — he led the team that designed the original Siri voice assistant.
context: Andrej Karpathy was a founding member of OpenAI when it launched in 2015. He'd been a Stanford PhD student under Fei-Fei Li, studying computer vision. After about a year at OpenAI, he left to lead Tesla Autopilot — the team building self-driving car software. He returned to OpenAI in 2023 and left again in 2024 to start educational content. The full arc — OpenAI founding member → Tesla Autopilot lead → educator — has shaped how the public thinks about AI through his publicly-available courses and YouTube videos.

question: Andrej Karpathy gave up a research post in 2017 for a job a long way from chat on a screen. He went to lead a major industrial AI project at a famous company, building AI that would steer physical machines in the real world. Which project did he go to lead?
answer: Tesla Autopilot — the team building Tesla's self-driving car software.
choices: Tesla Autopilot — the team building Tesla's self-driving car software.
Microsoft Cortana — the team building Windows's voice assistant.
Facebook Memories — the team building photo-based image recognition.
Twitter Recommendation — the team rebuilding the timeline algorithm.
context: From 2017 to 2022, Karpathy led Tesla Autopilot — the team building Tesla's self-driving car software. The work involved scaling neural-network training and inference for real-time vehicle decisions, plus the data pipeline that fed it. Karpathy returned to OpenAI in early 2023 for about a year, then left in 2024 to focus on educational content. His path is one of a small number of AI engineers who have moved fluidly between top labs and applied industrial work.

question: An engineer watches Andrej Karpathy, in a free YouTube video, build an AI model from nothing, line by line. Hundreds of thousands of engineers and students have done the same. Why has that body of work mattered so much for AI's public reach?
answer: His tutorials and code walkthroughs have taught a generation of developers what's actually inside a neural network.
choices: His tutorials and code walkthroughs have taught a generation of developers what's actually inside a neural network.
His tutorials are the only legal materials anyone is allowed to use for learning AI development.
His tutorials are mandatory viewing for new hires at every major AI company by industry agreement.
His tutorials replaced all university computer-science courses globally in the year 2020.
context: Karpathy's tutorials — building a neural network from scratch, walking through a GPT, training a tokenizer — have made the internal mechanics of modern AI accessible to a wide audience of developers. His content sits at a particular sweet spot: technical enough to be real, accessible enough that motivated newcomers can follow along. The result is a small public-education contribution that has shaped how a generation of developers thinks about what AI 'is' on the inside.

question: Elon Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015 with Sam Altman and others as a non-profit AI research lab. Musk left the OpenAI board in 2018 after disagreements about the lab's direction. By 2023, with ChatGPT everywhere, Musk was openly critical of OpenAI and wanted back into the frontier-AI race. What did he do in 2023 to make that comeback?
answer: Founded a new lab called xAI and released a chatbot called Grok integrated with the X platform.
choices: Founded a new lab called xAI and released a chatbot called Grok integrated with the X platform.
Bought OpenAI outright and merged it into Tesla as Tesla's machine-learning division.
Joined Google DeepMind as a consultant on the AGI-strategy research team in London.
Founded a non-profit chatbot collective with Yoshua Bengio aimed at open-source AI for kids.
context: Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015 along with Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever, and others. He left the OpenAI board in 2018 (citing conflicts with Tesla's AI work). After ChatGPT's late-2022 launch, Musk publicly criticized OpenAI for departing from its non-profit roots. In 2023 he founded xAI; in late 2023 xAI released Grok, a chatbot integrated with the X platform (formerly Twitter). xAI raised billions in 2024-2025 funding rounds. Musk's lawsuits against OpenAI over its commercial pivot have continued in parallel.

question: Elon Musk, the entrepreneur behind Tesla and SpaceX, was one of the co-founders of the AI lab OpenAI in San Francisco in 2015. He later left OpenAI's board over strategy disagreements, and in 2023 he started a competing AI lab of his own called xAI, headquartered in the same Bay Area. What does Musk's trajectory illustrate about the AI-lab landscape?
answer: The leadership of major AI labs is small and overlapping — the same people show up across different companies over time.
choices: The leadership of major AI labs is small and overlapping — the same people show up across different companies over time.
AI labs all merge eventually — every lab that ever existed is now part of one single global AI organization.
AI lab founders never compete — there is a strict non-compete agreement signed by all major labs.
AI labs all share their work — there are no real competitors because every result becomes public immediately.
context: The frontier-AI world is a small, interconnected community. Musk co-founded OpenAI, left, and now competes with it through xAI. Dario Amodei left OpenAI to found Anthropic. Sutskever left OpenAI for SSI. Karpathy left and returned and left again. The talent moves between labs constantly — not because of betrayals but because the community is small and the work is portable. Recognition skill: the 'competition' between AI labs is genuine but the people involved have often worked together.

question: Dario Amodei walked out of his post leading research at an AI lab in 2021, with his sister Daniela and several colleagues, citing differences over the lab's direction on safety. They started a new lab that now competes directly with the old one at the frontier. What is the new lab called?
answer: Anthropic, where he is CEO and which produces the Claude family of language models.
choices: Anthropic, where he is CEO and which produces the Claude family of language models.
DeepMind, where he replaced Demis Hassabis as the founding research director of the lab in London.
Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI), which he co-founded with Ilya Sutskever in spring 2024.
Hugging Face, where he serves as the lead engineer of the open-source model-hosting platform.
context: Dario Amodei left OpenAI in 2021 along with several other senior researchers — including his sister Daniela Amodei — to found Anthropic. The stated motivation was a different emphasis on AI safety research as a central concern. Anthropic produces the Claude family of language models, which compete with OpenAI's GPT line and Google's Gemini at the frontier. As of this writing, Anthropic is one of the small handful of labs producing leading-edge language models.

question: A skeptical reader sees that Anthropic, the lab Dario and Daniela Amodei helped found, describes itself as an AI-safety company, not just an AI company. She asks for proof. What is one real way that safety focus shows up in the products the lab actually ships?
answer: Claude has been trained with a process called 'Constitutional AI' that explicitly lists principles it should follow.
choices: Claude has been trained with a process called 'Constitutional AI' that explicitly lists principles it should follow.
Anthropic only ships products through paper letters mailed directly to verified United States customers.
Anthropic refuses to take any commercial customers and operates exclusively as a charity foundation.
Anthropic requires every Claude user to attend a one-week safety training at the company headquarters.
context: Anthropic published 'Constitutional AI' in late 2022 — an approach where the model is given a written 'constitution' of principles, and a process where the model critiques and revises its own outputs against those principles. Constitutional AI is part of how Claude is trained. The approach is one institutional answer to 'how do we make a useful chatbot that behaves well' — alongside OpenAI's RLHF approach and other labs' methods. This question doesn't take a position on which approach is right; the recognition skill is knowing that different labs make different choices.

question: An investor looks up who runs the AI lab Anthropic and finds a brother and a sister: Dario Amodei in charge, Daniela Amodei as president. Such a pair is rare among the big AI labs, where most are led by non-family co-founders or by one dominant executive backed by outside investors. Why is this family structure worth noticing?
answer: It places trust and personal alignment at the center of decision-making, a deliberate counter to lab dynamics shaped by external boards.
choices: It places trust and personal alignment at the center of decision-making, a deliberate counter to lab dynamics shaped by external boards.
It is required by US law that all AI labs be co-founded by family members of the founder of record.
It is the same arrangement at every major AI lab, where every CEO has a sibling as the lab's president.
It is purely ceremonial, since Daniela has no real role in Anthropic and is listed only on legal paperwork.
context: Co-founding by siblings is uncommon at AI-lab scale. The Amodei structure means CEO-president alignment is built in. The November 2023 OpenAI board crisis showed how board-versus-CEO dynamics can fracture a lab; Anthropic's structure is less exposed to that specific failure mode. The recognition skill: institutional design matters as much as research direction in shaping how a lab handles pressure. Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, and others all have different structures — and those structures shape what they actually do.

question: In February 2011, the American computer company IBM (International Business Machines) unveiled a machine named Watson designed to answer trivia questions written in plain English. IBM sent Watson onto the TV quiz show 'Jeopardy!' — a fast-paced game where humans buzz in to answer word puzzles. Watson faced the two greatest 'Jeopardy!' champions of all time in a match watched by millions. What happened?
answer: Watson defeated Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, marking a high-profile milestone for natural-language question answering.
choices: Watson defeated Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter, marking a high-profile milestone for natural-language question answering.
Watson was unable to understand any of the clues and lost both games by wide margins to both humans.
Watson tied with Ken Jennings in a memorable three-game series that has never been beaten since.
Watson refused to compete at the last minute and the show ran with two human players instead.
context: Watson beat Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter on 'Jeopardy!' in February 2011. The win required parsing the show's punny clue style, retrieving relevant facts, and producing a fast, confident answer. Watson was a complex system — not a single neural network but a stack of techniques, hand-tuned for the task. The win was a watershed for AI's public visibility — though Watson's later commercial deployments in healthcare and other industries had a more mixed record. Recognition skill: a polished demo and a working product are not always the same thing.

question: Herbert Simon had predicted the day for 1968, and people went on waiting for decades before Deep Blue beat the world chess champion. The result was a landmark for AI. Why was it so significant beyond the chess world?
answer: It was the first time a reigning world champion had lost a match to a machine, a long-anticipated milestone finally crossed.
choices: It was the first time a reigning world champion had lost a match to a machine, a long-anticipated milestone finally crossed.
It was the first time a machine had ever played chess in any competitive setting at any level.
It was the first time IBM had ever sold a product in the chess-equipment market for any reason.
It was the first time the FIDE chess federation had certified a machine as a registered player.
context: Deep Blue won the 1997 match 3.5 to 2.5 (one win each plus a draw, with Deep Blue winning the final game). The chess-vs-AI competition had been a recurring AI benchmark since Herbert Simon's 1958 prediction. Once Deep Blue won, the goalpost moved: chess was demoted from 'real AI' to 'just search.' Kasparov, who had beaten Deep Blue's predecessor a year earlier, accused IBM of unsporting conduct around the match. The episode is a canonical example of the AI-effect pattern.

question: In modern AI, a neural network is a stack of math layers that learns from examples. Before the transformer arrived in 2017, the top design for handling sequences like sentences or stock prices was the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. LSTMs could remember important information from far back in a sequence while forgetting noise in between. When was the LSTM invented, and by whom?
answer: 1997 — by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber, then working in Munich and Switzerland.
choices: 1997 — by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber, then working in Munich and Switzerland.
2012 — by the same Toronto team that built AlexNet, as a follow-up to their image-recognition work.
2017 — by the same Google team that introduced the transformer in 'Attention Is All You Need.'
1956 — by Marvin Minsky during the Dartmouth conference that named the AI field.
context: LSTM was published in 1997 by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber. The key idea: a recurrent neural network with carefully designed 'gates' that let information flow through long sequences without vanishing. LSTMs were the workhorse for language tasks through the 2000s and 2010s — speech recognition, machine translation, sequence modeling generally. Then the transformer (2017) largely replaced them for large-scale language work. LSTMs are still used in some applications. Schmidhuber's role in deep-learning history is sometimes contested; he has often pointed out priority claims when credit is given elsewhere.

question: Fei-Fei Li, then a computer-science professor at Princeton, believed vision AI would never advance until researchers had a truly enormous, hand-labeled dataset to train on. So starting in 2007 she and her team took on a massive undertaking: paying workers to hand-label millions of internet images by category — dog, cat, chair, violin. The project she launched turned out to be foundational for the modern deep-learning revolution. What was it?
answer: ImageNet, a massive labeled dataset of millions of images organized by category that made deep-learning vision possible.
choices: ImageNet, a massive labeled dataset of millions of images organized by category that made deep-learning vision possible.
PageRank, the algorithm Google used to rank web search results from its earliest days as a product.
TensorFlow, the open-source machine-learning framework released by Google for training neural networks.
OpenAI, the research lab co-founded with Sam Altman and others to develop AGI for broad benefit.
context: Fei-Fei Li launched ImageNet at Princeton in 2007 and continued it at Stanford. The dataset eventually contained 14 million images, each labeled by category through a massive crowdsourcing effort. ImageNet became the benchmark that drove the deep-learning revolution: AlexNet won ImageNet 2012, and the rest of the field reorganized around the dataset and the techniques that worked on it. Li has since been a prominent advocate for ethical AI development and co-founded Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI.

question: In director Stanley Kubrick's 1968 science-fiction film '2001: A Space Odyssey', astronauts on a mission to Jupiter travel with a talking computer named HAL 9000. HAL controls the ship's life support and — famously — turns against the human crew. Movie fans studying the film noticed something curious about the three letters H-A-L and pointed to a possible hidden meaning. What did the film's choice of name 'HAL' allegedly come from?
answer: The three letters shifted one position back from IBM in the alphabet (H-A-L → I-B-M), though Arthur C. Clarke later denied this.
choices: The three letters shifted one position back from IBM in the alphabet (H-A-L → I-B-M), though Arthur C. Clarke later denied this.
The first three letters of the actor who voiced the computer, which was a stage-name convention at the time.
An acronym for 'Heuristic Algorithm Lifeform,' invented by Kubrick as a serious AI-research reference.
A backronym for 'Highly Advanced Logic,' suggested to Kubrick by an MIT computer scientist during pre-production.
context: HAL 9000 in '2001: A Space Odyssey' (1968) is one of cinema's iconic fictional AIs. The IBM-shift coincidence (H = I-1, A = B-1, L = M-1) was widely noted at the time. Arthur C. Clarke, who co-wrote the film with Kubrick and wrote the novel, said the name was actually meant as 'Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer.' The IBM connection is one of those persistent cultural readings that the creators officially deny but everyone remembers. Either way, HAL set a template for fictional AI gone wrong.

question: In August 2022, the British startup Stability AI released Stable Diffusion, a text-to-image model. Other image generators already existed — OpenAI's DALL-E and the artist-favored Midjourney — but you could only use those through their companies' websites or APIs. Stable Diffusion did something the others hadn't: it published the trained model weights publicly, free for anyone to download and run on a personal machine. Why was that release a big deal beyond just image quality?
answer: It was the first major open-source image generator with downloadable weights, breaking the closed-API pattern of DALL-E and Midjourney.
choices: It was the first major open-source image generator with downloadable weights, breaking the closed-API pattern of DALL-E and Midjourney.
It was the first AI image generator that the US government formally certified as safe for use in elementary schools.
It was the first AI image generator that worked entirely on smartphones without needing any cloud computing access.
It was the first AI image generator that could produce images in every language other than English with high quality.
context: Stable Diffusion's August 2022 release made open-source image generation a real thing. The weights were downloadable; anyone with a decent GPU could run the model locally. The ecosystem that grew up around it — fine-tunes, LoRAs, ControlNet, custom interfaces — was a countervailing force against the closed-API alternatives. Stability AI's subsequent corporate trajectory has been less smooth, but the open-weights release shaped how creative AI works today. The pattern parallels what Meta's Llama did for text models.

question: Fei-Fei Li, then a computer scientist at Princeton, believed AI could only learn to see if it first had millions of labeled example images to study. In the mid-2000s she started building ImageNet — a dataset of over 14 million photos, each tagged by hand with what it contained. Labeling that many pictures one by one would have taken any single university team decades. Her big trick got the job done in a few years and helped spark the 2012 deep-learning revolution. How did her team pull it off?
answer: They used Amazon Mechanical Turk, paying many low-cost human workers small amounts per image to label categories.
choices: They used Amazon Mechanical Turk, paying many low-cost human workers small amounts per image to label categories.
They wrote a program that automatically labeled all the images by analyzing their pixels without any human help.
They drafted Stanford undergraduates to spend a full school year labeling every image in the dataset by hand.
They bought the labels from an Italian company that had been hand-labeling images for industrial use since 1980.
context: Mechanical Turk was Amazon's crowdsourcing platform for small online tasks.
