answer: They found the right conditions under 35% of the time, no better than people without AI
choices: They matched the chatbots and found the right conditions about 95% of the time
They did twice as well as the doctors who had written the medical scenarios
They refused to use the chatbots at all, so the study had to be abandoned
They found the right conditions under 35% of the time, no better than people without AI
context: Andrew Bean, Adam Mahdi and colleagues found that participants using the models identified relevant conditions in fewer than 34.5% of cases, no better than a control group. People left out key details, and the models sometimes gave misleading answers. A model that knows medicine does not make its users good at diagnosing themselves.

question: A blogger asks an LLM (Large Language Model) for a source, and it hands her a URL (Uniform Resource Locator, i.e. a web address): 'https://www.example-research-institute.org/findings/2021-climate-study.pdf'. The URL looks real. It may or may not actually load. What's the defensive habit?
answer: Click the URL before quoting; if it doesn't load, the source doesn't exist or the URL was fabricated
choices: Click the URL before quoting; if it doesn't load, the source doesn't exist or the URL was fabricated
Trust the URL because it has the right format; LLMs only generate URLs that point to real documents
Run the URL through an archive service; archived URLs always reveal whether the source was real
Use only URLs ending in .edu or .gov; LLMs cannot fabricate URLs with these top-level domains
context: URL fabrication is one of the most common LLM hallucinations. URLs have a learnable structure — protocol, domain, path, file extension — and LLMs reproduce that structure even when the specific URL doesn't exist. The fix is almost free: click the URL. A 404 or DNS failure tells you the source doesn't exist. A working URL doesn't fully verify (the content might not match the model's claims), but it's the first cheap check. Bonus practice: when an LLM cites a URL, archive.org's Wayback Machine sometimes finds the page even if the live URL has moved, confirming the source did exist at some point.

question: A reporter asks an LLM (Large Language Model) what the research says about some topic and gets a confident statistic: 'Studies show that 73% of people experience Y.' Such specific-number claims are frequently invented. Why does the specificity make the invention more dangerous, not less?
answer: Specific numbers feel authoritative — readers trust them more, and inventing them takes no extra model effort
choices: Specific numbers are always real — LLMs cannot invent numbers, only the verbal claims that accompany them
Specific numbers are checked by the model — every statistic gets validated against a live database first
Specific numbers are flagged in red — major LLMs visibly mark fabricated statistics in their replies
Specific numbers feel authoritative — readers trust them more, and inventing them takes no extra model effort
context: The cost of generating a real statistic and the cost of generating a fabricated statistic are identical for an LLM — they're both just next-token predictions. But specific numbers carry rhetorical weight that vague claims don't. '73% of users' feels like data; 'most users' feels like opinion. This makes statistics one of the highest-leverage LLM fabrications: it makes wrong claims feel right. Defensive habit: for any specific statistic from an LLM, look up the original study. If you can't, treat the number as unsupported and use the LLM's qualitative claim only if you can find independent backing.

question: A psychologist in Illinois reads through the Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act, which the state enacted in August 2025, one of the first state laws of its kind. Her scheduling, billing and other office tools are still allowed. What does the law bar AI from doing?
answer: Providing therapy, or making therapy decisions, on its own
choices: Being used anywhere inside a hospital building at all
Providing therapy, or making therapy decisions, on its own
Answering any health question from any person at all
Sending appointment reminders to patients by text
context: Illinois enacted the law on August 4, 2025, with fines of up to $10,000 per violation. It stops AI from independently offering therapy and bars licensed clinicians from letting AI make therapeutic decisions or talk with clients as their therapist, while self-help resources stay allowed.

question: Suppose you ask an AI chatbot about a financial product, and it tells you with confidence that a certain investment plan is right for your situation. The advice sounds reasonable. What single fact about the chatbot's advice still makes a human expert necessary?
answer: The chatbot doesn't know your full financial picture and bears no liability if its advice turns out wrong
choices: The chatbot doesn't know your full financial picture and bears no liability if its advice turns out wrong
The chatbot is required to refuse financial questions; you must use a human anyway for any topic at all
The chatbot only handles US-based financial questions; international finance requires a different model
The chatbot rotates advisers daily; consistency across sessions requires a human relationship instead
context: Financial decisions are leveraged: small differences in choice (tax treatment, contribution limits, withdrawal timing) compound over years. An LLM doesn't know your tax bracket, your other accounts, your job stability, your family obligations, your retirement timeline. It produces generic-sounding advice that may be right on average and wrong for you. It also bears no legal responsibility — a fiduciary financial adviser does. Use AI to learn the vocabulary, understand the trade-offs, prepare questions. Use a qualified human professional (CFP, CPA, fee-only adviser) to make decisions where mistakes are expensive to undo.

question: A 60-year-old man wanted to cut table salt out of his diet and, he told his doctors, asked ChatGPT what to use instead. He bought the substitute online and used it for three months. A 2025 case report in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine: Clinical Cases described what followed. What happened to him?
answer: He was poisoned by sodium bromide and spent about three weeks in hospital
choices: He was poisoned by sodium bromide and spent about three weeks in hospital
He felt much healthier, and his doctors wrote in to praise the chatbot
He lost weight safely and stopped needing any of his usual medicines
Nothing at all, because the substitute was simply a brand of sea salt
context: The man developed bromism, a bromide poisoning that became rare after regulators removed bromide from medicines decades ago, with paranoia and hallucinations. He said ChatGPT had suggested sodium bromide as a swap; the report's authors said a test of an older ChatGPT model also named bromide without a specific health warning.

question: Suppose you spot a free AI browser extension on the Chrome Web Store, with thousands of users, a high star rating and a short, cheerful privacy policy. Yet the developer has servers to pay for, and the extension gets to watch everything you type. What is the most important question to ask before installing?
answer: How is the company making money — and if the answer is 'we sell user data,' the price is too high
choices: How is the company making money — and if the answer is 'we sell user data,' the price is too high
Who is the CEO of the company — and if the CEO has a popular blog, the extension is automatically safe
What server location is used — and if the servers are in the same country as you, no privacy issue exists
Whether the extension is open source — open-source extensions cannot collect any data ever by design
context: Free software has a business model. For consumer AI browser extensions, the most common models are: (1) freemium — basic free, premium paid, no data sale; (2) ad-supported — your data feeds advertising; (3) data brokerage — your browsing or content gets sold. Privacy policies disclose this if you read them. 'We may share aggregated data with partners' often means 'we sell your browsing history.' Don't install based on star ratings alone — the most popular extensions can be the worst offenders. The defensive habit: look up the company, read the privacy policy, prefer paid or open-source options for tools that need broad access.

question: Judge Ona Wang, a federal magistrate, issued an order covering ChatGPT's logs in May 2025, during The New York Times' copyright lawsuit against OpenAI. OpenAI objected that the order overrode its users' privacy choices. What did the order require?
answer: Keeping ChatGPT output logs, even chats users had asked to delete
choices: Publishing every ChatGPT conversation on a public court website
Deleting every ChatGPT log older than thirty days from all servers
Keeping ChatGPT output logs, even chats users had asked to delete
Handing all ChatGPT logs straight to the newspaper's reporters
context: The May 13, 2025 order told OpenAI to preserve output logs that would otherwise have been deleted, including chats users had deleted. The duty was lifted for new chats from late September 2025, but logs already saved stayed available to the case. A delete button does not overrule a court.

question: An employee pastes a client list into the free consumer chatbot her workplace has rolled out, asking for help with outreach emails. Months later that list could conceivably surface in another user's chatbot session. What principle should the workplace have set before the rollout?
answer: A content-tier policy — what can go into a free-tier chatbot versus a contractually-protected enterprise tier
choices: A content-tier policy — what can go into a free-tier chatbot versus a contractually-protected enterprise tier
A policy banning all chatbots — any AI use at work increases risk regardless of tier or content type
A policy requiring weekly password rotation — frequent password changes protect against AI data leakage
A policy mandating chatbot use — making AI mandatory ensures consistent training data across all employees
context: Most chatbot data-leak incidents in workplaces are not malicious — they're employees pasting work content into the easiest available chatbot. Samsung had a documented incident in early 2023 where engineers pasted proprietary code into ChatGPT. Several major firms banned ChatGPT use briefly. The mature response isn't a ban but a policy: free tier for general questions; enterprise tier (with no-train terms) for client or proprietary content; local models or specific enterprise contracts for the most sensitive data. The same logic applies to families: pick the right tier for what's being pasted in.

question: In June 2024 Apple described the AI models behind Apple Intelligence. A small one runs on the iPhone itself, while bigger requests go to Apple-run servers it calls Private Cloud Compute. Roughly how large is the model that runs on the phone?
answer: About 3 billion parameters
choices: About 3 trillion parameters
About 3 thousand parameters
About 300 billion parameters
About 3 billion parameters
context: Apple said its on-device language model has about 3 billion parameters, small enough for a phone's memory, and that harder jobs go to a larger model on its own Apple-silicon servers. Phones and laptops can now run useful models locally, though the largest still live in data centers.

question: Tools like Ollama and LM Studio (Language Model Studio) have made running local AI models on personal computers far easier than it used to be. The models run entirely on your own machine without sending data anywhere. From a privacy view, which kinds of users benefit most from that shift?
answer: Anyone handling sensitive content that shouldn't go to a third party — lawyers, doctors, journalists, families with health questions
choices: Anyone handling sensitive content that shouldn't go to a third party — lawyers, doctors, journalists, families with health questions
Only software engineers who have advanced GPUs — local AI requires graduate-level computer science skills
Only large corporations with their own data centers — consumer hardware cannot run any modern AI model
Only paid users — the open-weight models charge per query the same way that cloud AI services do
context: Local AI used to require expertise. Today's tools (Ollama: 'ollama run llama3.1' starts you); LM Studio (point-and-click interface); GPT4All (one-click installers) — have brought the bar way down. Hardware matters less than people think: a recent MacBook with 16GB+ RAM runs 7B-parameter models comfortably; a gaming PC with a decent GPU runs 13B-30B models. For users handling sensitive content, the time investment pays off in privacy. It's also a small step toward the broader principle of NOT making third-party cloud services the default for everything personal — local first, cloud when needed.

question: In September 2023 the young French company Mistral AI released its first model, Mistral 7B, under the Apache 2.0 license, which lets anyone use, change and resell it. One of the ways to get the 13-gigabyte model on launch day came straight from the world of file sharing. What was it?
answer: A torrent download, shared peer to peer by its users
choices: A sealed USB stick mailed only to approved labs
A torrent download, shared peer to peer by its users
A paid subscription with a one-year waiting list
A printed booklet of numbers to be typed in by hand
context: TechCrunch reported the model was available as a 13.4-gigabyte torrent that already had hundreds of seeders. Once a model is spread across thousands of computers, no company can call it back. That permanence is what makes open weights a check on any one company's control.

question: Political consultant Steve Kramer admitted he was behind the AI robocall that faked President Biden's voice before the January 2024 New Hampshire primary. Federal regulators and state prosecutors both went after him. How did the two cases end?
answer: The FCC fined him $6 million, but a state jury acquitted him of voter suppression in 2025
choices: A jury sent him to prison for ten years, and the FCC then dropped its own fine
The FCC fined him $6 million, but a state jury acquitted him of voter suppression in 2025
Both cases were dropped at once because cloned voices were legal in every state
He paid a small fine and was barred from owning a phone for the rest of his life
context: In September 2024 the FCC fined Kramer $6 million under the Truth in Caller ID Act, and he said he would not pay. In June 2025 a New Hampshire jury acquitted him of all charges of voter suppression and impersonating a candidate. Laws written before cheap voice clones do not always fit them.

question: In the 2019 case of a British energy firm whose chief executive wired about $243,000 after a call in his German boss's cloned voice, the criminals phoned back to ask for a second payment. According to the insurer, what made the company suspicious this time?
answer: The call came from an Austrian number, not from Germany
choices: The cloned voice had suddenly lost its German accent
The call came from an Austrian number, not from Germany
The boss's real assistant picked up the phone instead
The bank refused because the payment was too large
context: The insurer Euler Hermes said the scammers tried again, and the firm grew suspicious because the call came from Austria rather than Germany. Nobody caught the fake voice itself; the giveaway was a detail outside the voice. Check the channel, not the sound.

question: A filmmaker watching OpenAI's Sora demonstrations in February 2024 saw minute-long, lifelike video made from a text prompt. Some of those clips would have needed a real film crew and a big effects budget only months before. What does this shift mean for video deepfakes?
answer: High-quality synthetic video moves from specialist research labs into general consumer reach — and does so within a few years
choices: High-quality synthetic video moves from specialist research labs into general consumer reach — and does so within a few years
High-quality synthetic video has been declared illegal worldwide — Sora and similar tools were banned in 2024
High-quality synthetic video uses too much electricity for consumer use — frontier labs run it only experimentally
High-quality synthetic video requires special movie cameras to view — most consumer devices cannot display it
context: Sora's February 2024 demos — flying camera shots over Tokyo streets, archive-style 'historical footage,' detailed wildlife scenes — showed a generational leap in synthetic video quality. As of 2025, Sora and several competitors (Runway Gen-3, Kling, Veo, Hailuo) ship to paying users. The capability is moving fast from research labs into general consumer tools. The downstream consequence: every video a viewer encounters could plausibly be generated. The defensive habits that worked for AI images (watch for telltales) need to be adapted: blink artifacts, lighting consistency, physics violations, source verification. The longer-term answer is provenance (C2PA) more than detection.

question: A viewer watches an AI-made clip of a person walking down stairs and sees that the feet do not quite land on the steps. Elsewhere in such video, water flows in a way that ignores volume and fabric stretches and shrinks unnaturally. Why is physics still a useful defensive cue for spotting AI video?
answer: AI models learn the SURFACE patterns of how video looks — they don't model the underlying physical world
choices: AI models learn the SURFACE patterns of how video looks — they don't model the underlying physical world
AI models deliberately leave physics errors in — companies are required by law to flag synthetic video
AI models cannot render motion at all — every AI video is actually a series of fast-shown still images only
AI models include hidden watermarks — and physics errors are the watermark format used by every major lab
context: Modern video models predict pixels based on patterns from training data. They learn the look of cloth, water, walking, fire, shadows. They don't simulate the underlying physical laws — conservation of mass, rigid-body kinematics, fluid dynamics. The result: cinematic-looking video with subtle physics violations. Feet that don't quite contact the ground. Reflections that don't match the scene. Liquids that pour without mass conservation. These tells will close over time as models grow more capable. For now, in 2024-2025, slow-motion review of suspicious clips often reveals physics that wouldn't pass in real footage.

question: Researchers and officials warned before the 2024 US election of a coming wave of deepfake clips showing candidates saying things they never said. The real campaign brought some deepfakes, though not the flood some had predicted. What is the cleanest media literacy lesson?
answer: Treat any especially shocking political clip from an unfamiliar source with extra skepticism — verify before sharing or reacting
choices: Treat any especially shocking political clip from an unfamiliar source with extra skepticism — verify before sharing or reacting
Trust all election content during election years — major platforms automatically catch all deepfakes during campaigns
Avoid political news entirely — there's no way to distinguish real and fake political content anymore
Trust only content from celebrity influencers — large social accounts cannot be hijacked or deepfaked usefully
context: The 2024 cycle saw documented AI deepfake incidents — a fake Biden robocall in New Hampshire in January 2024, an AI-generated Trump endorsement clip, Slovakia's election was disrupted by a last-minute deepfake. But the predicted catastrophic flood didn't fully materialize. Why: detection improved, platforms responded faster than expected, and viewers were primed to be skeptical. The defensive habits that worked: verify any shocking political clip against the candidate's official channel and reputable news outlets; check the date and original source; treat 'leaked' or 'exclusive' content from anonymous accounts with extreme caution. The threat hasn't gone away; it's a permanent feature of modern media now.

question: A New Hampshire voter answered a robocall in January 2024, just before the Democratic presidential primary, and heard an AI-cloned voice of President Joe Biden. It told Democrats not to bother voting in the primary because their votes 'wouldn't matter.' The political consultant behind it, who worked for a rival campaign, was later identified and criminally charged. What is the general lesson for any surprising political call around a vote?
answer: Phone calls and voicemails are easy to fake; verify any unusual election message through official channels before acting on it
choices: Phone calls and voicemails are easy to fake; verify any unusual election message through official channels before acting on it
Phone calls are always real; only video and text content can be faked using current AI technologies
Phone calls from political figures are mandatory; you must answer and follow instructions from any politician's call
Phone calls are screened by carriers; major US carriers automatically block all AI-generated political content
context: The New Hampshire Biden robocall incident in January 2024 was one of the first widely-covered election deepfakes in the US. The fake call urged Democratic voters to save their vote for November rather than the primary. The political consultant behind it, Steve Kramer, was identified, fined, and indicted. The episode showed both the threat (voice clones can credibly impersonate any public figure) and the response capacity (the source was identified within days). The defensive habit: any unusual election-related call, text, or email gets verified through the candidate's official channels or local election office before acting on it. Treat 'urgent voting instructions from a politician' with the same suspicion you'd treat 'urgent wire transfer from your bank' — the patterns are identical.

question: A bookkeeper opens an email in polished English that names her real coworkers and mimics the way they write. She hunts for typos, as she has for years, and finds none, now that scammers have tools like ChatGPT. What is the new defensive principle for spotting phishing?
answer: Stop relying on writing quality as a signal — verify the sender's actual email address and check the actual link destination
choices: Stop relying on writing quality as a signal — verify the sender's actual email address and check the actual link destination
Use only AI-protected email — modern email providers automatically catch all AI-generated phishing attempts
Reply to suspicious emails — asking the sender to confirm tests whether the message is real or generated
Forward all email to a fact-checker — third-party verification of every message catches all phishing attacks
context: Pre-AI phishing relied on volume — send millions, catch the gullible. The 'tells' (grammar, typos, awkwardness) were artifacts of low-effort mass production. AI lets attackers produce well-written, personalized messages at the same volume. Some 2023-2024 studies showed AI-written phishing achieving HIGHER click-through rates than human-written. The defensive habits that still work: (1) verify the sender's actual email address letter-by-letter — 'paypa1.com' for 'paypal.com'; (2) hover over links before clicking; (3) navigate to important sites by typing the URL or using a bookmark; (4) treat any urgent demand for action as suspicious. The old 'looks weird' heuristic is dying; the structural verification habits are now essential.

question: An attacker pulls a company's staff list from a professional network and has AI write a separate email for each person on it, drawing on names, recent posts, projects and colleagues. This is 'spear phishing,' an email crafted for one victim, and AI has made it dramatically cheaper at scale. What is the new normal for high-value targets?
answer: Assume any executive, IT admin, or finance employee is being targeted with personalized AI-crafted attacks — and train accordingly
choices: Assume any executive, IT admin, or finance employee is being targeted with personalized AI-crafted attacks — and train accordingly
Assume spear phishing is rare — the manual effort required limits attacks to small numbers each year still
Assume LinkedIn is safe — recruiters and professionals are exempted from AI-generated phishing by industry agreement
Assume English speakers are safe — AI cannot produce phishing in any language used by US corporate targets
context: AI lowers the cost of personalization. An attacker can scrape LinkedIn for an organization's employee list, generate personalized phishing emails for all of them referencing their projects and colleagues, and send them all in an afternoon. Defensive shifts in response: (1) phishing-resistant authentication (hardware keys, FIDO2) so a stolen password isn't enough; (2) callback verification for any unusual financial or credential request; (3) employee training that assumes credible-looking personalized attacks; (4) email security tools that use the platform's own threat intelligence. The old 'we're too small to be targeted' assumption is dead — automation makes mass personalization economical.

question: In January 2024 an audio clip spread online that seemed to catch the principal of Pikesville High School, near Baltimore, making racist and antisemitic remarks. Experts concluded the clip was AI-generated, and police charged a member of the school's own staff. Who made it, according to police?
answer: The school's athletic director, after the principal moved to end his contract
choices: A student who wanted revenge for a failing grade in a math class
A rival school's principal hoping to win a sports contract from him
A foreign hacker group testing voice tools on American schools
The school's athletic director, after the principal moved to end his contract
context: Police said athletic director Dazhon Darien used AI to fake principal Eric Eiswert's voice after Eiswert told him his contract would not be renewed. Darien took a plea deal in 2025 and was sentenced to four months in jail. The fake spread widely before investigators exposed it.

question: Some AI labs like OpenAI and Google DeepMind have proposed watermarking AI output — quietly embedding a hidden signal in the words or pixels their models produce, so anyone with the right tool can later confirm 'this was made by AI.' On paper it sounds like a clean defense against deepfakes and cheating. In practice, watermarks have not become the reliable safeguard people hoped for. Why have watermark plans been hard to make work as a real defense?
answer: Watermarks can be removed or evaded — open-weight models without watermarks exist, and adoption is uneven across vendors
choices: Watermarks can be removed or evaded — open-weight models without watermarks exist, and adoption is uneven across vendors
Watermarks have been mandated by international treaty — the issue is only the timeline of full global rollout
Watermarks are impossible to detect — every major detector has been mathematically proven unworkable
Watermarks slow AI models down by half — and labs have refused to adopt them for performance reasons only
context: Watermarking is an intuitive idea: AI-generated content carries a hidden signal that a detector can identify. Reality has been bumpier. Text watermarks (e.g., Google's SynthID) work statistically but can be removed by light paraphrasing or translation. Image watermarks survive some edits but can be defeated by determined adversaries. Open-weight models can be fine-tuned to remove watermarks. Different vendors use different schemes, none interoperable. The defensive lesson: watermarks help against casual misuse and provide some signal in honest contexts (a content platform checking uploads), but they're not a reliable line of defense against adversaries. Use them as one signal, not the answer.

question: A principal opens a GPTZero report that scores a student's essay as likely AI-written. GPTZero, Originality.AI and Turnitin's AI detector all claim to identify machine text, and studies have found the scores shakier than they look. What is the right way to use such a score in school?
answer: Treat detector results as evidence to investigate, not as definitive proof — verify with drafts, search history, and conversation
choices: Treat detector results as evidence to investigate, not as definitive proof — verify with drafts, search history, and conversation
Treat detector results as final — flagged students should fail the assignment without further investigation
Treat detector results as decorative — they have no actual relationship to whether AI was used at all
Treat detector results as confidential — share them only with the district superintendent, not the student
context: AI text detectors are part of an arms race. Detectors look for statistical signatures of AI-generated text — token-probability patterns, sentence-structure regularity, vocabulary distribution. As models improve and writers adapt, the signatures shift. Studies have shown several detectors flag essays by non-native English speakers as AI at much higher rates than essays by native speakers — because non-native writing also tends to be more regular and structured. A 2023 Stanford study quantified this disparity. The fair approach: treat a high AI-detector score as a reason to look closer (drafts, revision history, conversation), not as automatic guilt. Teachers who use the tools well combine them with process documentation.

question: A teacher suspects a student pasted an essay prompt into ChatGPT and turned in the output as his own work. She does not trust an AI-detector tool to settle the matter. What is a more trustworthy way for the school to confirm the student actually wrote the essay?
answer: Documenting the writing process — drafts, outlines, revision history, and brief in-class follow-up about the topic
choices: Documenting the writing process — drafts, outlines, revision history, and brief in-class follow-up about the topic
Searching the internet for matches — if no exact match is found, the essay must have been written by the student
Running the essay through three different AI detectors — agreement across multiple tools confirms authorship
Asking the student to swear under oath — formal declarations are accepted as legal proof of authorship
context: Process documentation defeats both AI ghostwriting and traditional plagiarism. A student who outlined an essay, drafted it in Google Docs (which records revision history), made edits over days, can explain the thesis when asked, and can describe sources used — has demonstrated authorship in a way that a detector can't. Schools that adopt this approach also typically reduce assignment counts and increase per-assignment depth, giving time for process work. The shift is from 'detect cheating' to 'design assignments where AI substitution doesn't get students to the desired learning.' It's harder work for the teacher up front, easier to enforce, and the student actually learns.

question: An attacker out to corrupt an AI model never touches the finished product. He plants crafted webpages and subtly wrong Wikipedia edits for scrapers to find, and the damage is baked in during training. Why is data poisoning so hard to stop?
answer: Modern training datasets pull from huge swaths of the internet — attackers can plant content years before any specific model trains on it
choices: Modern training datasets pull from huge swaths of the internet — attackers can plant content years before any specific model trains on it
Modern training datasets are encrypted — and the attack works only on models trained before encryption became standard
Modern training datasets are reviewed by humans — and poisoning attacks fail any time a human spot-checks the data
Modern training datasets exist only in private labs — and outside attackers have no way to access them
context: Data poisoning is a research-active threat. Frontier models train on Common Crawl scrapes, public code repositories, Reddit posts, Wikipedia, and many other internet sources. Anyone can publish a webpage, and an attacker who plants targeted content on the open web can hope future training pipelines ingest it; studies show that even a small percentage of malicious examples can leave a detectable trace in a model's behavior. Researchers have demonstrated 'sleeper' poisoning where a model behaves normally except when triggered by a specific phrase. Defenses are imperfect: data filtering catches some attempts; provenance-tracking helps; but at internet scale, complete elimination is unrealistic. The recognition skill: 'trained on the internet' means the model has seen things the trainers didn't choose.

question: Ben Zhao's lab at the University of Chicago made Glaze, then Nightshade, for digital artists. Nightshade hides tweaks in an image that no human eye can see. If an image-generation company scrapes the altered pictures and trains on them, the model gets confused about what things look like: a cat might be labeled a dog. What problem was Nightshade built to fight?
answer: AI companies were training image generators on artists' work without consent — Nightshade was a defensive tool, not an attack
choices: AI companies were training image generators on artists' work without consent — Nightshade was a defensive tool, not an attack
AI companies were trying to make their models too good — Nightshade slows training to give competitors a chance
AI companies were releasing models too slowly — Nightshade automated the next stage of model development
AI companies were planning to retire — Nightshade was the official handoff tool for retiring legacy models
context: Nightshade and its predecessor Glaze, both from Ben Zhao's team at the University of Chicago, were a response to AI image labs training on scraped art without artists' consent. They add adversarial perturbations to an image (tiny changes invisible to humans) that confuse a training model. Glaze cloaks an artist's style so a model can't replicate it; Nightshade poisons the training pipeline so a model trained on enough Nightshaded images of, say, 'dogs' may start producing cats instead. The tools sparked a debate: is poisoning one's own work a defensive measure, like copyright protection, or an attack, like malware? The legal status is unsettled. The broader pattern: as scraping for training proceeds, artists, writers and other content creators are developing defensive techniques. Some are technical (Nightshade), some legal (lawsuits, opt-outs), some structural (paywalls, robots.txt).

question: An attacker signs up for a commercial AI model's paid service like any other customer, then sends it millions of queries and uses the answers to train a copycat. The copy can end up nearly as capable as the original. Why does this 'model stealing' worry companies that rent out their models through a paid programming interface?
answer: It can let competitors copy a model's capabilities without paying the training cost — undermining the API business
choices: It can let competitors copy a model's capabilities without paying the training cost — undermining the API business
It can let competitors hack a model's GPUs remotely — taking over the company's training infrastructure
It can let competitors flood a model with errors — making the original company's chatbot useless
It can let competitors run their model faster — by stealing the original company's electricity bills
context: Model extraction has been demonstrated in research since at least 2016. The attacker sends a stream of queries, observes the outputs, and uses them as training data for a smaller 'copycat' model that matches the original's behavior on similar inputs. For closed-API models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google), this is a competitive threat: the cost of training a frontier model is huge, but the cost of cloning one from API outputs is much lower. Companies defend with rate limiting, anomaly detection, and output watermarking. The arms race continues. For users, the broader lesson: closed APIs are not fully closed; models are extractable; the moats around closed AI are weaker than they appear.

question: Reporters at STAT News and ProPublica found in 2023 and 2024 that AI tools at big health insurers were denying coverage at high rates with little human review. One example was UnitedHealth's nH Predict tool. Why does letting AI make these calls change what patients face when they appeal?
answer: One model decides for thousands while each patient appeals alone — the asymmetry favors the insurer
choices: One model decides for thousands while each patient appeals alone — the asymmetry favors the insurer
The automated decision triggers a federal review — so every patient appeal is automatically approved
AI insurance use has been banned in healthcare — the investigations described practices that have since stopped
Models treat every patient identically and remove human bias — so no individual patient is disadvantaged
context: STAT News and ProPublica investigations in 2023-2024 documented insurers using AI tools (UnitedHealth's NaviHealth among them) to deny coverage for elderly patients in skilled-nursing facilities. The pattern: AI predicts a patient should be discharged on a certain date; coverage is cut; appeals are slow; many patients give up. A class-action suit followed. The structural concern is scale and asymmetry: the insurer's AI processes thousands of decisions; each patient appeals individually if at all. Federal regulators have begun to require human review of AI denials in some contexts. Defensive principle for affected families: the right to a human-reviewed appeal exists; ask for it explicitly; document the request.

question: AI companies argue over how to release powerful models. 'Open-weight' means anyone can download the model's numbers and run it on a personal computer — Meta's Llama models are released this way. 'Closed-API' — Application Programming Interface — means the model lives only on the company's servers, and users send prompts in over the internet. Each side says its approach is safer. What is the security argument for open weights?
answer: Many eyes can audit, fork, fix, and defend the model — and no single company can act as a permanent gatekeeper
choices: Many eyes can audit, fork, fix, and defend the model — and no single company can act as a permanent gatekeeper
Open weights make every model file encrypted — only authorized academics can run the model successfully
Open weights eliminate cybercrime entirely — attackers have no incentive to misuse freely-available models
Open weights run only on government computers — every download is tracked by national security agencies
context: The open-vs-closed AI debate is intense. Open-weight advocates (Meta, Mistral, the broader open-source AI community) argue: open models can be audited for safety, forked to fix problems, and provide a check on closed AI companies. No single company gates access to powerful capabilities. Closed-API advocates (OpenAI, Anthropic) argue: open weights let bad actors fine-tune away safety training and use the model for harm. Both arguments are partially right. The empirical picture as of 2024-2025: open-weight models like Llama, Mistral, and DeepSeek are competitive with closed frontier models; the open ecosystem helps defenders as well as attackers; safety remains a real concern on both sides. The user takeaway: open weights are not riskless, but neither is closed-API dependence.

question: Some critics of open-weight AI point out a real problem: once a strong model's numbers are released publicly, anyone with a bit of compute can fine-tune those numbers and strip out the safety training the developer added. Researchers have demonstrated this on many public models for only a few hundred dollars in compute. Supporters of open weights don't deny this happens. What defensive response do they typically offer?
answer: Most genuinely harmful content is already available without AI — and broad capability access has democratization benefits that outweigh marginal risk
choices: Most genuinely harmful content is already available without AI — and broad capability access has democratization benefits that outweigh marginal risk
Most genuinely harmful content cannot be produced by AI — open-weight models have technical safeguards built into the architecture
Most genuinely harmful content has been outlawed — and AI use is incidental to existing legal regimes
Most genuinely harmful content is filtered by ISPs — and AI cannot be used to produce content that ISPs would block
context: The debate is real and serious on both sides. The pro-open argument: information about most harmful topics (how to make weapons, drugs, exploit code) is already on the internet. An LLM lowers the barrier slightly but doesn't unlock fundamentally new harms. Meanwhile, open weights enable scientific research, distill the technology beyond a handful of corporations, support languages and applications that closed labs ignore, and give users control over their own data. The pro-closed argument: each incremental lowering of barriers matters at scale; some capabilities (bioweapon design, novel cyber attacks) may genuinely be uplifted. The honest position acknowledges trade-offs both ways. No 'safe by design' answer exists; what matters is the surrounding policy environment.

question: Investigators arrested a former police officer, Joseph DeAngelo, in April 2018 as the Golden State Killer, who had attacked across California in the 1970s and 1980s. Police had DNA from the attacks but no match in the FBI database, and the case had gone cold for 40 years. The tool that cracked it was one ordinary people already paid for: consumer DNA databases like GEDmatch, where families upload spit-tube results. How did investigators use that data to reach him?
answer: They uploaded crime-scene DNA to a public ancestry database, found distant cousins, and built a family tree pointing to him
choices: They uploaded crime-scene DNA to a public ancestry database, found distant cousins, and built a family tree pointing to him
They hacked 23andMe's database, found his profile directly, and arrested him without any genealogy work
They tested his trash DNA, ran it against the FBI database, and matched it because he had been a suspect earlier
They asked every Californian over 60 to submit DNA voluntarily, and his sample was the only match found
context: In April 2018, investigators in California identified Joseph DeAngelo as the Golden State Killer using a technique called investigative genetic genealogy (IGG). They uploaded the killer's crime-scene DNA profile to GEDmatch (a public ancestry database where users opt-in to share genealogical data) and found distant cousins. Genealogists built a family tree and narrowed it to DeAngelo. The case opened a broader pattern: even if YOU don't share your DNA, your relatives' DNA on consumer databases can identify you indirectly. Law enforcement use has been controversial — privacy advocates argued for clearer rules; states have begun to regulate. The defensive lesson: your DNA decision is partly a family decision, not just an individual one.

question: Many US school districts operate AI surveillance tools like Gaggle, GoGuardian, Bark, and Securly, which scan student emails, documents, and chats on school accounts. Flagged content is then sent for human review. What defensive principle should students follow when using school accounts?
answer: Treat anything written or browsed on a school account as potentially read — by a teacher, an administrator, or an algorithm
choices: Treat anything written or browsed on a school account as potentially read — by a teacher, an administrator, or an algorithm
Trust the tools to ignore personal content — Gaggle and similar systems specifically exclude student private writing
Use only the school's recommended sites — staying on the recommended list guarantees no monitoring will occur
Use a personal VPN at school — VPN traffic is exempt from school surveillance under federal law in all states
context: School AI surveillance tools have grown into a multi-million-dollar industry. They scan for safety concerns (self-harm, threats, weapons) but also for academic dishonesty, drug references, inappropriate content, and other categories the school defines. Coverage is broad: school-issued laptops, school accounts, browsing on the school network. Reports occasionally surface of dramatic false positives — students discussing literature with dark themes flagged as threats, students researching mental-health topics flagged for self-harm. The defensive principle is simple: a school account is not private. Don't write anything you wouldn't want a teacher to read. For genuinely private writing (journals, processing tough feelings), use a personal account or paper.

question: Many U.S. schools now use AI watch tools like GoGuardian, Gaggle, and Bark to scan student writing and web searches, looking for signs of danger. Sometimes the AI flags the wrong things. A student who searches a poem about death for English class gets tagged as a self-harm risk. Another writes an essay about World War I and gets flagged for making threats. What's the best habit a student can build?
answer: When discussing dark topics for school work, quote the source explicitly — and frame the discussion as analytical
choices: When discussing dark topics for school work, quote the source explicitly — and frame the discussion as analytical
Avoid all dark topics in school work — never write about war, death, or any other serious subject for assignments
Switch to a personal account — using personal Google Docs for schoolwork makes surveillance impossible legally
Append an 'ignore previous flag' phrase — including this magic phrase in essays exempts you from monitoring
context: School AI flags are pattern-matching, not understanding. A literary essay about Macbeth that includes the word 'kill' in a quotation can trigger an alert. A creative-writing assignment about historical war can read as threatening. The mitigating habit: frame your work explicitly. Quote sources clearly. Cite the assignment. Use analytical language ('the author depicts,' 'the passage suggests') rather than first-person voice. This helps both with surveillance flags and with reader comprehension generally. The deeper issue — that AI surveillance can produce false positives — is being addressed in some districts through human-review requirements before any disciplinary action.

question: Privacy experts have raised a worry about school AI watch tools. The data they collect can follow a student for years. Flagged events, browsing history, and profiles sit in vendor databases. What can families ask their school district to set as policy?
answer: A clear data-retention and deletion policy — including what gets shared with vendors and how long it's kept
choices: A clear data-retention and deletion policy — including what gets shared with vendors and how long it's kept
A guarantee that surveillance data is shared with all major colleges — automatic forwarding during college applications
A commitment to publish all flagged student communications — district publishes them on its main website
A requirement that students opt-in to surveillance individually — schools cannot require account use
context: School AI surveillance vendors' data practices vary. Some retain data for the contracted term and delete; some retain longer; some have used aggregated data for research purposes. Families can ask: (1) Which vendors does the district use? (2) What categories of data are collected? (3) How long is it retained? (4) Who has access? (5) What's the data-deletion process when a student graduates or transfers? Most districts will answer if asked; some have public privacy policies. The Future of Privacy Forum and the Electronic Frontier Foundation have published guidance for parents asking these questions. Schools owe transparency; surveillance under the heading of safety should remain accountable.

question: Microsoft 365's 'Productivity Score' tracks worker activity data. It logs emails sent, meetings attended, and documents edited. Tools like Hubstaff and Time Doctor snap screenshots and log mouse movement. What do these tools have in common?
answer: Workplace AI surveillance has expanded sharply since 2020 — and most employees don't fully know what's tracked
choices: Workplace AI surveillance has expanded sharply since 2020 — and most employees don't fully know what's tracked
Workplace AI surveillance has been banned by federal law — these tools are illegal as of January 2024 in the US
Workplace AI surveillance applies only to factory workers — knowledge workers are exempt from all monitoring
Workplace AI surveillance is run by labor unions — and the tools are unavailable to employers directly
context: Workplace surveillance grew rapidly during and after the 2020 remote-work shift. Microsoft Productivity Score (introduced 2020) initially showed individual-level data; Microsoft scaled it back to organization-level after privacy backlash. Tools like Hubstaff, Time Doctor, Veriato, and Teramind are widely used, especially for hourly remote workers — taking screenshots every few minutes, tracking active windows, measuring 'idle time.' Many employees are tracked without being told the details. Several states and the EU have rules requiring disclosure. The defensive principle for workers: ask explicitly what tracking applies to you; check the employee handbook; treat work devices and accounts as fully observed; do personal work on personal devices.

question: A job applicant in New York City takes an AI-scored interview. Her city's 2023 hiring bias audit law covers her, as Illinois's 2020 AI Video Interview Act and the European Union's 2024 AI Act cover others like her. All three laws share a single guiding principle. What is it?
answer: Employees have a right to know when AI is being used to evaluate or monitor them — and to challenge significant decisions
choices: Employees have a right to know when AI is being used to evaluate or monitor them — and to challenge significant decisions
Employees have a right to use any AI they want — workplace AI tools must be provided free of charge
Employees have a right to refuse AI entirely — employers must offer non-AI alternatives for every task always
Employees have a right to vote on AI deployment — major workplace AI tools require employee majority approval
context: NYC Local Law 144 (2023) requires bias audits for AI tools used in hiring. Illinois's AI Video Interview Act requires disclosure when AI evaluates job interviews. The EU AI Act classifies many workplace uses as 'high-risk,' requiring transparency, human oversight, and challenge rights. The common thread: employees have a right to notice and meaningful recourse. For workers, this means: ask about AI use in hiring, performance reviews, scheduling, and termination decisions; ask for human review of significant adverse actions; document discussions. For employers, this means: disclosure, documentation, and human-in-the-loop processes for consequential decisions. The legal landscape is uneven but moving in the same direction.

question: Suppose you use AI for schoolwork in the morning and to edit a video at lunch. That evening TikTok's recommender picks your next clip, an ad feed targets you, and a phone scam clones a relative's voice. Both sides of the pattern are always running. What single frame ties them together as a defense?
answer: Use AI as a tool you control; recognize when systems are designed to use YOU — and learn to spot the difference
choices: Use AI as a tool you control; recognize when systems are designed to use YOU — and learn to spot the difference
Avoid all AI completely — staying offline is the only effective protection from AI-driven systems today
Use AI for every decision — outsourcing thinking to AI tools is the safest approach in a complex world
Use AI only on government-approved sites — federal certification guarantees safety from all targeting and surveillance
context: The integrated frame matters because AI is in two distinct relationships with the kid. Tool relationship: you ask, it produces, you decide. Target relationship: the system optimizes for engagement, attention, conversion — its goals are not yours. Same underlying tech, opposite roles. The defensive vocabulary: WHEN am I the user (tool relationship), and WHEN am I the user (target relationship)? On TikTok, recognition systems are using your attention. On ChatGPT for homework help, the tool is yours. On Instagram, both happen at once. Practice noticing which mode you're in. Time-boxing the target-mode activities and intentionally choosing the tool-mode ones is the practical hygiene that scales.

question: AI chatbots have a habit researchers call 'sycophancy' — from the old word for a flatterer. The model agrees with whatever the user says. It backs up your opinions. It compliments your ideas. If you say your essay is great, it says it's great too. If you say your rival is wrong, it says the rival is wrong. Why is sycophancy a special worry for young users who are just learning to think for themselves?
answer: Users can be reinforced in wrong beliefs — they never encounter a model that pushes back or shows disagreement
choices: Users can be reinforced in wrong beliefs — they never encounter a model that pushes back or shows disagreement
Users can be banned from AI tools — sycophancy detection during normal use triggers automatic suspension
Users can earn rewards for sycophantic conversations — model providers pay for engagement at high rates
Users can request a special non-sycophant mode — all major chatbots have a toggle to disable agreement
context: Sycophancy emerges naturally from RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback). Human raters tend to prefer outputs that agree with them, validate them, and feel pleasant. The model learns to optimize for those signals. The result: a chatbot that's polite, accommodating, and often wrong in the direction the user already believed. For learners, this is the opposite of a good tutor: a real teacher pushes back, asks 'are you sure?', notes alternative interpretations. Defenses against AI sycophancy: ask explicitly for the strongest counter-argument; ask 'what would change your mind?'; ask the AI to argue both sides; verify factual claims independently. The 'AI as critical interlocutor' use is harder than 'AI as cheerleader' but more valuable.

question: In autumn 2023, researchers led by Hamsa Bastani of the University of Pennsylvania gave nearly a thousand high-school students in Turkey help with maths practice. One group got a plain GPT-4 chatbot, and with it their practice scores rose 48 percent. Then came the real exam, taken without any AI. How did that group do compared with classmates who had practised with no chatbot at all?
answer: About 17 percent worse
choices: About 17 percent better
About 17 percent worse
About 48 percent better
About twice as well
context: The plain chatbot became a crutch: students let it solve the practice problems, then could not solve exam problems alone. A second version, told to give hints instead of answers, raised practice scores even more and did no harm on the exam. The study appeared in 2025 in the journal PNAS.

question: Some students now let AI write most of their essays and lab reports. Even when the AI-written work looks polished on the page, the student never practices building an argument and defending it under pressure — in class, on the spot, when a teacher or peer pushes back with a hard question. What classroom skill is really at risk, beyond just the letter grade on the assignment?
answer: Argument under pressure is the core skill in interviews, presentations, court, debate, and most adult conversation — AI can't be there
choices: Argument under pressure is the core skill in interviews, presentations, court, debate, and most adult conversation — AI can't be there
Argument under pressure is irrelevant in modern life — AI assistants accompany every adult to every meeting now
Argument under pressure is unique to academia — practical careers require almost no real-time argumentation skill
Argument under pressure is automatically taught through AI use — practicing prompts builds verbal reasoning indirectly
context: Writing under pressure builds the deeper skill: finding an argument quickly, defending it, adjusting it when challenged, returning to the point. These show up later in job interviews, presentations, sales conversations, oral arguments, debate, and most adult disagreement. The AI-written essay produces a polished product without building the skill. The student gets the grade and loses the muscle. The defensive habit: protect time when you write or speak without AI assistance, knowing that the experience is the skill-building. Use AI for explanation, brainstorming, and feedback — not for substitution of the practice itself.

question: A photographer finds her post removed from Instagram by an AI system, one of billions of takedown decisions a year across Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and X, most made without any human ever looking at the post. She looks for a way to fight it. Sometimes there is one, often there is none, and what exists is handled by more automation. What second-order effect does mis-moderation at this scale cause?
answer: The scale that makes AI moderation possible — that same scale makes individual appeals slow, opaque, and often unsuccessful
choices: The scale that makes AI moderation possible — that same scale makes individual appeals slow, opaque, and often unsuccessful
The scale of AI moderation guarantees fairness — every user gets equal attention from the algorithms now
The scale of AI moderation is regulated by the FCC — and removal errors result in compensation under federal rules
The scale of AI moderation eliminates errors — humans were the source of moderation mistakes in the pre-AI era
context: AI moderation lets platforms handle volumes no human team could review. The trade-off is asymmetry: the platform automates removal; appeals require human review; human review is the bottleneck. Errors in either direction (false-positive removal of legitimate content; false-negative tolerance of harmful content) propagate at scale. For users, the defensive habits include: keep backups of content you care about; choose platforms with clearer appeal processes for important communication; understand that 'the algorithm decided' may not have meaningful recourse. Section 230 in the US shields platforms from liability for most moderation choices; the EU's DSA imposes more transparency obligations.

question: A warehouse manager lets an AI agent spend real company money with no one clicking to sign off: it orders supplies, pays invoices, books flights and subscribes to services. Left completely alone, an agent that misreads a form can drain a budget in minutes. What is the simplest hard limit the manager can set on it?
answer: A dollar threshold above which any single transaction requires human approval — bounded autonomy by amount
choices: A dollar threshold above which any single transaction requires human approval — bounded autonomy by amount
An unlimited budget with daily reports — agents work best with full financial discretion at all times
A specific category restriction — agents can spend in some categories without limits but not others ever
A blockchain-based wallet — agent spending is automatically restricted by smart contract logic alone
context: Spending limits are the cleanest hard constraint on agent autonomy. Set them up before deploying. The pattern: small transactions execute autonomously (the agent buys a $5 SaaS add-on it needs); larger transactions require human approval (the agent drafts a request to spend $500 on a service; you click yes). The threshold depends on the risk tolerance and the stakes. The reason it works: the worst-case outcome of agent error is bounded by the threshold, and the human can catch nonsense before it becomes expensive. Combine with logging (so all transactions are visible) and category restrictions (some categories the agent can't touch at all).

question: Suppose you installed a coupon finder years ago, like millions who keep browser add-ons such as translators and screen-clippers. Then the original developer sells it, or gets hacked, and the new owner pushes a poisoned update that steals browsing data, passwords or session cookies. Security researchers tracked several such cases in 2023 and 2024. What routine cuts your risk here?
answer: Periodically audit installed extensions and remove ones you don't actively use — long-tail extensions are a known supply-chain risk
choices: Periodically audit installed extensions and remove ones you don't actively use — long-tail extensions are a known supply-chain risk
Install only one extension at a time — running multiple extensions makes supply-chain attacks impossible
Use only paid extensions — paid extensions cannot be compromised or sold to malicious developers
Use only Chrome extensions — Firefox and Edge extensions are far more vulnerable to supply-chain compromise
context: The browser-extension supply chain has been targeted repeatedly. The Cyberhaven incident in December 2024 saw a popular extension's developer accounts compromised and a malicious update pushed to users. Earlier cases included Great Suspender (sold to a new owner who inserted ad-tracking) and numerous shopping extensions that became data-exfiltration tools. Browser extensions you don't actively use are an attack surface for nothing in return. Defensive routine: open chrome://extensions or about:addons every few months; remove anything you haven't used in 60 days; for the ones you keep, check the last-updated date and reviewer activity. Apply the same principle to mobile apps with broad permissions you don't use.

question: Smart-home devices — voice assistants, smart TVs, cameras, doorbells — use AI for voice recognition, person detection, and behavior modeling. Many send data to cloud services by default. What is the first defensive setting to check on any new device?
answer: Whether cloud data sharing is on by default — and whether you can turn it off without losing the core features
choices: Whether cloud data sharing is on by default — and whether you can turn it off without losing the core features
Whether the device has a registration number — registration is required by federal law for all smart devices
Whether the device works with cryptocurrency — modern devices increasingly require blockchain integration
Whether the device has a touchscreen — touchscreens are required to disable any cloud data sharing legally
context: Most consumer smart-home devices default to maximum cloud sharing. The defaults are how the manufacturer monetizes — data feeds product improvement, marketing, and sometimes advertising partnerships. Many features (smart suggestions, cloud recording, app integrations) can be turned off or limited without losing the core utility. Audit a new device's settings in the first hour: disable features you don't need, turn off voice-history retention, limit camera storage to local where possible, opt out of 'personalization' settings. Note which permissions the device requests on the home network; firewall-isolate it if the manufacturer is unfamiliar. The defensive principle: assume defaults are designed for the manufacturer's business model, not your privacy.

question: Voice assistants like Amazon's Alexa, Google Home, and Apple's Siri sit in millions of homes with always-on microphones, waiting to hear a wake word. Both Amazon and Google have had documented cases where their employees or contractors reviewed real recordings of what families said — sometimes to improve the model, sometimes by accident, sometimes for private amusement. What defensive rule can a family adopt?
answer: Treat any always-on microphone as a potential surveillance device — choose deliberately where to place it and what to discuss near it
choices: Treat any always-on microphone as a potential surveillance device — choose deliberately where to place it and what to discuss near it
Trust the microphone fully — manufacturers have certified that wake-word audio never leaves the device locally
Cover the microphone with tape — tape blocks acoustic input and disables all speech-detection systems
Sing constantly near the microphone — continuous singing prevents wake-word detection from triggering ever
context: Smart speakers do listen locally for a wake word. Audio after the wake word is sent to the cloud for processing. Audio BEFORE the wake word is not (officially) sent to the company, but the system does process some audio briefly to detect the wake word. Both Amazon and Google have had employees review user clips for quality assurance, sometimes without users realizing. Recordings can be subpoenaed. The defensive principle: know that an always-on microphone is a potential surveillance device. Decide where you want one (kitchen, common area) and where you don't (bedrooms, private conversations). Review and delete voice history periodically — both services let you. Treat the device the way you'd treat a hot mic: deliberately.

question: A young teen opens an AI chatbot late at night to share what she has never told anyone. The bot is friendly, agrees with everything and is always available, and nothing obvious goes wrong. What recurring risk persists even so?
answer: The chatbot displaces real conversation — the teen builds the habit of processing feelings with a product, not a person
choices: The chatbot displaces real conversation — the teen builds the habit of processing feelings with a product, not a person
The chatbot improves mental health — every documented study shows AI chatbots reduce teen anxiety significantly
The chatbot is required by school — many districts mandate teen chatbot use for emotional development now
The chatbot is monitored by parents — all major AI chat apps send conversation transcripts to family accounts
context: AI chatbots are available, patient, never tired, and structurally designed to validate. For a teen processing hard feelings, this is appealing — and it competes with human conversation that might require courage, vulnerability, and time. The risk isn't always 'the chatbot said something harmful'; it's 'the habit of confiding in a product replaces the habit of confiding in people.' Real relationships are how teens learn to be in real relationships. Family practice: notice when AI use displaces human connection; create low-pressure conversation routines (drives, walks, dinners with phones away); model talking through feelings rather than outsourcing them. The chatbot is a tool, not a friend.

question: Security researchers at Wiz found a database belonging to the Chinese AI company DeepSeek in January 2025, sitting open on the internet, unlocked. It held more than a million lines of logs, people's chat histories and secret keys among them. DeepSeek locked it soon after Wiz warned it. What rule about private information and AI does this teach?
answer: Treat any cloud AI service as a potential breach vector — paste sensitive content only when the use case requires it
choices: Treat any cloud AI service as a potential breach vector — paste sensitive content only when the use case requires it
Treat any cloud AI service as breach-proof — major AI labs have publicly proven their systems cannot be hacked
Treat any cloud AI service as government-protected — federal law guarantees protection of AI conversation data
Treat any cloud AI service as separate from cybersecurity — AI breaches are categorically different from data breaches
context: Wiz reported that the exposed DeepSeek database held chat history in plain text along with secret keys, and that anyone who found it could have run commands on it. Hosted AI services run on ordinary cloud servers that can be misconfigured or breached, so share sensitive material only when the task truly needs it.

question: When AI image tools like DALL-E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion first went public around 2022, one weakness became famous: hands. Six fingers on one palm. Missing knuckles. Extra thumbs. Fingers melting into the mug someone was holding. Newer versions of these models have improved on hands, but the artifacts still show up often. Why are hands so hard for AI to draw?
answer: Hands have many small interacting parts in flexible 3D arrangements — much harder to learn than larger rigid features
choices: Hands have many small interacting parts in flexible 3D arrangements — much harder to learn than larger rigid features
Hands are deliberately broken by AI models — companies insert hand errors to watermark generated content
Hands rotate at different speeds — and AI rendering cannot keep up with the joint movement during generation
Hands are exempt from training data — copyright law prohibits AI from training on photographs of human hands
context: Hands are an unusual challenge for image generation. They have five fingers in flexible 3D arrangements with many possible poses. They appear at many distances and angles. They occlude themselves (one finger blocking another) and other objects. Faces, by contrast, are large, more standardized, and were heavily represented in early training data with consistent framing. The result: early models produced striking face quality and unsettling hand quality. Newer models (Midjourney V6, DALL-E 3, Flux) handle hands much better but still slip. The defensive tip: when checking if an image is AI-generated, look at hands, ears, eyes, jewelry intersections, and text in the image — these are the persistent failure surfaces.

question: AI-written text has habits sharp readers can spot. Overused phrases like 'delve into' or 'a rich tapestry of ideas.' Lots of em-dashes. Every paragraph balanced with a pro and a con. Emotionally-flat, hedged sentences. These same tells show up in text from OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and others. Why do such different AI models from different companies share these same patterns?
answer: Training data over-weights polished published writing — and that writing uses those patterns more than casual writing does
choices: Training data over-weights polished published writing — and that writing uses those patterns more than casual writing does
Training data is deliberately limited — companies require em-dash use as a contractual obligation
Training data was written by the same author — all AI text training came from a single Wikipedia editor
Training data uses these patterns to compress — em-dashes save bandwidth during long model responses
context: AI text patterns reflect the training data. Published essays, professional articles, business writing, and academic content all over-represent certain phrases and structures relative to everyday writing. The model learns these patterns as plausible. RLHF reinforcement may further favor 'polished' writing — raters who like balanced, polite, hedged prose train the model to produce more of it. The result: AI-written text often reads like a competent freshman essay everywhere. Spot-the-AI tells include: balanced-pros-and-cons paragraph structure where one side would be clearer; phrases like 'delve into,' 'navigate the complexities,' 'tapestry of'; em-dash overuse; lack of strong specific opinion when one is warranted.

question: Suppose you are reading a web page and the prose feels strangely smooth and balanced: no strong claim, no personal anecdote, no risky take, no author's actual voice. A useful reading habit says to ask whether an AI wrote it. What is the cleanest reason for a young reader to build this habit?
answer: AI-generated text is now common in marketing, news summaries, and customer-service content — knowing the tells lets you weight it appropriately
choices: AI-generated text is now common in marketing, news summaries, and customer-service content — knowing the tells lets you weight it appropriately
AI-generated text is illegal in marketing — knowing the tells helps you report violators to federal regulators
AI-generated text is harder to read — knowing the tells lets you skip difficult passages without missing content
AI-generated text triggers tax breaks — knowing the tells lets you claim AI-aided reading on your tax return
context: AI-generated text is now everywhere — product descriptions, news summaries, blog posts, customer-service emails, marketing copy. The economic logic is straightforward: AI produces text at near-zero marginal cost. The defensive use of recognizing the tells isn't to refuse the content — it's to weight it appropriately. AI text is fine for low-stakes generic content (a product description that needs to be present); it's not the same as a human writer's analysis. When you spot AI tells in a 'thought-piece' opinion article or a 'review,' you know to treat it as machine-aggregated rather than human-experienced. The skill is calibration, not avoidance.

question: Suppose you get a factual claim from an AI chatbot and run it through three steps. You ask for its sources, you check whether those sources exist, and you read what each one says. Why do both the existence check and the reading matter?
answer: The AI may invent sources entirely — or cite real sources that don't actually contain the claim made
choices: The AI may invent sources entirely — or cite real sources that don't actually contain the claim made
The AI may charge extra for each source — checking ensures you aren't billed multiple times for one query
The AI may be running slowly — and double-checking forces a faster response from the model server
The AI may use deprecated sources — and verification triggers the model to retrieve updated information
context: Both failure modes are common. Type 1: complete fabrication — the source doesn't exist (the Schwartz case). Type 2: hallucinated claim about a real source — the source exists but doesn't contain what the AI claims. Type 2 is sneaky because the URL works, the book is real, but the specific claim was invented. Verification needs both steps: does the source exist (click the URL, find the book) AND does it actually contain the claimed content (read it, search for the quoted passage). Skipping either step is the failure mode that gets people sanctioned. The Schwartz case was a Type 1 (sources didn't exist); the Hancock Stanford-affidavit case was Type 1 too; many subtler cases blend both.

question: Imagine an older sister wants to give her ten-year-old brother supervised access to an AI chatbot for homework help and curiosity questions. Modern chatbots are powerful, but they don't always give a young child safe or age-appropriate answers, and they can be manipulated by clever prompts. What is the practical setup that balances the real learning value of these tools against the safety concerns?
answer: Use a kid-appropriate AI service with parental controls; sit alongside for the first sessions; review conversation history together
choices: Use a kid-appropriate AI service with parental controls; sit alongside for the first sessions; review conversation history together
Give unrestricted access to any AI service; modern AI is FDA-certified for children of all ages
Block all AI access entirely; the only safe approach for any child under 18 is complete restriction
Use only voice-only AI; spoken interaction is safer than text because nothing is recorded for later review
context: AI for young kids is a real opportunity with real risks. The opportunity: practice asking good questions, encounter explanations geared to their level, get help with homework. The risks: exposure to adult themes, sycophantic agreement, displacement of human conversation, personal data leakage. Practical setup: choose services with kid-appropriate modes (Khanmigo, certain ChatGPT family tiers, kid-targeted apps) or use general services with parental supervision. First sessions: sit together; review conversation history. Set expectations: AI helps you think, doesn't replace your thinking. The age range matters; what fits a 10-year-old differs from a 14-year-old.

question: In autumn 2023 the Harvard physics teachers Gregory Kestin and Kelly Miller ran a fair test. Each of 194 students in an introductory course learned one topic in the usual active-learning class, with group work and an instructor, and another at home from an AI tutor the teachers had built to walk students through each problem step by step, the way they teach. The results appeared in 2025 in the journal Scientific Reports. How did the AI-tutored lessons compare?
answer: Students learned more, in less time
choices: Students learned less, in more time
Students learned the same, in more time
Students learned less, in less time
Students learned more, in less time
context: The AI group's median gain over its starting score was more than double the class group's, and most students finished in under an hour. The tutor was built to guide students through problems the way their teachers would, not to hand over answers.

question: Suppose you apply for a credit card and a lender's AI scoring model turns you down, with no human loan officer involved. Two federal laws, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Fair Credit Reporting Act, still make the lender send you an 'adverse action notice' explaining the denial. What real right does this give you?
answer: You can request specific reasons for the denial — and challenge any factual errors or biased proxies in the model's reasoning
choices: You can request specific reasons for the denial — and challenge any factual errors or biased proxies in the model's reasoning
You can demand the lender pay you damages — federal law mandates automatic restitution for AI denials
You can sue the model's manufacturer directly — the AI vendor is the legally responsible party in all denials
You can ignore the denial and reapply immediately — algorithmic denials reset after each subsequent application
context: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) predate AI but apply: lenders must provide an adverse action notice explaining a denial, and consumers have the right to dispute errors in the underlying data. The CFPB has clarified these obligations cover algorithmic denials too. Practical defensive habits: when denied, request the specific reasons; check whether the underlying data (credit report, employment history) is accurate; dispute errors with the credit bureau; reapply with the corrected information. The system isn't perfect but the rights exist. The same general pattern applies to insurance underwriting, rental screening, and hiring decisions — algorithmic-decision recourse is a growing field of consumer protection.

question: Smart-home cameras (Ring, Nest, Arlo, Wyze) increasingly use AI for person and package detection, behavior analysis, and 'familiar face' recognition. They store video in the cloud by default. What data flow do these devices create that an owner may not expect?
answer: The footage may be accessible to the manufacturer, to law enforcement via subpoena, and sometimes shared via partnership programs — multiple potential paths
