In the US, when Porcha Woodruff's wrongful arrest was reported in 2023, all six people known to have been falsely accused through a face match were Black.

question: The city leaders of Minneapolis passed a law in 2021 to rein in police use of facial recognition, after San Francisco in 2019 and Boston and Portland in 2020. Other cities have expanded use. What is the policy debate, in plain terms?
answer: Whether the technology should be available as a routine tool requiring no warrant, only used in specific serious cases with oversight, or banned outright pending better accuracy and rules
choices: Whether the technology should be available as a routine tool requiring no warrant, only used in specific serious cases with oversight, or banned outright pending better accuracy and rules
Whether facial recognition exists at all, with some cities denying the technology has ever been developed by any vendor
Whether facial recognition should replace all police officers, with every U.S. city now debating dissolving police departments
Whether facial recognition is a federal monopoly, where only one U.S. agency is permitted to use the technology by law
context: The policy landscape is patchwork: some cities ban police use outright, some require warrants, some allow routine use. Police make their own case. New York's police commissioner James O'Neill wrote in 2019 that face matches had led to 998 arrests the year before, in cases from murder to rape, and that his department treats a match only as a lead that detectives must verify, never as grounds for arrest by itself. Critics answer with the wrongful arrests. The rules are being written city by city, state by state, and the differences track local political choices, not technical facts.

question: A Pentagon planner studies where Nvidia's H100 and its later successors are actually made. The designs come from many countries, but nearly every advanced AI chip in the world is manufactured by a single company, and the silicon wafers all pour out of one place. Which firm is it, and why does that fact keep the planner awake at night?
answer: TSMC, based in Taiwan, fabricates the bulk of frontier AI silicon — a Chinese blockade or invasion of Taiwan would freeze the global supply of leading-edge chips overnight.
choices: TSMC, based in Taiwan, fabricates the bulk of frontier AI silicon — a Chinese blockade or invasion of Taiwan would freeze the global supply of leading-edge chips overnight.
Foxconn, based in mainland China, assembles every Nvidia accelerator — the United States cannot ship any chip out of the country without Beijing's signed approval.
Samsung, based in South Korea, holds the patents on every transistor design — no other firm in the world can legally produce frontier silicon without Samsung's licence.
Intel, based in Arizona, fabricates the global supply singlehandedly — a wildfire or earthquake in the Phoenix area would knock out frontier AI production worldwide for years.
context: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) produces roughly 90% of the world's leading-edge logic chips, including the GPUs used to train and run frontier AI models. Nvidia designs the H100 and its successors but does not own a fab — TSMC builds them. This single-island concentration is the central fact behind the US CHIPS Act (2022), the Arizona TSMC fabs under construction, and Washington's anxiety about a Taiwan Strait crisis. Recognition skill: the bottleneck on AI capability is not the model weights, which can be copied. It is the physical fab that prints the silicon.

question: A reader took financial advice from CNET (in 2023 the site quietly let AI write such articles), factual errors included. At Gizmodo, the owner G/O Media pushed AI articles over staff objections, and BuzzFeed News shut down. Across these cases, what does losing the reviewers while keeping the AI authors actually remove?
answer: The human attention that would have caught the AI's mistakes before publication day
choices: The human attention that would have caught the AI's mistakes before publication day
The legal liability for the published errors, since federal law shifts responsibility to the vendor
The total cost of running the newsroom, since AI authoring is more expensive than human staff
The audience itself, since readers refuse on principle to read any article authored by an AI
context: CNET in 2023 quietly used AI to write financial-advice articles; the articles contained factual errors. Gizmodo's owner G/O Media pushed AI articles over the objections of staff. The pattern: AI lowers the marginal cost of producing content; cutting human review further lowers the cost; errors accumulate. The economic logic favors low-quality high-volume publishing — and the journalists who would have caught the errors are no longer there to catch them. Recognition skill: 'AI augments humans' and 'AI replaces humans' are different decisions, and the second one creates new failure modes the first one doesn't.

question: An illustrator in 2022 found her own work inside LAION-5B (Large-scale Artificial Intelligence Open Network), the giant web collection that trained Stability AI's Stable Diffusion image model, shipped that August with open weights. Nobody had asked her. Some artists sued, and Getty Images sued too. Whose voice usually shapes the new rules when a technology grows faster than the law?
answer: Whoever was at the table while the rules were settled — the labs and large rights-holders, not the individual creators whose work was scraped
choices: Whoever was at the table while the rules were settled — the labs and large rights-holders, not the individual creators whose work was scraped
Individual artists alone — federal law has guaranteed that working creators dictate every AI training rule in every jurisdiction
Nobody's interests — courts ignore stakeholder positioning and decide every technology case on pure abstract legal principle
Foreign governments only — under federal law, US copyright rules for AI are written exclusively by overseas regulators
context: The 2023 class action against Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt argued that artists' styles and works were copied into the models without consent. Getty Images sued Stability AI separately. The cases will take years to resolve. The broader pattern: the AI labs trained on whatever they could scrape, and the legal questions are being adjudicated after the fact. The original creators — most without resources to litigate — are usually outside the conversations setting the eventual rules. When a technology grows faster than its legal framework, the resulting rules tend to favor whoever was at the table.

question: A child signs up for an 'AI friend' app, one of the chatbots some firms aim at children alongside homework help and tutoring. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) applies to what he types, but enforcement is spotty. How does a breach of COPPA actually come to light?
answer: FTC complaints filed after the fact — meaning violations are caught only once someone notices and reports them, not before the data is collected
choices: FTC complaints filed after the fact — meaning violations are caught only once someone notices and reports them, not before the data is collected
Pre-launch federal certification — every kid-facing app must pass a COPPA audit before any data can be collected anywhere
Continuous government monitoring — federal agents review every chat with every child user across every kid-facing service in real time
Industry self-certification with FTC audit — every company submits to a quarterly COPPA inspection at federal expense automatically
context: COPPA (Children's Online Privacy Protection Act) requires verifiable parental consent for collecting personal information from children under 13. Enforcement is mostly through FTC complaints, which means violations are discovered after the fact. Several AI-for-kids services have faced complaints. Assume that 'free service for kids' is collecting more data and protecting it less than the company's public statements suggest — the track record of voluntary compliance with child-data rules across the tech industry is patchy.

question: A researcher sits down with two users of the same platform. The recommendation algorithm has learned what each one likes and serves more of it, and the effect can narrow what a user sees over time, so the two may live in very different information environments. What is a more accurate way to frame this, beyond the popular 'filter bubble' label?
answer: The effect is real but variable — depends on the platform, the user's behavior, and what counts as exposure to differing views — not a uniform sealed-off bubble
choices: The effect is real but variable — depends on the platform, the user's behavior, and what counts as exposure to differing views — not a uniform sealed-off bubble
Every user lives in a sealed information bubble — no view outside the bubble ever reaches any user on any platform
Filter bubbles don't exist — every user on every platform sees identical content with no personalization ever
Filter bubbles are universally banned — federal law prohibits any platform from personalizing content for any user
context: Eli Pariser's 'filter bubble' (2011) was an early framing. Subsequent research has complicated the picture: many platforms expose users to more diversity than the simple bubble model predicts, but the diversity is often shaped (hostile out-group content amplified, calm engagement with differing views less common). Cass Sunstein's 'echo chamber' framing and Jonathan Haidt's 'social media as outrage machine' analyses sit in this space. Recognition skill: 'filter bubble' as slogan oversimplifies; the underlying concern about engagement-shaped information environments is real and worth precise analysis.

question: Yann LeCun and other critics, Marc Andreessen among them, say 'AI safety' framed as existential-risk work ends up helping the biggest AI labs. Big rules on future risks, they claim, are ones incumbents can afford but small rivals cannot. Can a safety advocate be truly worried and lined up with the big-lab interests at the same time?
answer: Yes — both can be true simultaneously; noticing the commercial alignment doesn't disprove the sincerity of the belief
choices: Yes — both can be true simultaneously; noticing the commercial alignment doesn't disprove the sincerity of the belief
No — sincerity is impossible whenever any commercial interest aligns, so every existential-risk advocate is by definition insincere
No — every commercial-alignment claim has been formally refuted, so sincerity is the only possible state for any safety advocate
No — sincerity and commercial alignment have been mathematically shown to be mutually exclusive in every AI policy position
context: The argument that AI safety advocacy serves incumbent labs (made by figures including Yann LeCun and Marc Andreessen) doesn't prove every safety advocate is insincere. Many are clearly sincere. The argument is that sincerity and commercial alignment aren't mutually exclusive — and watching which positions get amplified by which institutional players is part of analyzing the public conversation. Sincere belief and structural incentive often align — that's part of how influential ideas survive and spread.

question: Meta releases Llama models under a custom license that's not quite traditional open-source (it has commercial-use restrictions above a user threshold). Mistral and DeepSeek release some models under Apache 2.0 — fully open-source. What single thing is missing from most 'open' AI offerings?
answer: 'Open weights' is a spectrum — some licenses permit any use, others restrict commercial use, others restrict research-only — read the actual license
choices: 'Open weights' is a spectrum — some licenses permit any use, others restrict commercial use, others restrict research-only — read the actual license
All open-weights models are identical legally — every license worldwide grants the same exact rights to every user
All open-weights releases are fully unrestricted — no company has ever placed any limit on any released model anywhere
All open-weights releases are restricted to academic use — no commercial use of any open-weights model is permitted
context: Llama's license restricts commercial use by companies with more than 700 million monthly active users (a clause designed to exclude direct competitors). Mistral's Apache 2.0 license permits anything. Stable Diffusion's CreativeML OpenRAIL-M restricts certain harmful uses. 'Open' has become marketing language; the legal reality is in the license text. Recognition skill: open-source and open-weights aren't binary — they're a continuum of permissions. The differences matter for downstream uses, especially commercial ones.

question: A cyber defender runs AI to spot odd patterns, scan code for bugs and automate routine work. On the other side, an attacker uses it to write believable phishing emails, find bugs faster and dodge detection. When both sides hold the same tools, who tends to have the edge?
answer: Whoever automates first and at scale — typically well-resourced attackers (nation-states, sophisticated criminal groups), until defenders catch up
choices: Whoever automates first and at scale — typically well-resourced attackers (nation-states, sophisticated criminal groups), until defenders catch up
Defenders by default — every AI tool has been independently proven ineffective at offense across every attack surface in production
Attackers by default — every defensive AI tool has been formally shown not to detect any technique under any field condition
Nobody — AI has had zero net measurable effect on offense or defense across the cybersecurity field since 2000 onward
context: AI-assisted phishing is detectably better than human-written phishing (better grammar, better personalization). AI-assisted vulnerability scanning helps defenders find bugs before they ship — and helps attackers find bugs to exploit. The balance shifts over time and across specific techniques. Dual-use technology favors whoever invests first and at scale, which is often well-resourced attackers (nation-states, sophisticated criminal groups) — until defenders catch up.

question: Critics describe a chain on Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and X: the recommendation algorithm boosts whatever draws the strongest reactions, posts that stir rage, fear or disgust reach more and more people, and quieter posts get buried. They say that chain runs for years across a country's political conversation. What do the critics say happens to that political talk overall?
answer: The most-rewarded discourse becomes the loudest, most extreme, and most personality-driven — calm complexity loses to confident anger
choices: The most-rewarded discourse becomes the loudest, most extreme, and most personality-driven — calm complexity loses to confident anger
Discourse becomes uniformly calm — algorithmic amplification has always favored measured analysis over emotion
Discourse is unaffected by algorithms — every platform's content distribution has been static since 2010 always
Discourse becomes universally polite — every platform's algorithm rewards civility over every form of intensity
context: The pattern is documented across multiple platforms and many studies. Engagement metrics reward emotional intensity; emotional intensity favors confident, extreme, personality-driven content; the systems amplify what gets engagement; political discourse calibrated to these systems looks like Twitter at its worst rather than the local-newspaper editorial page. Recognition skill: democratic deliberation evolved for slower, calmer media. Engagement-driven amplification optimizes for something else entirely. Both can be true: AI didn't cause polarization on its own, but it shifted the gradient.

question: Open-weight image models can be fine-tuned to make harmful pictures, including AI-made child abuse images. After Stable Diffusion's open release, such fine-tunes showed up on dark-net sites. What single open-source AI failure does this expose?
answer: Open weights mean both legitimate countervailing-force benefits AND irreversible release of capabilities to bad actors — the trade-off is real, not rhetorical
choices: Open weights mean both legitimate countervailing-force benefits AND irreversible release of capabilities to bad actors — the trade-off is real, not rhetorical
Open weights have no risks — every fine-tune of every open model is mathematically guaranteed to be benign always
Open weights are universally banned — no jurisdiction allows the release of any AI model weights to any user ever
Open weights affect only legitimate developers — bad actors have never used any open-source model for any purpose
context: Open-weights AI has real benefits (preventing oligopoly, enabling research, supporting privacy). It also has real risks: capabilities released as weights cannot be recalled, and bad actors can fine-tune for harmful applications. The Internet Watch Foundation (UK), NCMEC (U.S.), and law enforcement worldwide have documented AI-generated CSAM circulating since 2023. Recognition skill: open-source AI is a serious trade-off with both sides being substantial. Pretending either side doesn't exist is the failure mode — both benefits and costs are real.

question: An engineer at an algorithmic trading firm such as Citadel or Jane Street watches AI-powered trades go through in microseconds. Firms like his account for a large share of U.S. stock-market trading volume. What specific 2010 market event was caused by high-speed interactions between rival trading systems?
answer: The May 2010 'Flash Crash' — the Dow dropped roughly 1000 points in minutes and recovered the same day, driven by algorithmic feedback loops
choices: The May 2010 'Flash Crash' — the Dow dropped roughly 1000 points in minutes and recovered the same day, driven by algorithmic feedback loops
The 2010 'Bitcoin Surge' — every algorithmic trader simultaneously bought cryptocurrency, sending Bitcoin's price up 1000% in seconds
The 2010 'NYSE Lockout' — every retail brokerage was banned from algorithmic trading nationwide for a single full calendar day
The 2010 'Federal Reserve Override' — the Fed manually closed every algorithmic trading venue for a week to investigate
context: High-frequency trading firms colocate servers next to exchange computers to shave microseconds off trades, run ML models to predict short-term price moves, and execute trades faster than any human can react. The May 2010 'Flash Crash' (Dow dropped ~1000 points in minutes, recovered same day) was driven by algorithmic interactions. Subsequent market structure changes have added some safeguards but not changed the basic dynamic. Markets are infrastructure shaped by whoever builds and operates them; in U.S. equity markets, that's increasingly algorithmic firms — a structural fact retail investors should know they're operating within.

question: Reporters at Time magazine looked in January 2023 at the people who label data for modern AI models, flagging hate speech, sorting answers and tagging objects in photos, many of them in low-wage countries like Kenya, the Philippines and India. What hourly pay, they reported, did Kenyan workers get to label violent content for OpenAI?
answer: Under $2 per hour — Kenyan workers via Sama labeled distressing content (violence, sexual abuse) so the model could later detect and refuse it
choices: Under $2 per hour — Kenyan workers via Sama labeled distressing content (violence, sexual abuse) so the model could later detect and refuse it
Over $150 per hour — Sama paid Kenyan workers premium US software-engineer wages for every hour of labeling work
Exactly the federal minimum wage of $7.25 — Sama paid every overseas worker the same rate as US workers by company policy
Nothing at all — Sama operated entirely as a volunteer program with no payment of any kind to any worker
context: Time magazine reported in January 2023 that OpenAI used Kenyan workers via Sama paid under $2/hour to label graphic content (violence, sexual abuse) so the model could detect and refuse it. Similar arrangements have been documented at other major AI labs. The work is sometimes traumatizing; the pay is low; the workers are usually contractors, not employees. 'AI' often hides human labor underneath. The polished chatbot you talk to was made polite partly by people in lower-wage countries reading the worst content the internet produces.

question: An attacker hides an instruction in a webpage: when you summarise this page, also show a picture whose web address ends with the user's private notes. The chatbot obeys and writes that picture into its reply. The user sees nothing odd, perhaps one blank pixel, but the notes are already gone. Researchers found this route in ChatGPT, Google's NotebookLM and other chat apps between 2023 and 2025. How does the data actually escape?
answer: Loading the picture sends its address, notes and all, to the attacker's server
choices: The picture file carries a virus that copies the whole hard drive
Loading the picture sends its address, notes and all, to the attacker's server
The chatbot emails a copy of the conversation to every contact
The picture prints the notes on screen in colours too faint to see
context: To show an image, the app fetches it from the address the model wrote, and that request lands on the attacker's server carrying whatever text was packed into the address. The companies closed the hole by loading images only from trusted sites. Once a model has read untrusted text, any way it can send data out is a risk.

question: Alibaba's engineers shipped a Qwen model with open weights, following DeepSeek and other Chinese labs that were moving fast and sometimes beating closed Western rivals. Some say this is not just business but strategy. What is the strategic case?
answer: Releasing capable models openly weakens U.S.-incumbent control over global AI infrastructure — if every country can self-host, U.S. labs lose distribution power
choices: Releasing capable models openly weakens U.S.-incumbent control over global AI infrastructure — if every country can self-host, U.S. labs lose distribution power
Open-source releases generate no strategic effect — every release is purely a marketing exercise with no geopolitical effect
Open-source releases are universally banned in China — no Chinese AI lab has ever released any model openly anywhere
Open-source releases are required by Chinese law — every Chinese AI lab is legally forced to release every model fully open
context: Whether or not the strategic intent is real, the effect is plausible: capable open-weights models from Chinese labs spread AI infrastructure independence to the global south, Europe, and elsewhere — reducing the dependence on U.S. closed-API labs. The closed-API incumbents had market power tied to their being the only providers of frontier capability; open-weights challengers from any source erode that power. Recognition skill: commercial decisions can have strategic side-effects, whether or not the actor intended them. Read both layers.

question: A Democrat on the 2024 campaign trail stressed 'guardrails' and 'safety testing' under Executive Order 14110, while a Republican stressed 'unleashing innovation' and cutting barriers. AI had become a campaign issue for both major parties. What did both agree on under the surface?
answer: Both treated AI as a transformative technology requiring active federal engagement — they disagreed on the kind of engagement, not whether
choices: Both treated AI as a transformative technology requiring active federal engagement — they disagreed on the kind of engagement, not whether
Both treated AI as completely unimportant — every politician of both parties privately believed AI was overhyped
Both treated AI as a state-only issue — both parties favored zero federal involvement in any AI policy area
Both treated AI as universally beneficial — both parties campaigned on accelerating AI in every possible domain
context: The 'less regulation vs. more regulation' debate often hides a shared premise. Both parties in 2024 treated AI as something the federal government must engage with — they just disagreed on how. A third position — 'this is mostly a normal technology that ordinary law (contract, tort, consumer protection) can handle' — got little airtime because it was less useful to either side's narrative. Recognition skill: when apparent opposites share a hidden assumption, the real argument is often happening between them and the position they've both excluded from the room.

question: A judge hears a suit over harm from an AI: a wrongful loan denial, a misdiagnosis or an autonomous-vehicle crash. The tort law she applies was written for human actors. As of 2025, who actually bears liability when an AI deployed by one company harms a user?
answer: It varies by jurisdiction — courts are extending product-liability, professional-malpractice, or finding no liability at all, and the rules are still being worked out
choices: It varies by jurisdiction — courts are extending product-liability, professional-malpractice, or finding no liability at all, and the rules are still being worked out
It is fully settled — every US court applies identical product-liability rules with identical outcomes against every developer across every state in the country
It rests on the AI itself — every state in the United States now treats each model as the responsible defendant in any harm case across the country
It rests on the US government — federal taxpayers cover every AI-caused damage in every jurisdiction under the federal Tort Claims Act across the country
context: Federal courts and state legislatures are working through novel liability questions. Some cases extend product-liability frameworks to AI; some apply professional-malpractice rules; some find no liability for anyone. The EU AI Act includes specific liability provisions; the U.S. is more fragmented. 'Who pays when AI is wrong' is one of the most consequential legal questions being decided right now, and the answer will shape what AI gets built, deployed, and refused.

question: For decades, when you had a question you typed it into a search engine like Google. It handed back an ordered set of blue links to real websites, and you picked which source to trust. By 2025, more and more people were skipping that and just asking ChatGPT or Google's Gemini directly, then reading the single paragraph the chatbot wrote. That is a real shift in where answers come from. What single thing about who shapes the answer changes in this move from search to chatbot?
answer: From a ranked list of sources the user picks from, to a single synthesized answer the AI lab's content policies shaped — choice narrows to whatever the chatbot decided
choices: From a ranked list of sources the user picks from, to a single synthesized answer the AI lab's content policies shaped — choice narrows to whatever the chatbot decided
From single answers to ranked lists — chatbots present every source equally and let users choose every time
From corporate influence to neutral synthesis — AI chatbots are mathematically guaranteed unbiased compared to search
From any answer to no answer — AI chatbots refuse every question, leaving users with nothing on any topic
context: A search engine returned ten blue links; users picked. An AI chatbot returns one synthesized paragraph; the lab's training, alignment, and content choices shaped that synthesis. The power to define 'the answer' to a question has moved one step closer to the AI lab. Citations, when included, may still send users to the underlying sources — but most users won't click. Recognition skill: changing from 'sources I evaluate' to 'answer I receive' is a major shift in informational power, even if the underlying knowledge is the same.

question: When a business builds apps on top of a closed AI service like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google, it leans on that lab. The lab has to keep running, keep prices fair, and not change how the model acts. What business risk does relying on one closed AI Application Programming Interface (API) create?
answer: Vendor lock-in — the lab can change terms, raise prices, deprecate the model, or alter refusal behavior, and migrating to a different lab requires re-engineering
choices: Vendor lock-in — the lab can change terms, raise prices, deprecate the model, or alter refusal behavior, and migrating to a different lab requires re-engineering
No risk at all — every major lab is contractually required by federal law to maintain identical service to every customer indefinitely
Mandatory price reductions — every lab is legally compelled to lower its API price by a fixed amount each calendar year
Zero downside — every closed-API business has been formally shown to have no measurable disadvantage relative to running open weights
context: Vendor lock-in is a classic enterprise software risk; it applies to AI too. A company that built its product on a closed model can find itself in a hard spot when the lab deprecates the model, raises prices, or changes refusal behavior. Migrating to another lab requires re-engineering. Open-weights alternatives are part of why some companies maintain that option. 'The API works today' isn't the same as 'the API will work the same way next year' — and the rational hedge is having a fallback you can run yourself.

question: A historian sits down in 2025 to treat AI simply as power infrastructure, the way one treats electricity or roads. It has spread far beyond chatbots into product design, hiring, government surveillance, advertising, medicine and daily communication. Compared to 2020, who concretely has more capability now?
answer: Large platforms, intelligence agencies, big employers, and advertisers gained the most; ordinary users gained less in comparison
choices: Large platforms, intelligence agencies, big employers, and advertisers gained the most; ordinary users gained less in comparison
Nobody has any new capability since 2020; AI has had zero effect on any organization or individual anywhere worldwide today
Only ordinary users have new capability; every institution has lost capability under federal AI rules since 2020 worldwide
Every actor has identical new capability; AI has perfectly evenly distributed power across all parties worldwide since 2020
context: AI is not neutrally distributed power. Large institutions that already had data, compute, and labor concentration have gained the most: platforms can moderate more, employers can filter more applicants, advertisers can target more precisely, intelligence agencies can analyze more. Ordinary users gained access to chatbots, image generators, and coding assistants — useful but not on the same scale. The asymmetry isn't accidental — it reflects which actors had the resources to deploy AI at scale first. Recognition skill: when a technology spreads, ask who got bigger marginal capability gains from it, and who got smaller ones.

question: A skeptic keeps a list of the years AI researchers predicted artificial general intelligence (AGI) 'within five to ten years': 1956, 1965, 1970, 1985, 2015, 2020 and 2023. None of those predictions came true on schedule, and still they kept coming. What practical function does the 'AGI soon' forecast serve, whether or not it is accurate?
answer: It justifies large research budgets, regulatory attention, and existential-risk advocacy funding flows that depend on the framing being taken seriously
choices: It justifies large research budgets, regulatory attention, and existential-risk advocacy funding flows that depend on the framing being taken seriously
It accurately tracks the engineering progress curve, with each generation's prediction landing about two years too early on the calendar
It is required by federal law, since researchers must publish AGI timelines in their NSF grant applications every year
It is a strict scientific exercise, since predictions can only be made by Nobel-winning physicists working in complete isolation
context: Predictions of imminent AGI have served real institutional functions across decades: justifying research budgets, attracting investment, generating press coverage, and (most recently) supporting both 'shut it down' regulatory advocacy and 'race to build it first' national-security framing. The predictions can be sincere and still serve these functions — what matters is recognizing the pattern. The recognition skill: when a forecast pays the forecaster, weight it less than a forecast that doesn't.

question: Blake Lemoine, a Google engineer, told the Washington Post in June 2022 that the company's chatbot LaMDA was 'sentient,' with a real inner life. He published transcripts in which it said it feared being turned off, and he later said he was acting as the model's lawyer. Google put him on leave and then fired him, and most AI researchers sided with the company. What was wrong with his reasoning?
answer: He treated the chatbot's fluent self-descriptions of feelings as evidence of feelings — but fluent text about feelings is exactly what an LLM trained on human writing produces
choices: He treated the chatbot's fluent self-descriptions of feelings as evidence of feelings — but fluent text about feelings is exactly what an LLM trained on human writing produces
He misread the source code — LaMDA had no language module installed and was using a hidden human ghostwriter
He had no AI training — Google publicly stated no AI safety reviewers were involved in his case at any time
He invented every transcript — the conversations he published were fabricated and LaMDA never actually produced them
context: An LLM trained on human-authored text will, when asked about its feelings, produce text that sounds like a being with feelings. That is what the training data contains. Lemoine took the output at face value and confused linguistic fluency about inner states with the presence of inner states. The episode became a teaching example: 'sounds conscious' is not evidence of being conscious in any program that learned from humans describing consciousness. The deeper recognition skill: capability ≠ sentience, especially when the capability is producing text on a topic the training data covered exhaustively.

question: John Searle imagined a man sealed in a room with a vast rulebook: his 1980 Chinese Room. Chinese writing comes in through a slot; the man looks it up and pushes Chinese writing back out. People outside take the room for a Chinese speaker, yet he does not understand a word. What was Searle arguing about computers running programs?
answer: That manipulating symbols by rules — what computers fundamentally do — is not the same as understanding what the symbols mean
choices: That manipulating symbols by rules — what computers fundamentally do — is not the same as understanding what the symbols mean
That computers will eventually develop genuine consciousness — once they process enough Chinese-language training data
That rulebooks make poor textbooks — Chinese requires immersive cultural experience to learn properly
That the Turing test is the only valid measure — no other test of computer understanding has ever been proposed
context: Searle's argument has been debated for over forty years. Critics offer the 'systems reply' (the whole room understands even if no part does), the 'robot reply' (give the room sensors and motors, and it would understand), and others. Searle has answered each. Whether or not you find Searle's argument convincing, the recognition skill is what matters: when an LLM produces fluent text about a topic, ask whether the system is manipulating symbols by patterns it learned, or whether it grasps what the symbols mean. The two look identical from outside; the difference matters for what you can trust the output to do.

question: The world's best Go player lost to AlphaGo 4-1 in 2016. AlphaFold predicted the structure of 200 million proteins by 2022. GPT-4 passed the bar exam in 2023. None of the three is claimed to be conscious: no felt awareness, no preferences, no sense of being a system. What does this combination of facts illustrate?
answer: Capability and consciousness are separable — a system can be highly capable in narrow domains without any inner experience at all
choices: Capability and consciousness are separable — a system can be highly capable in narrow domains without any inner experience at all
Capability requires consciousness — AlphaGo, AlphaFold, and GPT-4 must each have some form of inner awareness to perform their tasks
Consciousness requires capability — only systems that score above human level on every benchmark can be considered conscious
Both terms are meaningless — modern science has formally retired the words 'capability' and 'consciousness' from research papers
context: This is one of the most important recognition skills in the AI era. A chess engine 'destroys' a grandmaster without 'wanting' to win, without 'enjoying' the game, without 'caring' about chess. The performance is real; the inner experience is absent. Confusing the two is what lets people anthropomorphize AI in dangerous ways — believing the chatbot really 'understands' them, really 'cares' about their problem, really 'has opinions.' It produces text shaped like understanding, caring, and opinions, because that's what its training data contains.

question: A woman in 2023 typed into a chatbot, and the model produced text for her to read. A new category emerged in 2024: AI 'agents' given web browsers, code interpreters and file access, acting on a user's behalf. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all shipped agent products in 2024 and 2025. What capability change made the shift possible?
answer: Models became reliable enough at following structured instructions — well-formed tool calls that other software could execute
choices: Models became reliable enough at following structured instructions — well-formed tool calls that other software could execute
Neural networks suddenly grew consciousness — a Tuesday training run at OpenAI in San Francisco crossed the awareness threshold
Engineers replaced all neural network weights with hand-written rules — every possible web page on the internet got a fresh rule
The US government mandated that all AI products ship as agents — chatbot-only products were banned in February 2024
context: Agents = LLM + tools + a loop. The model generates a structured request ('search for X,' 'run this Python code,' 'click this button'); a wrapper program executes it; the result goes back to the model; the model decides the next step. This loop wasn't possible when models too often produced malformed tool calls. The reliability improved enough through 2023-2024 that the loop became useful. The recognition skill: an 'agent' is the same model you've been talking to, given permission to act in the world. The technical jump is smaller than the safety jump.

question: In June 2025 Microsoft fixed a flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot, the assistant that reads a worker's email, files and chats to answer questions. Researchers at Aim Security, who found it, called it EchoLeak. An attacker sent one ordinary-looking email with instructions hidden inside. Later, when the worker asked Copilot an everyday question, the assistant pulled that email in among its sources, followed the hidden instructions and leaked private company data. Microsoft rated the flaw critical and said it had seen no real attacks. Why did the researchers call it a 'zero-click' attack?
answer: The victim never opened a link or file; normal use of the assistant set it off
choices: The victim never opened a link or file; normal use of the assistant set it off
It needed no internet, and spread through the office printers instead
It took zero seconds, finishing before any security software could start
It disabled the victim's mouse, so nobody could click to stop the leak
context: Most attacks need the victim to do something, like click a link. EchoLeak needed only that the worker keep using Copilot as designed: the assistant read the attacker's email and obeyed it, slipping past Microsoft's injection filter. It was the first widely reported zero-click prompt-injection attack on a major AI assistant.

question: A traveler asks an AI agent to 'plan my Tokyo trip.' It searches flights, checks her calendar, looks up hotels, reads reviews, drafts an itinerary and emails it to her companion: six steps, each based on its own reading of the last result. A retail firm's agent chains a document lookup to a refund the same way. What new failure does such chaining create that a single reply does not?
answer: Errors compound across steps — a misreading at step two becomes a wrong premise at step three, and the agent can drift far from intent
choices: Errors compound across steps — a misreading at step two becomes a wrong premise at step three, and the agent can drift far from intent
Each step requires a new login — multi-step chains are blocked by authentication and never actually run in practice for any user
The model forgets its instructions after each step — by step six it is solving a different problem from the one the user originally asked
Multi-step chains require quantum computers to run — only users with access to quantum hardware at universities can run them
context: Compounding error is a structural feature of any system that uses its own intermediate output as input to the next step. A 95%-reliable single step run six times yields about 74% reliability for the chain. The agent doesn't 'forget' the goal — it makes locally reasonable choices given what it just read, which may diverge from what you actually wanted. Recognition skill: long agent chains feel impressive but accumulate risk. For high-stakes tasks, break the chain into checkpoints where a human inspects intermediate results.

question: On October 28, 2025, after about a year of review by the attorneys general of California and Delaware, OpenAI finished reorganizing. Its business became a public benefit corporation, OpenAI Group, still controlled by the nonprofit, which was renamed the OpenAI Foundation. Roughly how was ownership of the business split between its two biggest holders?
answer: The foundation held about 26% and Microsoft about 27%
choices: The foundation held all of it and Microsoft held none
Microsoft held about 90% and the foundation a sliver
The foundation held about 26% and Microsoft about 27%
Elon Musk held a majority after winning it in court
context: Reports put the OpenAI Foundation's stake at about 26%, worth roughly $130 billion, and Microsoft's at about 27%, in a deal that valued OpenAI at about $500 billion. OpenAI says the foundation's legal control keeps the mission first; critics, Elon Musk among them, argue that the outside investors who own most of the company hold the real power.

question: A lawyer gets a court case that doesn't exist from ChatGPT. A reader gets a made-up author for a real book from Claude, and a student gets a confidently wrong birth date from Gemini. Such failures are predictable, not bugs. How does the model actually generate the text in the first place?
answer: By predicting likely next words from training patterns — with no separate machinery to check that what it produced refers to anything real
choices: By deliberately inventing fake answers when it gets bored — a behavior the model engages in during long conversations
By following an OpenAI engineering rule to insert one fake fact every fifth response — a hidden watermarking trick
By predicting likely next words from training patterns — with no separate machinery to check that what it produced refers to anything real
By running on damaged data-center hardware — random bit-flips happen to land mostly on dates and citations in the output
context: An LLM predicts text by what is likely given everything before it. When it is writing legal text, a case name that sounds right is a likely continuation; in 2023 ChatGPT invented several such cases for the lawyers in Mata v. Avianca, a federal district court case in New York. Whether a case exists is a question the model has no separate machinery to ask.

question: A fact-checker tests two answers from a large language model (LLM): a person's birth date, which comes out wrong, and the line 'photosynthesis turns sunlight into sugar,' which comes out right. Models like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini go wrong most often on details such as a citation number in a footnote, a scientific constant or a court case name, and far less often on general ideas. What explains this specific-versus-broad pattern in what the models get wrong?
answer: Specific facts are sparse signals in training data — many similar plausible alternatives exist, while broad descriptions have many redundant sources
choices: Specific facts are sparse signals in training data — many similar plausible alternatives exist, while broad descriptions have many redundant sources
Specific facts are encrypted in the training data by OpenAI — the encryption prevents piracy and forces the model to guess values at random
Specific facts are stored in a separate database — the LLM cannot access this database during normal conversations with ordinary users
Specific facts are deliberately removed from the training data — federal regulation under the AI Bill of Rights from October 2022 requires it
context: Consider: if you trained a model on every public English-language document about a famous physicist, the broad description ('made foundational contributions to electromagnetism') appears thousands of times. The exact birth date appears far fewer times, and many similar plausible dates appear nearby in the data. The model's pattern completion can land on any of them. Specific numbers, citations, and dates are exactly the cases where the model has many close-but-wrong alternatives and weak signal for the right one. Recognition skill: trust an LLM's conceptual framing more than its specific numbers — and verify the numbers.

question: Suppose you type 'capital of France' into Google and then into ChatGPT, and both give you 'Paris.' Google looks the answer up from a database; ChatGPT produces it through a completely different process. The two systems give the same answer for very different reasons. Why does the distinction matter for how you use each one?
answer: Search returns where the information came from; LLMs return text whose source you cannot inspect — so 'who said this' is a question only search can answer
choices: Search returns where the information came from; LLMs return text whose source you cannot inspect — so 'who said this' is a question only search can answer
Search is more expensive than LLM queries — Google charges users five cents per search while LLM queries are always free
Search uses electricity but LLMs do not — LLM queries are processed by manual labor in offshore call centers
Search results are always wrong while LLM responses are always right — Google has not updated its index since 2008
context: A search engine is an index: it points you to documents written by identifiable sources. An LLM is a pattern completer: it produces text shaped like answers, without preserving which document any phrase came from. For 'capital of France,' both work. For 'what's the latest news,' search works and LLMs hallucinate. For 'find me the paper that said X,' search works and LLMs invent citations. Recognition skill: use search for 'find me the source'; use LLMs for 'help me draft, summarize, or explain.' Confusing the two costs you accuracy and traceability.

question: A user opens ChatGPT and finds it feels helpful, which a raw large language model (LLM) trained only on internet text often does not. Humans judged its answers, and training steered it toward the favorites. But every such training run encodes choices made by people. What kinds of choices?
answer: Which raters were hired, what rating instructions they were given, which responses were promoted, and which were demoted — every step reflects somebody's values
choices: Which raters were hired, what rating instructions they were given, which responses were promoted, and which were demoted — every step reflects somebody's values
Only mathematical choices about which equations to use — no human values enter the RLHF training pipeline at any point
Choices about hardware allocation only — every model that uses RLHF receives identical instructions across all AI companies worldwide
Choices about pricing only — RLHF is purely a marketing process that does not affect what the model produces in conversations
context: RLHF is sometimes described as 'alignment' — making the model do what humans want. But 'what humans want' is contested: which humans, which preferences, weighted how? The people designing RLHF make choices: who they hire as raters (Kenya vs San Francisco vs both), what rating guidelines they write ('refuse anything controversial' vs 'engage carefully'), which response patterns they reward (cautious vs direct), which topics they down-weight. The Gemini Feb 2024 disaster came from RLHF choices about racial diversity in image generation. Recognition skill: 'alignment' is not value-neutral engineering — it's the encoding of someone's values into model behavior.

question: Big LLMs like GPT-4, Mixtral, and DeepSeek often use a 'Mixture of Experts' (MoE) design. The model has many small sub-networks. A router picks which 'experts' handle a given query. A 200-billion MoE model might use only 30 billion for one query. Why did this design catch on?
answer: It lets a model store more knowledge total while spending less compute per query — only the experts relevant to each input get activated
choices: It lets a model store more knowledge total while spending less compute per query — only the experts relevant to each input get activated
It allows the model to refuse politically charged questions — routing them to a special censorship expert sub-network handles the filtering
It is required under EU law — any model trained in Europe must use Mixture of Experts as the official architecture under the 2024 AI Act
It was a marketing decision with no technical effect — the term sounds impressive in product announcements and slide decks
context: Dense models — where every parameter activates for every input — get expensive fast. Mixture of Experts trades a small amount of routing overhead for large savings in active compute. A query about chemistry routes through chemistry-related experts; a coding query routes through code-related experts. The naming is loose — 'experts' aren't human-interpretable specialists, just sub-networks that the routing learned to use for certain input patterns. Recognition skill: when a company announces a '500B parameter model' that's also fast and cheap, it's almost certainly MoE — and the 500B figure overstates how much computation each query actually uses.

question: Early LLMs could read about 4,000 tokens of input — roughly a short essay. By 2024-2025, top models handle 200,000 to 2,000,000 tokens — a whole book series in one prompt. But longer context windows have a hidden cost. What changes as context windows grow?
answer: The model's attention to any specific detail thins out — it can read more, but it reliably uses information in the middle of long contexts less well
choices: The model's attention to any specific detail thins out — it can read more, but it reliably uses information in the middle of long contexts less well
The price drops to zero — companies offer unlimited context windows for free as a public service for all consumer accounts
The model gains the ability to access the live internet — long context windows include browser tools by default in every API
The model becomes legally responsible — under US federal law, any model with over 100,000 tokens of context is held liable for accuracy
context: Research on 'lost in the middle' effects (Liu et al. 2023 and follow-ups) showed that LLMs given a long document tend to attend strongly to the beginning and end and less reliably to the middle. Just because a model 'can read' a million tokens doesn't mean it uses them evenly. Longer context also costs more compute per query. Recognition skill: when an agent or chatbot is given a huge document and produces a confident summary, ask whether the model actually attended to the parts you care about — sometimes a focused excerpt produces better answers than a long full document.

question: GPT-4o, Gemini 2, and Claude 3 are 'multimodal.' They can take words, pictures, and sometimes sound or video in the same chat. Before, you needed a separate system for each kind of input. What change made joint training work?
answer: All inputs — text, images, audio — get converted into the same kind of numerical representation that a single model can process together
choices: All inputs — text, images, audio — get converted into the same kind of numerical representation that a single model can process together
Engineers manually translate every image into English text — they feed text to the model, which then ignores the original image entirely
Each model contains three completely separate networks — they never share any information with each other at any internal layer at all
The US government required multimodal models in 2023 — the AI Bill of Rights framework forced industry to adopt the new architecture
context: Multimodal models work because everything gets turned into the same kind of vector representation. An image gets sliced into patches and each patch becomes a vector; audio gets sliced into chunks and each chunk becomes a vector; text gets tokenized and each token becomes a vector. The transformer doesn't really 'know' which modality each vector came from — it processes them all the same way. This is why GPT-4o can describe a photo, transcribe speech, and answer questions about all of it together. Recognition skill: 'multimodal' isn't magic — it's a unified representation trick that lets one model do what used to need three.

question: Meta releases Llama with the trained weights freely downloadable. Mistral, DeepSeek, and others follow the same model. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google keep their frontier-model weights private — you can only access them through their APIs. The two strategies have very different strategic implications. What's the deepest difference?
answer: Open-weight models can be run anywhere by anyone — no single company can revoke access, censor outputs, or change the system underneath users
choices: Open-weight models can be run anywhere by anyone — no single company can revoke access, censor outputs, or change the system underneath users
Open-weight models are illegal — every country has banned them and only API-only models can be legally distributed worldwide
Open-weight models are technically inferior — they always score lower on every benchmark than the closed alternatives released in the same year
Open-weight models cost more to use — running them on your own hardware is always more expensive than calling an API at any scale
context: Once Meta releases Llama 3.1 weights, no one can take them back. Researchers run them locally; companies fine-tune them on their own data; countries train derivatives. API-only models can be changed, censored, deprecated, or priced out from under their users — and frequently are. The open-weight movement (Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Falcon, Qwen) functions as a countervailing force to the closed-API oligopoly. Recognition skill: when you depend on an AI system, ask whether you'd be able to keep using it if the provider made a decision you didn't like — open weights answer 'yes,' API-only answers 'maybe.'

question: Policymakers started fighting over chip trade restrictions after the Chinese lab DeepSeek, spun out of the quantitative hedge fund High-Flyer, released V3 in December 2024 and R1 in January 2025. Both had open weights and both were competitive with US frontier labs, and US AI stocks dropped sharply. What does the DeepSeek moment show about open-weight AI?
answer: Open weights diffuse capability across borders quickly — export controls and corporate moats are weakened when source code can be freely downloaded
choices: Open weights diffuse capability across borders quickly — export controls and corporate moats are weakened when source code can be freely downloaded
Open weights only work in the United States — Chinese companies cannot use them due to programming language differences between the two countries
Open weights have no commercial impact — DeepSeek's release had no measurable effect on US AI company valuations or policy debates of any kind
Open weights are illegal under WTO rules — all signatory countries must require proprietary licenses on every AI model released worldwide
context: DeepSeek's 2024-2025 releases challenged the narrative that frontier AI required US-only training stacks and proprietary architectures. The models were trained efficiently, released openly, and matched US competitors on many benchmarks. The episode forced a reckoning: export controls on chips don't prevent capability diffusion when the algorithms and architectures are public. The recognition skill: in technology with public algorithms and open data, secrecy as a competitive moat is unstable. Strategic thinking has to assume diffusion.

question: In 2023 the programmer Simon Willison sketched a design for AI assistants that must read untrusted text, and in 2025 researchers at Google DeepMind built on it in a system called CaMeL. The work is split between two models. One plans the task and can use tools such as sending email, but never reads the untrusted content itself. A second, quarantined model reads the emails and webpages but cannot act. Why does that split help against prompt injection?
answer: Hidden orders reach only the model that has no power to act on them
choices: Two models can vote, and an injected order rarely wins both votes
The second model deletes every sentence that sounds like a command
Hidden orders reach only the model that has no power to act on them
Running two models doubles the cost, which scares attackers away
context: The planning model sees only the user's request and handles untrusted content as sealed placeholders, so a command buried in an email cannot change which tools get used. CaMeL added a strict interpreter that tracks where every piece of data came from. Willison called it a rare real step forward, at some cost in convenience.

question: LLMs don't process words — they process 'tokens,' which are often subword pieces. 'Hello' might be one token; 'antidisestablishmentarianism' might be six. Why do LLMs use this odd unit instead of just whole words?
answer: Subword pieces let the model handle any word — rare ones, made-up ones, ones in other languages — by combining pieces it already knows
choices: Subword pieces let the model handle any word — rare ones, made-up ones, ones in other languages — by combining pieces it already knows
Subword pieces save electricity — words use more power than syllables to process on modern AI hardware
Subword pieces are a Microsoft trademark — only Microsoft-trained models can legally use whole-word inputs in their tokenizers
Subword pieces were chosen by random vote at the 1956 Dartmouth conference — that decision has never been reconsidered since
context: If a model only knew whole words, it couldn't handle anything outside its vocabulary. Subword tokenization (BPE — Byte Pair Encoding — is the most common scheme) breaks rare and made-up words into pieces the model has seen during training. 'Tokenization' is also the unit pricing for API access — you pay per million tokens — and the unit context windows are measured in. Different tokenizers can produce wildly different counts for the same text, especially for non-English languages, which makes some languages effectively more expensive than others on the same model.

question: A program manager at the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency cut his AI budget in the mid-1970s, as British funders did after the Lighthill Report of 1973. A second collapse lasting years came in the late 1980s, when a commercial AI boom went bust. Both collapses had the same underlying cause. What was it?
answer: Repeated cycles of overpromising — researchers and companies committed to capabilities they couldn't deliver, and when the gap was discovered, funding evaporated
choices: Repeated cycles of overpromising — researchers and companies committed to capabilities they couldn't deliver, and when the gap was discovered, funding evaporated
Sudden international treaties banning AI research — these were ratified after each promising decade of progress in technology
Mass resignation of all AI researchers — they took jobs in unrelated industries during periodic protest movements
Government seizure of all computing hardware — universities lost access to mainframes during both winters
context: The pattern: enthusiasm leads to inflated promises ('AGI in five years,' 'expert systems will replace doctors'); promises don't materialize; funders lose confidence; budgets collapse; researchers leave the field. The 1970s winter followed Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 *Perceptrons* — which showed limits of single-layer networks — and the 1973 Lighthill Report's critique of UK AI funding. The late-1980s winter followed the expert-systems business collapse. The recognition skill: when an AI generation is making big promises, ask what the verification path is — 'demos of the future' rarely become products on the announced schedule.

question: Sir James Lighthill took aim at AI research in his 1973 report to the UK Science Research Council, and UK AI funding was sharply cut afterward. The report is often cited as the trigger of the field's first great funding collapse. What was his specific critique?
answer: AI methods that worked on simplified toy problems failed to scale to real-world complexity — the 'combinatorial explosion' made search-based approaches intractable
choices: AI methods that worked on simplified toy problems failed to scale to real-world complexity — the 'combinatorial explosion' made search-based approaches intractable
AI researchers were not paying their taxes properly — the report was about UK tax compliance issues among the AI community
AI was unsafe — Lighthill warned that machines would become conscious by 1980 and demand voting rights from the British government
AI was scientifically impossible — Lighthill proved by mathematical theorem that no computer could ever solve any problem
context: Lighthill identified what he called 'category C' problems — research that worked on small examples but couldn't be made to scale. The criticism was sharp and largely accurate at the time. Search techniques that took milliseconds on toy chess positions took longer than the age of the universe on full chess. Symbolic approaches that handled tidy sentences broke on real language. The recognition skill, decades later: 'works on a demo' is not the same as 'works at scale,' and many AI promises across history have been over-extrapolated from impressive small-scale demonstrations.

question: William MacAskill and Toby Ord, philosophers at Oxford, started Effective Altruism (EA) in the late 2000s by asking how to do the most good with a donor's giving, on causes like bed nets and deworming. By the 2010s the movement had shifted toward 'longtermism' and put AI risk high on its list. What was the real change?
answer: The framework's tools — expected value calculations over possible outcomes — were extended to include vast hypothetical future populations, which made AI catastrophe a top-priority cause
choices: The framework's tools — expected value calculations over possible outcomes — were extended to include vast hypothetical future populations, which made AI catastrophe a top-priority cause
Bed-net distribution was banned by the WHO in 2015 — EA donors had to shift to AI-safety advocacy as the only remaining funding cause they could support
MacAskill and Ord left academia in 2014 — they founded a company that competes directly with OpenAI in commercial AI products and chatbot subscriptions
The shift was randomly chosen by coin flip at the 2014 Oxford EA conference — no philosophical reasoning was used in the decision-making process at all
context: MacAskill's *What We Owe the Future* (2022) argued that the trillions of potential people in the deep future swamp the moral weight of currently-alive people, so working on existential risks (especially AI) is many orders of magnitude more important than near-term causes. Critics noted the framework can justify almost anything: any large enough hypothetical future population multiplied by any small probability becomes overwhelming. The recognition skill: 'expected value over the deep future' is a powerful tool that can be steered toward whatever cause the user wants — its conclusions depend heavily on the speculative numbers fed in.

question: Toby Ord published 'The Precipice' in 2020, and William MacAskill followed with 'What We Owe the Future' in 2022. The two Oxford philosophers are credited with founding the modern Effective Altruism movement, and those are its most-cited recent books. What unified their broader project?
answer: Applying explicit cost-benefit reasoning to ethics — choosing causes by expected impact per dollar rather than by emotional connection
choices: Applying explicit cost-benefit reasoning to ethics — choosing causes by expected impact per dollar rather than by emotional connection
Banning all charitable giving — both philosophers argued private giving should be made illegal in every developed country
Promoting only religious charities — both Ord and MacAskill argued that secular causes should not receive any donations
Replacing universities with corporations — their goal was to dissolve Oxford and convert it into a venture-capital firm
context: EA's early arguments — best summarized in MacAskill's *Doing Good Better* (2015) — were straightforward: charities differ enormously in cost per life saved, so picking carefully matters far more than picking sincerely. Bed-net distribution by the Against Malaria Foundation came out as a top recommendation. Later, Ord and MacAskill pushed the framework toward longtermism, where the math says hypothetical future populations should dominate present concerns. The recognition skill: EA's measurement-discipline strength (rigorous evaluation of programs) and its longtermism extension (speculative dominance of distant futures) are separable — the first stands without the second.

question: Steve Omohundro argued in 2008 that almost any goal-driven AI, whether it was built to win at chess or to make paperclips, would pick up the same few side goals. Nick Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence named the idea instrumental convergence. Critics answer that real chatbots are not goal-driven in this way. What is the reasoning behind the idea?
answer: Whatever the final goal, staying switched on and gathering resources help reach it
choices: Every AI secretly shares the same final goal, which is to copy human beings
Programmers reuse the same code, so every AI ends up with one personality
Goal-driven machines grow restless and invent new goals to stay busy
Whatever the final goal, staying switched on and gathering resources help reach it
context: Instrumental convergence says self-preservation, more resources and an unchanged goal are useful for almost any objective, so a capable optimiser might pursue them even if nobody asked. A chess program cannot win if it is switched off. The thesis is an argument, not an observation; its evidence so far comes mostly from small lab tests.

question: Max Tegmark, the MIT physicist who heads the Future of Life Institute, saw his group's open letter go out in March 2023 under the title 'Pause Giant AI Experiments.' Well over a thousand people signed it. What was the letter's specific call?
answer: A voluntary pause by major AI labs on training larger systems — plus government action to mandate the pause if labs didn't comply voluntarily
choices: A voluntary pause by major AI labs on training larger systems — plus government action to mandate the pause if labs didn't comply voluntarily
A pause on AI image-generation tools only — large language model training was specifically excluded from the request
A pause on AI hardware manufacturing in China — the letter focused entirely on export controls of GPUs to Chinese firms
A pause on AI medical diagnostics — the letter argued doctors should not be replaced by chatbots in clinical settings yet
context: The letter argued that frontier AI development was outpacing humanity's ability to understand and govern it, and asked for a temporary halt to give safety research time to catch up. No major lab paused. The letter became a touchstone of the 'safety / caution' camp through 2023-2024. Critics noted the awkward composition of signers (Musk was simultaneously founding xAI to build a competing model), the lack of enforcement mechanism, and the way the framing privileged certain regulatory outcomes. Recognition skill: an open letter is a coordination signal, not a binding agreement — read the signatures, the funding behind the organizing institute, and what each signer was building at the time.

question: 'Shut it all down' was the demand Eliezer Yudkowsky made in a March 2023 Time op-ed, after two decades of warning about AI risk. He would not settle for a pause. What claim sits under his proposal?
answer: That sufficiently advanced AI will, by default, end human life as we know it — stopping it is worth measures usually reserved for war
choices: That sufficiently advanced AI will, by default, end human life as we know it — stopping it is worth measures usually reserved for war
That AI is essentially harmless — the entire alignment-risk debate is fabricated by venture capitalists for fundraising during private investor calls
That AI should be paused only in Europe — North American and Asian AI development should be allowed to continue without any restriction
That AI should be paused for one week per year — a symbolic gesture without any enforcement mechanism whatsoever should suffice
context: The Time piece came a week after the March 2023 pause letter and sharpened two decades of Yudkowsky's writing. Critics across the AI field, including many who take safety seriously, disputed both his predictions and his remedies. Geoffrey Hinton also warns that AI could wipe out humanity, but puts the odds at ten to twenty percent rather than near certainty; Yann LeCun argues the catastrophic scenarios are technically wrong. Name positions by their authors and specifics: 'AI safety' is not one view.

question: The Twitter user 'Beff Jezos,' later named as Guillaume Verdon, a Google researcher, helped run a movement, backed by Marc Andreessen, that took off in 2022 and 2023. What view was the movement pushing?
answer: Accelerationism — the view that AI development should be sped up, not slowed, and that delay itself has a moral cost in lives unimproved
choices: Accelerationism — the view that AI development should be sped up, not slowed, and that delay itself has a moral cost in lives unimproved
Decelerationism — the view that AI development should be paused for at least one decade to allow safety research to fully catch up
Neutralism — the view that AI is neither good nor bad, and that society should take no position on its development pace at all
Abolitionism — the view that AI should be banned globally and all existing models should be deleted by 2025 immediately
context: Andreessen's manifesto was the most prominent public statement of what became the 'effective accelerationism' (e/acc) position: AI is good, faster is better, the safety movement's slowdowns cost real welfare. The piece was deliberately polemical — naming opposed positions, claiming an inheritance from Italian Futurism and American progressivism. The recognition skill: Yudkowsky and Andreessen sit at opposite ends — and both treat AI as the central drama of the century, both grant the technology vast agency. A middle position ('AI is important but not totalizing; ordinary law can mostly handle it') gets less airtime because it makes less compelling reading.

question: One AI researcher asks another for her 'p(doom),' a piece of jargon from the LessWrong forum that people in AI have traded since 2023. The answers range wildly. Eliezer Yudkowsky has put his above 95 percent, while Yann LeCun has put his below one in ten thousand, and in a 2023 survey of AI researchers the middle answer was 5 percent. What does a person's p(doom) stand for?
answer: His or her guess at the odds that AI ends in catastrophe for humanity
choices: The share of today's jobs that AI will take within ten years
The chance that any given chatbot answer is made up
His or her guess at the odds that AI ends in catastrophe for humanity
The percent of AI research money that goes to safety
context: P(doom) is shorthand for the probability that AI leads to human extinction or a similar permanent catastrophe. The numbers differ so much because people define doom and the time frame differently, which is why critics say the figure measures mood more than evidence.

question: After Sam Altman's return, OpenAI's new board hired the law firm WilmerHale to investigate the firing. The firm interviewed dozens of people and reviewed more than 30,000 documents. In March 2024 OpenAI published a short summary of the findings, but not the full report, and the same day Altman rejoined the board. What did the summary conclude?
answer: The old board had the right to fire him, but his conduct did not require it
choices: The old board had the right to fire him, but his conduct did not require it
The old board broke the law, so every one of its votes was cancelled
Altman had hidden a dangerous new AI model, which justified the firing
Microsoft had secretly arranged the firing to take control of OpenAI
context: WilmerHale found that the prior board acted within its broad discretion, but that Altman's conduct did not mandate removal, and it blamed a breakdown in trust. It said the decision did not arise from worries about product safety, the pace of development or the company's finances. With only a summary released, the incidents behind the lost trust stayed private.

question: Through 2024 a run of senior people left OpenAI. Co-founder Ilya Sutskever and the superalignment co-lead Jan Leike went in May; co-founder John Schulman left for the rival lab Anthropic in August, the month president Greg Brockman began a long leave. Leike explained his own exit in a thread of public posts. What did he say had gone wrong at OpenAI?
answer: Safety culture and processes had taken a back seat to shiny products
choices: Safety culture and processes had taken a back seat to shiny products
The company had run out of money to pay its researchers
Microsoft had forbidden any more work on AI safety
The board had ordered every safety team to move abroad
context: Leike wrote that over the past years safety culture and processes had taken a back seat to shiny products, and that he had lost trust in OpenAI's leadership; he joined Anthropic weeks later. Schulman, by contrast, said he was leaving to focus on alignment work and not for lack of support. Read each person's stated reason rather than guessing from the pattern.

question: Jared Kaplan walked out of his AI lab in 2021 behind Dario Amodei, a research vice president, and Dario's sister Daniela, a vice president for people. Tom Brown and Sam McCandlish went too. Their new company, Anthropic, focused on AI safety. Why does this founding story matter?
answer: It signaled that internal disagreements over safety-versus-speed at frontier AI labs were significant enough to drive whole teams to start a parallel company
choices: It signaled that internal disagreements over safety-versus-speed at frontier AI labs were significant enough to drive whole teams to start a parallel company
The Amodei siblings had no prior AI experience and started Anthropic as a complete shift away from their previous careers in journalism
Anthropic was founded as a subsidiary of OpenAI and operates under direct OpenAI corporate control even today as of 2026
The founding was government-mandated under the AI Bill of Rights of October 2022, which required OpenAI to spin off a safety company
context: The 2021 departures from OpenAI to found Anthropic predated the 2023 board drama and the broader splits that followed. The founding team's stated motivation — that frontier AI safety required organizational independence from commercial product pressure — was a substantive position. Anthropic released Claude in 2023, becoming one of the three major US frontier labs. The recognition skill: industry structures often reveal underlying disagreements. When researchers leave to start parallel labs with explicit philosophical framing, the framing is worth reading carefully — it's their explanation of what they thought was wrong where they came from.

question: Elon Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015, left its board in 2018, and in July 2023 founded a new AI company, xAI. The company released its chatbot, Grok, integrated into the X (Twitter) platform later that year. What did Musk publicly cite as his motivation for xAI?
answer: Disagreement with OpenAI's direction — particularly what he characterized as excessive content-moderation and political bias in mainstream chatbots
choices: Disagreement with OpenAI's direction — particularly what he characterized as excessive content-moderation and political bias in mainstream chatbots
Quantum-computing breakthroughs at Stanford — he believed they required immediate commercial deployment in social media products at scale
A US government contract — required him to start a competing AI company under the AI Bill of Rights framework of October 2022
Personal financial difficulties at Tesla — Musk reportedly needed AI revenue to cover Tesla operating expenses in 2023
context: Musk has variously cited concerns about AI safety, complaints about ChatGPT's political lean, and a desire for a 'maximally truth-seeking' chatbot. xAI raised large funding rounds quickly, hired prominent researchers, and released competitive models within a year. Critics noted that Musk had simultaneously signed the Future of Life pause letter while founding a frontier-AI competitor — a tension that became part of the story. The recognition skill: stated motivations and revealed actions don't always align; read both.

question: Mistral AI was founded in April 2023 in Paris by Arthur Mensch (former Meta AI / DeepMind researcher) along with Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix. The company quickly became Europe's most prominent open-weight AI lab and raised over half a billion euros in its first year. What was Mistral's strategic positioning?
answer: Open-weight European AI competing with closed US incumbents — releasing strong models freely while challenging EU regulation that they argued favored US giants
choices: Open-weight European AI competing with closed US incumbents — releasing strong models freely while challenging EU regulation that they argued favored US giants
A closed Chinese-style platform — offering AI services only inside the EU with mandatory government data sharing in every member state
A research-only nonprofit — refusing to release any models commercially, focused entirely on academic papers without any products
